title: API Overview
description: Base address, versioning and the shape of every response.
content: api overview the server you run is the api. there is no central endpoint to call: every request goes to your own machine, and the data never leaves it. the base address your server answers on its own domain, issued when you registered it. the address is shown in the dashboard under server. it resolves to your machine, and the certificate is issued for it, so an ordinary https client works with no special handling. the port is the one your server was configured with. it is the same port the apps use. versioning the version is part of the path. everything documented here is version 1. a few routes sit outside the versioned tree because they are not part of the media api: for liveness, for the local control surface, and for artwork. the shape of a response a successful response is json. anything returning a list wraps it in . screens that the apps render are described rather than sent as raw rows. those endpoints return a list of components, each with its own props, and the client draws them. the home screen and library screens work this way, which is why one server change reaches web, phone and tv at once. what you need before calling anything two things: a token, and a user account on that server. a token alone is not enough. the server checks that the account behind the token exists on that server, so a token minted for a different nomercy server is rejected. see authentication. reading the reference every endpoint page lists the method, the path after , and the permission the endpoint requires. four permissions appear: | permission | held by | |------------|---------| | | any user allowed to use the server | | | a user allowed to drive the disc drive | | | a user who can manage the server | | | the one account that owns the server | the owner satisfies all four. see users for what each switch grants. where to go next - authentication - pagination - errors

title: Home
description: The home screen, its rows, and the trailer endpoints.
content: home the home screen is described by the server. it returns a list of components with their content, and the client draws them in its own idiom. that is why the phone, the web app and the tv agree without three implementations. the screen | method | path | needs | |--------|------|-------| | get | | mediaaccess | | get | | mediaaccess | | get | | mediaaccess | is the same screen shaped for a ten-foot display. filling a row | method | path | needs | |--------|------|-------| | post | | mediaaccess | | post | | mediaaccess | the screen describes its rows; these fill them. returns what the user was watching, so it changes as they watch. trailers | method | path | needs | |--------|------|-------| | head | | mediaaccess | | get | | mediaaccess | | delete | | mediaaccess | asks whether the server has the trailer ready, and prepares it if not. plays it. drops the copy the server made. where to go next - libraries - user data

title: Libraries
description: What a signed-in user can see, and how a library is listed for each surface.
content: libraries these endpoints answer what the calling user may see. they return only libraries that user has access to, which is why two accounts on one server can get different lists. administering libraries is a separate surface: see libraries admin. listing | method | path | needs | |--------|------|-------| | get | | mediaaccess | | get | | mediaaccess | | get | | mediaaccess | and return the same libraries shaped for those screens. they describe rows and cards for the client to draw, rather than raw records, which is how one server change reaches every client at once. one library | method | path | needs | |--------|------|-------| | get | | mediaaccess | | get | | mediaaccess | the letter form returns the titles starting with that letter. titles that do not start with a letter are grouped under . this is how the apps page a large library, rather than by number. import failures | method | path | needs | |--------|------|-------| | get | | mediaaccess | media that failed to import after the server had retried. pass to see only the ones still outstanding. where to go next - libraries admin - home - libraries for the concepts behind them.

title: Movies
description: Read one film, change how it is held, or ask the server to look at it again.
content: movies everything about a single film hangs off its id. the id is the film's themoviedb id, so the same number identifies it everywhere in the system. reading | method | path | needs | |--------|------|-------| | get | | mediaaccess | | get | | mediaaccess | | get | | mediaaccess | answers whether the server actually holds a playable file. returns what a player needs to start. user actions | method | path | needs | |--------|------|-------| | post | | mediaaccess | | post | | mediaaccess | both act for the calling user, not for the server. managing | method | path | needs | |--------|------|-------| | post | | moderator | | post | | moderator | | post | | moderator | | delete | | moderator | takes an optional and puts the film in that library. fetches the details and artwork again. looks at the files on disk again. a wrong title is usually a refresh; a file the server has not noticed is a rescan. where to go next - tv shows - libraries - metadata for how matching works.

title: TV Shows
description: Read a series, act on it as a user, or ask the server to look again.
content: tv shows a series is addressed by its themoviedb series id. seasons and episodes are returned inside the series rather than addressed on their own. reading | method | path | needs | |--------|------|-------| | get | | mediaaccess | | get | | mediaaccess | | get | | mediaaccess | | get | | mediaaccess | lists episodes the series is known to have and the server does not hold. it is the quickest way to see a gap in a season. user actions | method | path | needs | |--------|------|-------| | post | | mediaaccess | | post | | mediaaccess | managing | method | path | needs | |--------|------|-------| | post | | moderator | | post | | moderator | | post | | moderator | | delete | | moderator | and both take an optional . anime lives here too. an anime series is a series with an anime library behind it, so it uses these same endpoints. where to go next - movies - libraries - specials

title: Collections
description: Film series held together as one entry.
content: collections a collection is a film series that themoviedb groups, such as a trilogy. it behaves like a film: same actions, same ids, one level up. reading | method | path | needs | |--------|------|-------| | get | | mediaaccess | | get | | mediaaccess | | get | | mediaaccess | | get | | mediaaccess | the listing takes and . see pagination. user actions | method | path | needs | |--------|------|-------| | post | | mediaaccess | | post | | mediaaccess | managing | method | path | needs | |--------|------|-------| | post | | moderator | | post | | moderator | | post | | moderator | | delete | | moderator | adding a collection brings in the films it contains, so it saves adding each one. where to go next - movies - specials

title: People
description: Cast and crew, and what they appear in.
content: people people are the cast and crew of what your server holds. the id is the themoviedb person id. | method | path | needs | |--------|------|-------| | get | | mediaaccess | | get | | mediaaccess | the listing takes and . see pagination. a person page combines two sources: the biography and images come from themoviedb, and the credits are the titles your own server holds. because the details are fetched live, a person your server knows about can still answer 404 while themoviedb is unreachable. if the server is set to hide adult content, a person marked adult is refused rather than returned. where to go next - search - genres

title: Genres
description: Browse video genres and what sits under one.
content: genres video genres, and the titles on this server filed under one. music has its own genres: see music genres. | method | path | needs | |--------|------|-------| | get | | mediaaccess | | get | | mediaaccess | both take and . see pagination. the id is the themoviedb genre id, so the same number means the same genre everywhere. anime anime carries extra groupings of its own, addressed the same way. | method | path | needs | |--------|------|-------| | get | | mediaaccess | | get | | mediaaccess | | get | | mediaaccess | | get | | mediaaccess | | get | | mediaaccess | | get | | mediaaccess | an anime season here means the broadcast season, such as a year and a quarter, not a season of one series. where to go next - search - libraries

title: Search
description: Search your own library, for video and for music.
content: search search looks at what your server holds. video and music are separate, and each has a variant shaped for a tv. | method | path | needs | |--------|------|-------| | get | | mediaaccess | | get | | mediaaccess | | get | | mediaaccess | | get | | mediaaccess | ::properties ::property name: 'query', type: 'string' what to look for. accents and case are normalised, so a query without them still matches. ::property name: 'type', type: 'string' narrows the result to one kind of thing. :: the variants return the same matches described as screen components, so a tv client draws them without a second layout. each category is capped, so a very broad query answers quickly with the best matches rather than everything. where to go next - music - genres

title: User data
description: Continue watching, watched state and favourites for the calling user.
content: user data what one person has watched and liked. every endpoint here acts for the account behind the token, so two users on one server never see each other's progress. | method | path | needs | |--------|------|-------| | get | | mediaaccess | | delete | | mediaaccess | | get | | mediaaccess | | get | | mediaaccess | continue watching returns cards for what the user has started and not finished, ready to render. hides one item from that row. it takes the item's type and id, and it does not change the watched state or delete anything on disk. watched answers for one item. give it the same type and id pair. films and series use their numeric id. items that live only on your server, such as a special, use their own id instead. where to go next - home - streaming for how progress is reported during playback.

title: Specials
description: Hand-made collections that mix films and episodes in an order you choose.
content: specials a special is a collection you build yourself: films and episodes in a deliberate order, such as a viewing order across two series. it is the one grouping the metadata sources cannot give you. its id is generated by your server, so it exists only there. reading | method | path | needs | |--------|------|-------| | get | | mediaaccess | | get | | mediaaccess | | get | | mediaaccess | | get | | mediaaccess | the listing takes and . see pagination. user actions | method | path | needs | |--------|------|-------| | post | | mediaaccess | | post | | mediaaccess | managing | method | path | needs | |--------|------|-------| | post | | moderator | building and editing a special is a dashboard job with its own endpoints, under . those add and remove items and set their order. where to go next - specials for what one is and how to build it. - collections

title: Content segments
description: The marked ranges that let a player skip an intro or roll credits early.
content: content segments a segment marks a range on the timeline: an intro, a recap, an outro or the credits. players read them to offer a skip button and to move on when the credits start. a segment belongs to one episode or one film, never to both. reading | method | path | needs | |--------|------|-------| | get | | mediaaccess | | get | | mediaaccess | | get | | moderator | the two by-item routes are what a player calls. the bare listing is for review and takes , and . editing | method | path | needs | |--------|------|-------| | post | | moderator | | put | | moderator | | delete | | moderator | the shape of a segment ::properties ::property name: 'segmenttype', type: 'string' one of , , or . ::property name: 'startseconds', type: 'number' where the range starts, in seconds on the source timeline. ::property name: 'endseconds', type: 'number' where it ends. the end itself is outside the range. ::property name: 'source', type: 'string' how it got there: for automatic detection, for one entered by hand, for community data. ::property name: 'confidence', type: 'number' between zero and one. always one for a manual entry, so a player can prefer human answers and ignore weak detections. :: times are seconds, not milliseconds, and they are measured on the source, so they stay right whichever version is being played. where to go next - content analysis for how detection is run. - streaming

title: Authentication
description: How the server decides who is calling, and how to get a token.
content: authentication every request carries a token issued by the nomercy account service. the server validates it, then looks the account up in its own user list. getting a token tokens come from the nomercy identity service, not from your server. it speaks openid connect, so any standard oidc client library can obtain a token. the apps use authorization code flow with pkce on desktop and web, and device code flow where there is no browser, such as a tv. point your client at the discovery document and let the library do the rest. sending it put the token in the header. where a header cannot be set, such as a browser opening a signalr websocket, the token may travel as a query parameter instead. what the server checks three things, in order. the token is genuine. signature, issuer and audience are verified against the identity service. signing keys are cached, so a server that has lost its internet connection can still validate a token it has seen keys for. the token is for the api. it has to carry the api scope. the account exists here. the subject of the token has to match a user on this server. one identity service serves every nomercy install, so this last check is what keeps your server yours: a token from someone else's account is a valid token and still gets a 401 here. permissions passing authentication answers "who are you". each endpoint then asks "may you do this". ::properties ::property name: 'mediaaccess' allowed to use the server: browse libraries, play, manage own playlists. ::property name: 'opticalaccess' allowed to drive the disc drive: probe, play and rip a disc. ::property name: 'moderator' allowed to manage the server: libraries, encoding, tasks, logs, users. ::property name: 'owner' the account that owns the server. satisfies every other permission. :: each endpoint page names the permission it needs. which switches a user holds is set in the dashboard, described in users. where to go next - errors for what a rejected request looks like. - api overview for the base address and response shape.

title: Pagination
description: How to page through a long list.
content: pagination endpoints that can return a long list take two query parameters: and . ::properties ::property name: 'page', type: 'integer' which page to return, counting from zero. a negative value is treated as zero. ::property name: 'take', type: 'integer' how many items on the page. defaults to 300 and is capped, so a very large value returns the cap rather than the whole table. :: the endpoint pages say which endpoints accept these. where they are absent, the endpoint returns its full result in one response. letter pages library and music listings page by first letter instead of by number, because that is how the apps present them. titles that do not start with a letter are grouped under . where to go next - api overview - errors

title: Errors
description: The shape of a failed response, and what each status means here.
content: errors a failed request answers with a problem document: the standard shape, plus the trace id for that request. ::properties ::property name: 'type', type: 'string' an identifier for the kind of failure. stable, so it is safe to branch on. ::property name: 'title', type: 'string' the category, translated to the caller's language. ::property name: 'detail', type: 'string' what went wrong in this particular request. read this one first. ::property name: 'instance', type: 'string' the path that was called. ::property name: 'status', type: 'integer' the http status, repeated in the body. ::property name: 'traceid', type: 'string' identifies this request in the server log. quote it when reporting a problem. :: the statuses you will meet | status | means | |--------|-------| | 400 | the request was malformed | | 401 | no token, an invalid token, or an account this server does not know | | 403 | authenticated, but without the permission this endpoint needs | | 404 | no such item, or none you may see | | 409 | the change conflicts with the current state | | 422 | the request was understood but the values will not do | | 429 | too many requests | | 500 | the server failed | | 503 | the server is not ready to answer yet | telling 401 and 403 apart this pair is worth getting right, because the fix differs. 401 means the server did not accept the token. either it is missing or expired, or the account behind it is not a user on this server. a token for a different nomercy server lands here. 403 means the token was fine and the account is real, but it lacks the permission. granting the permission is a change the server owner makes in the dashboard. finding the request in the log every problem document carries , and the same id is written into the server log. search for it there to see what the server was doing. log locations are listed in logs. where to go next - authentication - api overview

title: Music
description: The music home screen and music search.
content: music music has its own home screen, described by the server the same way the video home is. the screen | method | path | needs | |--------|------|-------| | get | | mediaaccess | | get | | mediaaccess | the two are the same endpoint. it takes and . filling the rows | method | path | needs | |--------|------|-------| | post | | mediaaccess | | post | | mediaaccess | | post | | mediaaccess | | post | | mediaaccess | each fills one row of the screen for the calling user. search | method | path | needs | |--------|------|-------| | get | | mediaaccess | takes , and optionally to narrow it. the result is shaped for the music view: one top result, a handful of tracks, and carousels for the rest. each category is capped so a broad query stays fast. where to go next - artists - albums - playlists

title: Tracks
description: Favourite tracks, lyrics, and reporting a play.
content: tracks track endpoints are per user. the listing is the user's favourites rather than every track on the server, which is browsed through albums and artists instead. | method | path | needs | |--------|------|-------| | get | | mediaaccess | | post | | mediaaccess | | post | | mediaaccess | records that the track was played. players call it themselves; nothing else has to. lyrics | method | path | needs | |--------|------|-------| | get | | mediaaccess | | patch | | mediaaccess | lyrics are cached on the server after the first look-up. where a look-up found nothing, that answer is remembered too, so the providers are not asked again for the same track. shifts synced lyrics in time for a track whose timing is out. it is saved, so it applies on every later play. where to go next - albums - playlists

title: Playlists
description: Music playlists and video playlists, which are two separate things.
content: playlists there are two kinds, and they share nothing. a music playlist holds tracks. a video playlist holds films, series, episodes and specials. neither can contain the other, which is why they live at different addresses. music playlists | method | path | needs | |--------|------|-------| | get | | mediaaccess | | get | | mediaaccess | | post | | mediaaccess | | patch | | mediaaccess | | delete | | mediaaccess | tracks are added and removed one at a time. | method | path | needs | |--------|------|-------| | post | | mediaaccess | | delete | | mediaaccess | | post | | moderator | video playlists | method | path | needs | |--------|------|-------| | get | | mediaaccess | | get | | mediaaccess | | post | | mediaaccess | | patch | | mediaaccess | | delete | | mediaaccess | these are ordered, so the order is part of what you save. | method | path | needs | |--------|------|-------| | post | | mediaaccess | | delete | | mediaaccess | | put | | mediaaccess | every action here is scoped to the caller's own playlists. another user's playlist answers as if it were not there. playlist or special? a playlist is yours. a special belongs to the server and everyone sees it. reach for a special when the order is part of the library, and a playlist when it is a personal list. where to go next - tracks - specials

content: configuration the settings the dashboard edits. everything here is stored on the server, so a change applies to every client at once. | method | path | needs | |--------|------|-------| | get | | moderator | | post | | moderator | | patch | | moderator | what you can set ::properties ::property name: 'name', type: 'string' the server's display name, as clients show it. ::property name: 'internalport / externalport', type: 'integer' the ports the server listens on and is reached at. ::property name: 'allowadultcontent', type: 'boolean' whether adult titles may be shown at all on this server. ::property name: 'swagger', type: 'boolean' whether the built-in api explorer is served. ::property name: 'usesynthesizeddns', type: 'boolean' whether the server resolves its own name locally instead of going out to dns. :: worker counts the rest of the settings are worker counts, one per kind of work: , , , , , , and . each is how many of that job may run at once. raising the encoder count uses more of the machine; lowering it leaves room for other things. languages and countries | method | path | needs | |--------|------|-------| | get | | mediaaccess | | get | | mediaaccess | these are the lists clients offer in their pickers. they need only media access, because a normal user chooses their own language. where to go next - server - configuration

title: Libraries (admin)
description: Create libraries, attach folders, choose encoding, and run scans.
content: libraries admin this is the administrative side of libraries: what exists, which folders feed it, how it encodes, and when it looks again. what a viewer can see is a different surface, described in libraries. the library | method | path | needs | |--------|------|-------| | get | | moderator | | post | | moderator | | patch | | moderator | | delete | | moderator | | patch | | moderator | sets the order libraries appear in for everyone. deleting a library removes it from the server. it does not delete the files. folders | method | path | needs | |--------|------|-------| | post | | moderator | | patch | | moderator | | delete | | moderator | a library holds folders, and a folder is where its media lives. see libraries for how to lay them out. encoding | method | path | needs | |--------|------|-------| | post | | moderator | | delete | | moderator | encoding is chosen per folder, not per library, so two folders in one library can be treated differently. looking again | method | path | needs | |--------|------|-------| | post | | moderator | | post | | moderator | | post | | moderator | | post | | moderator | | post | | moderator | | post | | moderator | three different jobs, and picking the right one saves a lot of work: scan-new looks only for files the server has not seen. this is the everyday one. rescan looks at everything again, including what it already knows. refresh fetches details and artwork again, without touching the files. repairs | method | path | needs | |--------|------|-------| | post | | moderator | | get | | moderator | | post | | moderator | moves media into a different library. where to go next - libraries - encoder profiles - tasks for watching a scan run.

title: Encoder profiles
description: Read, build, validate and share the profiles that decide how media is encoded.
content: encoder profiles a profile decides what the encoder does with a file. this is the current surface for working with them. built-in profiles come with the server and cannot be edited. to change one, clone it and edit the clone. reading | method | path | needs | |--------|------|-------| | get | | moderator | | get | | moderator | | get | | moderator | | get | | moderator | the listing takes , and an optional . built-in profiles are returned first. a profile can inherit from another, so what is stored is not always the whole picture. returns it with everything inherited filled in, which is what the encoder will actually use. building one | method | path | needs | |--------|------|-------| | post | | moderator | | put | | moderator | | post | | moderator | | delete | | moderator | checking before you commit | method | path | needs | |--------|------|-------| | post | | moderator | | post | | moderator | says whether a profile can work at all. shows what it would do to a given source, which is the honest answer to "will this re-encode or copy". sharing | method | path | needs | |--------|------|-------| | get | | moderator | | post | | moderator | an exported profile can be signed. on import the signature is checked against the publishers you trust; importing an unsigned one is a deliberate choice, made with . deprecated routes and are deprecated. encoding presets lists which route here to call in place of each. where to go next - encoding profiles for what the settings mean. - encoder bundles - hardware benchmark

title: Encoder bundles
description: Finding encoded output on disk that nothing points at any more.
content: encoder bundles an encode writes a bundle: the output files for one title under one profile. over time a bundle can be left behind, for example when the profile that made it was deleted. | method | path | needs | |--------|------|-------| | get | | owner | the sweep walks every folder in every library and reports three kinds of problem: a bundle whose profile no longer exists, a bundle with duplicate manifests, and a bundle whose recorded files do not match what is on disk. it reports only. nothing is deleted by this call, so it is safe to run and read before deciding anything. remote storage is handled through its own driver, so a library on a network share or object store is swept the same way a local one is. where to go next - encoder profiles - encoding history - storage

title: Encoding history
description: What has been encoded, how it went, and clearing the record.
content: encoding history every finished encode leaves a row: what was encoded, with which profile, how long it took and what came out. it is the record you read when you want to know whether a setting actually helped. | method | path | needs | |--------|------|-------| | get | | moderator | | get | | moderator | | delete | | moderator | | post | | owner | the listing takes and . summarises the rows rather than returning them, which is what the dashboard charts. clears history in bulk and is owner-only. it removes the record, not the encoded files. where to go next - encoding history for what the fields mean. - hardware benchmark

content: encoding presets every route under is deprecated. it answers, so code calling it keeps working. write new code against encoder profiles. which route to call | deprecated | call instead | |-----|-----| | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | all paths above are relative to , and all need moderator. is deprecated too. its create route answers 410 and names the route to call in the response. where to go next - encoder profiles - encoding profiles

title: Hardware benchmark
description: Measuring what this machine can encode with, and watching it work.
content: hardware benchmark the benchmark measures what your machine actually manages, rather than what its parts claim. the result is what the server uses when choosing an accelerator. the cached result | method | path | needs | |--------|------|-------| | get | | moderator | | post | | owner | the result is kept, so reading it is cheap. running it again is owner-only, because it puts the machine under load for as long as it takes. the encoder view | method | path | needs | |--------|------|-------| | get | | moderator | | get | | moderator | | post | | moderator | | get | | moderator | | get | | moderator | lists what this machine can do: which accelerators are present and what each can encode and decode. is the live picture while encoding runs. starting a benchmark here returns a job id. poll that id for the result, rather than holding the request open. where to go next - hardware acceleration - encoder profiles

title: Optical media
description: Drives, discs, and the path from an inserted disc to a ripped title.
content: optical media everything to do with the disc drive: what is in it, what is on the disc, and turning that into files. reading a disc needs . changing the library because of one needs . the drive | method | path | needs | |--------|------|-------| | get | | opticalaccess | | get | | opticalaccess | | post | | moderator | | post | | moderator | the drive path identifies the drive, so a machine with two drives is handled without ambiguity. looking at the disc | method | path | needs | |--------|------|-------| | get | | opticalaccess | | get | | opticalaccess | | post | | opticalaccess | | post | | moderator | lists the titles on the disc. a disc usually holds many, most of them menus and trailers. asks what film or series this disc is. is you agreeing, or correcting it. nothing is written until you confirm. ripping | method | path | needs | |--------|------|-------| | post | | moderator | | post | | moderator | ripping is queued, not done in the request. watch it through the ripper hub. playing straight from the disc | method | path | needs | |--------|------|-------| | post | | opticalaccess | | post | | opticalaccess | onboarding a disc | method | path | needs | |--------|------|-------| | post | | moderator | | post | | moderator | | get | | moderator | this is the guided path the dashboard uses: start it with the library the disc should land in, and the server keeps the state so the page can be closed and reopened. where to go next - discs for the flow as a person walks it. - ripper hub

title: Plugins
description: Installing plugins, consenting to what they ask for, and the screens they add.
content: plugins plugin management is owner-only, because installing one is letting code run inside your server. installed plugins | method | path | needs | |--------|------|-------| | get | | owner | | get | | owner | | post | | owner | | delete | | owner | | post | | owner | | post | | owner | takes an uploaded file, so a plugin can be installed without a repository. consent | method | path | needs | |--------|------|-------| | post | | owner | | delete | | owner | | get | | owner | | post | | owner | a plugin that asks for more than the ordinary set installs switched off and waits here. withdrawing consent disables it and clears what was granted. grants are the narrower requests a plugin makes while running, such as one network host. they are answered one at a time. see plugins overview. repositories | method | path | needs | |--------|------|-------| | get | | owner | | post | | owner | | delete | | owner | | post | | owner | | get | | owner | | post | | owner | is what the configured repositories offer. installing from one takes an optional . the screens plugins add | method | path | needs | |--------|------|-------| | get | | authenticated | | get | | authenticated | | get | | authenticated | | get | | authenticated | these are what a client calls to draw plugin screens. a plugin describes its view and each client renders it in its own style, which is why one plugin looks native on web, phone and tv. takes a so a client asks only for what it can show. where to go next - plugins overview - repositories and trust - writing a plugin

title: Recommendations
description: Suggestions built from what your library already holds.
content: recommendations suggestions of titles you do not have, worked out from what you do. they are separated by kind, because the reasoning differs. | method | path | needs | |--------|------|-------| | get | | mediaaccess | | get | | mediaaccess | | get | | mediaaccess | | get | | mediaaccess | each listing takes to cap how many come back. the detail route returns one suggestion in full, so a client can show why it was suggested before you act on it. diagnostics | method | path | needs | |--------|------|-------| | get | | moderator | explains what the recommender had to work with. useful when the suggestions look thin: usually the answer is that the library is small or one-sided. where to go next - movies for adding one you decide to keep. - recommendations

title: Server activity
description: The record of what happened on the server, and who did it.
content: server activity the activity log answers "what happened here". sign-ins, playback, configuration changes, encoder work, scans and the server's own defensive actions all land in one place. | method | path | needs | |--------|------|-------| | get | | moderator | | post | | mediaaccess | | delete | | moderator | reading it needs moderator, because it shows what everyone did. writing needs only media access, because clients record their own playback here. categories rows are filed under one category, and the listing filters by it. | category | covers | |----------|--------| | auth | signing in and out | | connection | clients connecting and dropping | | playback | what was played, and where | | configuration | settings that changed | | failure | something that went wrong | | encoder | encode jobs starting, finishing or giving up | | library | scans, and files arriving or leaving | | security | addresses the server banned or released by itself | clearing it takes and , so you can drop one kind of row, or everything older than a date, without losing the rest. where to go next - activity - logs for the technical log, which is a different thing.

title: Storage browser
description: Browsing folders on the server, and creating one.
content: storage browser the folder picker in the dashboard runs on these. they browse the server's own filesystem, so what you see is what the server can reach, not what your own machine has. all of them need moderator, and all take their arguments in the body rather than the path, so a path with slashes and spaces needs no escaping. through a storage driver | method | path | needs | |--------|------|-------| | post | | moderator | | post | | moderator | | post | | moderator | these go through the storage driver, so they work the same for a local disk, a network share and an object store. checks that a location can be reached and written to. use it before saving a folder, so a wrong address is caught while the user is still looking at it. the local filesystem | method | path | needs | |--------|------|-------| | post | | moderator | | post | | moderator | | post | | moderator | | post | | moderator | lists the drives or mount points to start from, and the account's own folder. together they give a picker somewhere sensible to open at on any platform. where to go next - storage - libraries admin

title: Tasks and the queue
description: Watching the queue, reordering it, and dealing with what failed.
content: tasks and the queue work the server does in the background: scans, imports, artwork, and encodes. everything here needs moderator. the queue | method | path | needs | |--------|------|-------| | get | | moderator | | get | | moderator | | get | | moderator | | get | | moderator | is the summary the dashboard header shows. estimates when the queue drains. is what is executing right now. changing the order | method | path | needs | |--------|------|-------| | post | | moderator | | patch | | moderator | | delete | | moderator | the queue runs in order, so moving an item is how you get one film encoded tonight instead of tomorrow. pausing | method | path | needs | |--------|------|-------| | post | | moderator | | post | | moderator | | post | | moderator | | post | | moderator | pausing the queue lets what is running finish and starts nothing new, so the machine frees up without losing work. what failed | method | path | needs | |--------|------|-------| | get | | moderator | | post | | moderator | | post | | moderator | retrying without an id retries all of them. encodes that stopped part way | method | path | needs | |--------|------|-------| | get | | moderator | | post | | moderator | | delete | | moderator | | delete | | moderator | an encode interrupted by a restart or a power cut lands here. retrying queues that title's encode again from its source file. where to go next - queue for the same view from the command line. - dashboard hub for live progress.

title: Distribution workers
description: Extra machines that take encoding work from this server.
content: distribution workers a worker is another machine that encodes for your server. the server keeps the library and the queue; the worker just does the work and reports back. distributed encoding is switched on by giving the server a signing key. until then every route here answers 503 and the registry stays empty, so a single-machine install is unaffected by any of this. the worker list | method | path | needs | |--------|------|-------| | get | | owner | | delete | | owner | | get | | owner | the same routes answer under . what a worker calls | method | path | needs | |--------|------|-------| | post | | owner | | post | | owner | | post | | owner | a worker registers itself on boot, then keeps a heartbeat going to stay active. it either unregisters cleanly on shutdown, or drops out of the registry after a short silence. dispatching | method | path | needs | |--------|------|-------| | post | | owner | | get | | owner | reading the source | method | path | needs | |--------|------|-------| | get | | signed link | a worker reads its source file over this route. the link is signed and timestamped rather than open, so it grants one file for a short window instead of access to the library. where to go next - tasks and the queue - hardware benchmark

title: Logs
description: Reading the server log, and the levels and types to filter it by.
content: logs the technical log: what the server itself wrote. for a record of what people did, read server activity instead. | method | path | needs | |--------|------|-------| | get | | moderator | | get | | moderator | | get | | moderator | ::properties ::property name: 'limit', type: 'integer' how many lines to return. ::property name: 'types', type: 'string' which parts of the server to include, such as the encoder or the queue. ::property name: 'levels', type: 'string' which severities to include. ::property name: 'filter', type: 'string' free text to match within the message. :: and return the values the server actually uses, so a client can build its filter from the server rather than hard-coding a list that drifts. following along live the local control surface streams the log as it is written: that route answers on the machine itself, which is why it needs no token and is unavailable from elsewhere. where to go next - logs for where the files live. - diagnostics

title: Streaming
description: Live transcode sessions: starting one, playing it, and steering it.
content: streaming a live session transcodes a file while it plays, for a client that cannot play the original as it stands. every route needs mediaaccess. starting | method | path | needs | |--------|------|-------| | post | | mediaaccess | | get | | mediaaccess | | delete | | mediaaccess | the client says what it can play, and the server works out what to do with that. ::properties ::property name: 'videofileid', type: 'string' which file to play. ::property name: 'clientcaps', type: 'object' what this client can decode. the server transcodes only what it has to. ::property name: 'starttimeseconds', type: 'number' where to begin, so resuming does not start at the beginning. ::property name: 'preferredquality', type: 'string' an optional starting quality. ::property name: 'audiolanguage', type: 'string' the language of the audio track the viewer chose. leaving it out lets the server pick. :: the audio track is chosen by language, not by its position in the file, so the choice survives a file whose track order differs. playing | method | path | needs | |--------|------|-------| | get | | mediaaccess | | get | | mediaaccess | | get | | mediaaccess | ordinary hls: hand the master playlist to a player and it follows the rest. steering it | method | path | needs | |--------|------|-------| | post | | mediaaccess | | post | | mediaaccess | | post | | mediaaccess | | post | | mediaaccess | is the client saying where it is, so the server transcodes ahead of the viewer instead of racing to the end. moves the session, rather than asking the player to wait for segments that will never be wanted. the epoch in the segment path says which run of the transcoder produced that segment, so a seek or a quality change does not leave the player fetching segments from the run before it. ending the session frees the machine. a session nobody is watching expires on its own after an idle period. where to go next - content segments - encoding overview

title: SignalR overview
description: How live connections work, and which hub does what.
content: signalr overview rest answers a question. a hub keeps a conversation open, which is how playback stays in step across devices and how progress reaches a dashboard while it happens. connecting hubs sit at the root of the server, not under . two things are fixed: websockets only. long polling and server-sent events are turned off, so a client that cannot open a websocket cannot connect. a token is required. the same token the rest api takes. browsers cannot set headers on a websocket, so it goes in the query string. the connection closes when the token expires, so a client keeps its token fresh and reconnects. who receives what the server sends to a user, not to everyone. a message about your devices reaches your connections and nobody else's, which matters on a server with several households on it. your own devices are one group, so an action on the phone reaches the tv without either knowing the other's address. the hubs | hub | for | |-----|-----| | /nomercy-api/signalr/video-hub | video playback, progress, and handing playback to another device | | /nomercy-api/signalr/music-hub | music playback and the shared queue | | /nomercy-api/signalr/device-hub | which devices are here, what they can do, waking one | | /nomercy-api/signalr/cast-hub | chromecast and the nomercy receiver | | /nomercy-api/signalr/dashboard-hub | live server resources for the dashboard | | /nomercy-api/signalr/ripper-hub | disc ripping as it runs | | /nomercy-api/signalr/drives-hub | discs going in and out of a drive | | /nomercy-api/signalr/content-analysis-hub | progress of analysis work such as transcription | | | live transcode sessions | | | plugins. one hub for all of them, joined by group | where to go next - authentication - video hub

title: Video hub
description: Starting playback, reporting progress, and moving a film to another screen.
content: video hub the video hub holds one playback state per user. every device of that user sees the same state, which is what makes "carry on in the bedroom" work. starting playback says what kind of thing is being played, such as a film or a series. identifies it, and picks an episode within it. the server builds the queue itself. a client asks for a title and receives a state to render, rather than assembling a playlist of its own. while it plays carries the transport actions: play, pause, seek, next and so on. the state that comes back says which of them are allowed right now, so a client greys out what cannot be done instead of guessing. reports where the viewer is, which is what keeps continue watching honest. moving to another screen playback moves to that device. the queue and position stay with the user, so nothing restarts. which devices are available comes from the device hub. clearing progress drops the recorded progress for one item. where to go next - device hub - music hub - user data

title: Music hub
description: The shared music queue, position reporting, and volume across devices.
content: music hub music works the way video does: one playback state per user, shared by all their devices. a phone can drive what plays in the living room without either knowing the other's address. starting playback the server builds the queue. what it sends back is the state to render, including which transport actions are allowed. reading the state returns the current state directly, for a client that would rather ask than wait to be told. every state carries the server's own clock reading. a client works out elapsed time against that stamp, so a slow connection shifts nothing. while it plays position is reported in milliseconds. the form also says when the client took the reading, which keeps the timeline right when the message itself is delayed. for a queue of mixed items there are per-item forms, and , which name the item they refer to. crossfade the client says a fade has begun and, when the next track has taken over, which track that is. the state follows the audio rather than the other way round. devices and volume changes the device that is playing. names a device, so a phone can turn down the speaker it is driving. where to go next - video hub - device hub - tracks

title: Device hub
description: Which of your devices are here, what each can play, and waking one.
content: device hub this hub answers "what can i send this to". it lists your own devices only. saying what a device can do a client declares what it can play: audio codecs, how many channels, roughly how much memory it has. the server remembers it, so the answer survives the app closing. this is what lets the server decide between sending a file as it is and transcoding it. a device that never declares gets safe defaults instead of the best it could have had. the device list returns your devices with, for each one, its name, its type, whether it is online, its address on the local network, when it was last seen, and whether it is in the foreground with the screen on. that last pair is the difference between a device that is reachable and one someone is actually looking at. when the list changes, connected clients are told, so a picker updates itself rather than polling. waking one asks a device to come forward and be ready to play. the result says whether it worked, so a client can say something useful when the tv does not answer. notices anything the server needs to tell this device that happened while it was away, such as playback having been moved off it. where to go next - video hub - music hub - devices

title: Drives hub
description: Discs going in and out of a drive, pushed as it happens.
content: drives hub a listening connection. the server pushes drive changes to it: a disc inserted, a disc ejected, a drive appearing or going away. there is nothing to call on this hub. connect and receive. that is the point of it: a dashboard open on the disc page reacts the moment a disc goes in, without polling the drive and without spinning it up to ask. for the state of one drive on demand, ask the ripper hub instead. where to go next - ripper hub - optical media - discs

title: Content analysis hub
description: Progress of analysis work, such as transcribing a track.
content: content analysis hub analysis work runs long, so it reports here. connect, start the work through its endpoint, and read progress on this connection. there is nothing to call on this hub. connect and receive. transcription progress arrives as each chunk of audio is processed. starting the work the work itself is started over rest: these need owner. detecting an intro works across a season, because that is where a repeated opening can be found. where to go next - content segments - content analysis

title: Cast hub
description: Driving a Chromecast, and the receiver reporting back.
content: cast hub this hub carries both halves of casting: the app telling a receiver what to do, and the receiver saying what it is doing. choosing a receiver and starting pick a receiver by name, launch on it, then hand it what to play. ends playback; gives the receiver back. transport tracks what the receiver reports the receiver uses the same connection to say what it has: carries the position, the duration, how far through it is and how much is left, so a controller draws a progress bar without doing arithmetic of its own. asking where things stand for a controller that joined part way through, rather than one that has been listening from the start. where to go next - video hub - device hub

title: Dashboard hub
description: Live server resources and log lines while the dashboard is open.
content: dashboard hub the dashboard's live feed: processor, memory and disk as they move, plus log lines as they are written. a moderator connecting joins the moderators group and receives what is broadcast to it. resource monitoring both need moderator. measuring costs something, so it runs only while a dashboard is watching. start it when the page opens, stop it when the page leaves. the server also stops on its own once the last dashboard connection has gone, so a client that closes abruptly leaves nothing running. where to go next - tasks and the queue - logs - diagnostics

title: Ripper hub
description: The state of a drive, and rip progress as it runs.
content: ripper hub ripping takes a while, so it reports here rather than through a request the client holds open. connect before starting a rip and watch it work. asking about a drive needs moderator; anyone else gets nothing back. what comes back depends on what is there: no disc. the drive itself: path, label, and that it is empty. a disc the server can read. a light probe as well, so the page can name the disc without a full scan. a disc of a type with no reader. the drive-level answer only, rather than a failure. the probe is deliberately light. reading every title on a blu-ray takes minutes, and this call is what a page makes on open. watching a rip progress arrives on this connection while the rip runs. start the rip through optical media and read the progress here. where to go next - optical media - drives hub - discs

title: NoMercy API
description: The REST and SignalR surface your own server speaks.
content: ::hero nomercy api your server is the api. every request goes to the machine you run, so what you build with this talks to your library and to nothing of ours. classname: 'lead' ::iconcards ::iconcard href: '/nomercy-api/overview', name: 'overview', icon: 'api' the base address, versioning, and the shape of every response. ::iconcard href: '/nomercy-api/authentication', name: 'authentication', icon: 'app' getting a token, sending it, and what the server checks. ::iconcard href: '/nomercy-api/signalr/overview', name: 'signalr hubs', icon: 'server' live connections: playback, devices, progress and casting. :: start here anchor: false read overview for the base address and the response shape, then authentication for the token. between them they cover everything the reference pages assume. classname: 'lead' each endpoint page lists the method, the path, and the permission it needs. errors explains what a rejection looks like, and pagination how to walk a long list.

title: What the app is
description: The client you watch and listen in, and how it relates to your server.
content: what the app is the app is where you watch. your server is where your media lives. they are two different things, and knowing which is which explains most of what follows. open that, sign in, pick your server, and you are watching. nothing of yours passes through us the app is a page. when it plays something, it fetches it from your server directly. the video goes from your machine to your screen. that is why the app works on your home network with the internet down, and why a big library costs you nothing in hosting. one app, every server you are allowed on sign in once and the app lists the servers you have access to: your own, and any a friend has invited you to. switching between them is a menu, not a second account. what runs where your server holds the media, the library, the users, and everything the dashboard changes. it does the encoding. the app shows what the server describes. screens are built from what the server sends, so a server that gains a feature shows it in the app you already have. your account lives with the nomercy identity service, so one account gets you into every server you are allowed on. the dashboard is part of the app administering the server happens in the same app, under dashboard. if you own a server you get it; if you were invited to someone else's, you do not. where to go next - supported platforms - connecting to your server - install the server if you do not have one yet.

title: Where the app runs
description: Browsers, installing it like an app, and the other clients.
content: where the app runs anywhere with a current browser. there is nothing to install to get going. browsers current versions of chrome, edge, firefox and safari all work, on desktop and on a phone. what differs between them is which formats the browser itself can play. where a browser cannot take a file as it stands, the server converts it while it plays, so every browser gets a picture. see quality. installing it the app can be installed from the browser, and it then behaves like any other app: its own window, its own icon, no address bar. chrome and edge offer an install button in the address bar. safari on iphone and ipad installs through share, then add to home screen. installing changes the frame around the app, not the app. it is the same page, signed in the same way. on a television an android tv app is the way to watch on a television. it talks to the same server and shares your progress, so a film paused on the sofa carries on in bed. you can also cast from the app to a chromecast. see casting. where to go next - connecting to your server - what the app is

title: Connecting to your server
description: Signing in, picking a server, and what the app does about your network.
content: connecting to your server open app.nomercy.tv, sign in with your nomercy account, and the app lists the servers you can reach. what the app connects to your server has its own address, issued when it was set up. the app connects straight to it, so the media never travels through anything of ours. at home the app reaches your server across your own network, which is the fastest path. from elsewhere it reaches the same server over the internet. you do not choose between them; the app uses what works. first time on a device three short steps, and only the first time: 1. sign in. 2. name this device, so you recognise it later in the device list. 3. pick a server, if you can reach more than one. see name this device and selecting a server. switching servers from your profile menu. it is a separate action from signing out, so you keep your session. ::troubleshooting the list is empty. usually a different account, or a server that has not finished its own setup. see selecting a server. the server is listed but will not connect. see server offline. it works away from home but not at home. your browser is holding back a request from a public page into your own network, and it wants your permission first. see web app can't reach my server on my home network. :: where to go next - the first-run wizard - home

title: Naming your device
description: What the device name is for and where it shows up.
content: naming your device the first time you sign in on a new phone, tv, browser or computer, nomercy asks what to call it. why it asks your account works on many devices at once, and several features need to tell them apart. the name appears when you cast from your phone to your tv, in the list of devices in your settings, and in your server's activity so you can see what was watched where. a device with no useful name makes all of those harder to read. choosing a name you get suggestions based on what the device appears to be. pick one, or type your own. say where it is rather than what it is. "living room tv" is easier to pick out of a list later than "android tv" when you own two. skipping you can skip. the device gets a generic name. the cost is a device list that is harder to read, and casting targets that are harder to tell apart. changing it later the name is not permanent. change it in your settings under devices, on any device, at any time. where to go next - selecting a server if you have more than one.

title: Selecting a server
description: Choosing which server to browse, and what to do when none are listed.
content: selecting a server your nomercy account can reach more than one server: your own, and any that other people have shared with you. when there is a choice to make, nomercy asks which one you want. when you see this with exactly one server, nomercy picks it and you never see this screen. with more than one, you choose. you can switch later from your profile menu without signing out. what is in the list every server your account can reach. that means servers you own, and servers whose owner has given your account access. each one shows whether it is currently reachable. an unreachable server cannot be selected. see server offline. no servers listed three things cause this, in order of likelihood. you are signed in with a different account. the account that owns the server is the one that sees it. your server has not finished its own setup. a server that has not been claimed does not exist as far as your account is concerned. finish first-run setup on the server itself. nobody has shared one with you. if you do not run a server yourself, the owner has to add your account before it appears. switching servers use your profile menu. switching servers is a separate action from signing out. where to go next - server offline if the one you picked cannot be reached. - first-run wizard if the server is new.

title: First-run wizard
description: Name your server and create your first libraries.
content: first-run wizard the first time you open nomercy against a newly claimed server, it takes you through a short wizard instead of the home screen. three steps, and then you are done with setup for good. this runs after the server itself is set up. if you have not done that, start at first-run setup. only someone who can manage the server sees the wizard. everyone else waits until it is finished. step 1: base info give the server a name. this is the name you and anyone you share with will see when picking a server, so something recognisable is better than something clever. "living room" beats "server1". the step also links the privacy policy and terms of service. nothing else is asked here. you cannot continue until the name has something in it. step 2: media libraries create at least one library. this is the substantial step and it is worth doing carefully. for each library: 1. choose a type: movies, tv shows, anime, or music. this decides how file names are read, so it is the choice that matters most. 2. add a folder. the picker browses the server's disks, not the device you are on. you can create the folder here with new folder. the wizard does not ask about encoding. each folder is given a preset automatically, and you can change it later from library management. libraries can be dragged into the order you want them to appear in. you cannot continue until at least one library exists. see library management for what each type means and how to choose folders. step 3: finish a summary of what was set up, and a button that takes you into nomercy. the home screen is empty that is correct. the wizard built your shelves and left them empty. titles appear once you add a disc or some files. go to the dashboard and either rip a disc or add content. see discs or scanning and importing. where to go next - library management for choosing types and folders. - discs to add your first title.

title: Server offline
description: What to check when NoMercy cannot reach your server.
content: server offline this screen means the app could not reach the server you selected. the app is fine. something between it and the server is not. work through these in order. they are ordered by how often each one turns out to be the cause. is the server running check the machine it runs on. on windows and macos, look for the nomercy tray icon. on linux, on a nas, or in docker, check that the service or container is up. if the machine sleeps, it is not running while it sleeps. a server needs a machine that stays awake. are you away from home if it works at home and not elsewhere, the problem is remote access rather than the server. the server tries to arrange a route by itself. when your router blocks that, you need to add the rule yourself. see networking. is setup actually finished a server that never completed setup answers every request with "setup required", which reaches the app as unreachable. open the server's setup page and finish or retry it. see first-run setup. did the certificate lapse your server renews its certificate automatically. a server that was switched off for a long stretch can come back with an expired one. leave it running for a few minutes. the renewal runs on its own. if it does not recover, the server log says why. still nothing check the server's own logs. on the machine, or the container log for docker. the log says which of the above it is, and it is faster than guessing. where to go next - selecting a server to pick a different one. - networking for access from outside your home.

title: Home
description: The first screen, and what decides what is on it.
content: home home is rows of cards, built from what your server holds and what you have been watching. continue watching the first row is what you started and have not finished, most recent first. it updates as you watch, on whichever device you watched on. to take something off it, remove it from the row. that hides the item without marking it watched and without touching the file. the rest of the rows the other rows come from your own library: what was added recently, what sits under a genre, what belongs together. a server with one library shows fewer rows than a server with five, because there is less to group. the server decides the rows, not the app. that is why the same account shows different rows on different servers, and why a server update can change the screen without an app update. getting anywhere else the sidebar has your libraries, music, search, and, if you administer the server, the dashboard. ::troubleshooting home is empty. the server has nothing in it yet, or the scan has not finished. watch it from libraries in the dashboard. continue watching does not update. progress is saved as you watch, and a player closed immediately after starting saves nothing. if it stays empty across devices, check that the item plays to begin with. :: where to go next - libraries - search

title: Libraries
description: The libraries your server offers, and the other ways in.
content: libraries a library is a shelf: films in one, series in another, music in its own. what you see is what the server owner has made and given your account access to. opening libraries with only one library takes you straight into it. other ways to browse the same media is reachable by more than one path, because different moods want different routes. | route | shows | |-------|-------| | genres | everything filed under one genre | | collections | film series held together, such as a trilogy | | specials | hand-made collections the server owner built | | people | cast and crew, and what they are in | | favorites | what you have liked | | my lists | your own playlists | anime adds three more of its own: themes, demographics and seasons. a season here is the broadcast season, not a season of one series. where to go next - inside a library - title details - libraries for how the owner sets them up.

title: Inside a library
description: Browsing one library, and finding a title in a large one.
content: inside a library a library is a grid of what it holds. each card is a film, a series, or an album, with its artwork and enough to recognise it. finding something in a big library large libraries are browsed by first letter. pick a letter and you get that page of titles, rather than scrolling through everything. titles that do not start with a letter are grouped under . knowing the name already? search is quicker than either. opening a title a card opens its details page: what it is, who is in it, and what you can play. see title details. ::troubleshooting a title is missing. the server may not have scanned it yet. a scan is started from the dashboard, on libraries. a title is here with the wrong name or artwork. the match went to the wrong title. fixing it is a dashboard job: see metadata. :: where to go next - title details - search

title: Search
description: Finding something on your own server.
content: search search looks at your server: what it holds, not what exists in the world. video and music are searched separately, so a band and a film with the same name do not crowd each other out. what it matches titles, and the people in them. accents and case are ignored, so a query typed the easy way still finds the title spelled the proper way. results come back grouped: the best match first, then the rest by kind. when nothing comes back either the server does not hold it, or it holds it under a different name than you expect. a film matched to the wrong entry carries the wrong name, and searching the name you expect then finds nothing. browsing the library will show you what it actually calls itself. where to go next - inside a library - title details

title: Title details
description: The page for one film or series, and what you can do from it.
content: title details the details page is where you decide to watch something: the artwork, what it is about, who is in it, and what your server actually has. play, or not yet a title your server holds plays from here. a title it knows about and has no file for says so instead of failing when you press play. that difference matters on a series: a season can be half there, and the page shows which episodes are and which are not. episodes a series lists its seasons, and each season its episodes. an episode you have started shows how far in you are, so carrying on is one press. liking and lists the like button marks it as yours; it shows up under favorites. adding to a list puts it in a playlist you built. both are per account, so nobody else's screen changes. people cast and crew link through to their own page, which shows what else of theirs your server holds. ::troubleshooting the details are for the wrong title. the match went astray. fixing it is a dashboard job: see metadata. play does nothing. if the page says the title is unavailable, the server has no file for it. if it says nothing and play still fails, see common app issues. :: where to go next - watching - people

title: People
description: A person page, and what it shows from your library.
content: people a person page shows who someone is, and what of theirs your server holds. the biography and photograph come from themoviedb. the list of titles is your own library, so a long career shows only the part you have. getting there from the cast list on any title details page, or from people in the sidebar, which lists everyone your library involves. ::troubleshooting a person page will not open. the details are fetched while you open the page, so a server that cannot reach the metadata service shows nothing rather than a stale page. try again once it is back. someone is missing from a cast list. cast comes with the title's metadata. refreshing that title from the dashboard fetches it again. :: where to go next - title details - search

title: Watching
description: The video player: controls, skipping, and carrying on where you left off.
content: watching press play on a title details page and the player takes the screen. the controls the usual set: play and pause, a progress bar you can drag, volume, fullscreen, and pickers for subtitles, audio and quality. controls fade while you watch and come back when you move the pointer or press a key. on a touch screen, a tap brings them back. volume is remembered between sessions, so a player opened later starts where you left it rather than at full. keyboard | key | does | |-----|------| | space | play and pause | | left and right | seek | | up and down | volume | | | mute | | | fullscreen | | and | next and previous item | | | cycle subtitle track | | | cycle audio track | | and | slower and faster | | | back to normal speed | holding a modifier with left or right changes how far a seek jumps: shift for a nudge, alt for a few seconds, control for a minute. media keys on a keyboard work too, and so do the coloured buttons on a tv remote. skipping an intro where the server has marked an intro, a recap or the credits, a skip button appears while that part is playing. press it, or let it play; nothing is skipped without you. the server's own marks are used where it has them, and chapter marks in the file where it does not. marking is done by content analysis, described in content segments. carrying on progress is saved as you watch, on the server rather than in the browser. that is why a film paused on the laptop resumes on the tv. casting the player has a cast button when a receiver is on your network. see casting. ::troubleshooting playback stutters or drops quality. the server may be transcoding to suit this device. see quality. subtitles do not appear. they may not be selected, or the file may carry none. see subtitles. nothing plays at all. see common app issues. :: where to go next - subtitles - quality - casting

title: Music
description: The music screen, and how playback follows you between devices.
content: music music has its own screen, reached from the sidebar. it opens on what you listen to: favourites, favourite artists and albums, and your playlists. browsing artists, albums and genres each have their own list, browsed by first letter. names that do not start with a letter are grouped under . music search is separate from video search, so a band and a film with the same name stay out of each other's way. the player the player sits along the bottom and stays there while you browse, so opening an album does not stop the music. lyrics show where they are available, following along with the track when the file's lyrics are timed. it follows you playback lives on the server, not in the tab. start something on the laptop and the phone picks up the same queue at the same position. that is also what lets a phone drive what plays on a speaker or a television, without either knowing the other's address. ::troubleshooting an artist or album has no picture. artwork is fetched separately from the music itself, and one that could not be found stays blank rather than blocking the track. a track will not play. check the album page: a track the server cannot read shows there too. :: where to go next - artists - albums - playlists

title: Artists
description: An artist page, and what you can do from it.
content: artists an artist page shows their albums and tracks as your server holds them, with the artwork and details that came with the music. from here play everything, open an album, or like the artist so they show up under your favourites. liking is per account. another person on the same server has their own favourites. editing an artist someone who administers the server can correct an artist's details or replace the picture from this page. everyone else sees it as it is. where to go next - albums - music

title: Albums
description: An album page, its tracks, and lyrics.
content: albums an album page lists its tracks in order, with the cover and what is known about the release. play the album, play one track, or add tracks to a playlist. lyrics where lyrics are available for a track, they show with it. timed lyrics follow along as it plays. if the lyrics run ahead of or behind the music, they can be shifted for that track. the offset is saved, so it applies every time you play it. editing an album someone who administers the server can correct the details or replace the cover from this page. ::troubleshooting a track is on the album but will not play. the album came from the metadata source; the file has to be there as well. a track your server has no file for shows on the list and cannot be played. no lyrics. they were looked for and not found. that answer is remembered, so the providers are not asked again for the same track. :: where to go next - artists - playlists

title: Playlists
description: Building a playlist, and how it differs from a special.
content: playlists a playlist is yours. you build it, you order it, and nobody else on the server sees it. building one make a playlist, then add tracks to it from an album or an artist page. tracks are added and removed one at a time, and the order is yours to set. a playlist can have its own cover. music and video are separate a music playlist holds tracks. a video playlist holds films, series, episodes and specials. neither can hold the other, so a mixed list is not possible. video playlists live under my lists, alongside your libraries. playlist or special a playlist is personal. a special belongs to the server and everyone with access sees it. build a special when the order is part of the library, such as a viewing order across two series. build a playlist when it is just what you feel like. where to go next - music - albums

title: Subtitles
description: Choosing a subtitle track, styling it, and why your choice sticks.
content: subtitles pick a subtitle track from the player's subtitle button, or cycle through them with . your choice is remembered the player remembers the language you chose and applies it to the next thing you watch. it remembers the language, never the position in the list. track order comes from however the file was made, so "the second track" is english on one episode and japanese on the next. remembering the language means the next episode gives you the language you asked for. the same holds for audio: see watching. styling size, colour and background are yours to set, and are remembered along with the choice of track. subtitles that carry their own styling, such as signs and songs in anime, are drawn as the file describes them. those keep their own look rather than taking yours, because the styling is part of what is being said. where subtitles come from two places. subtitles inside the file are used as they are. subtitles fetched for a title are stored beside it. ::troubleshooting no subtitle button, or an empty list. the file carries none and none have been fetched for it. subtitles are out of step with the speech. the timing belongs to the subtitle file, not to the player. a different track for the same language is usually the fastest fix. the wrong language keeps coming back. the saved choice is per language. if a title has no track in that language, the player falls back to what the file offers. :: where to go next - watching - subtitle preferences

title: Casting
description: Sending playback to a Chromecast or a TV, and controlling it from here.
content: casting the cast button appears in the player when there is something on your network to cast to. casting to a chromecast press the cast button, pick the device, and playback moves there. the app becomes the remote: play, pause, seek, volume, subtitles and audio all still work from the screen in your hand. chapters travel with it, so the chapter bar on the television is the same one you had here. sending to your tv app a television running the nomercy app is also a target. that is not casting in the chromecast sense: the tv plays from the server itself, and the app tells it what to play. the advantage is that the tv does the work, so closing the browser does not stop the film. ::troubleshooting no cast button. nothing castable was found on this network. casting discovery needs the device and the receiver on the same network, and some networks block the discovery traffic between wireless clients. the tv is listed but does not start. it may be asleep. the app asks it to wake, and a device that does not answer is reported rather than silently ignored. volume changes nothing. on a television connected over hdmi, the volume belongs to the television or the amplifier, not to the app. :: where to go next - watching - devices

title: Quality
description: What the quality picker changes, and when the server transcodes.
content: quality the quality button offers auto and whatever rungs the title was encoded at. auto auto follows the connection. it starts where it can and moves up or down as bandwidth allows, so playback keeps going rather than stalling at a quality the line cannot carry. this is the right setting almost always. choosing one yourself pick a rung and the player stays there. useful on a metered connection, where you would rather cap the data than have auto reach for the best. the choice is remembered by height, not by its position in the list, so it survives a title whose ladder differs. when the server transcodes where a browser cannot take a file as it stands, the server converts it while it plays. it happens without asking, and playback starts either way, whatever the library is stored in. a modest machine can struggle to convert a heavy source in real time. where that shows, the answer is on the server side: encode those titles ahead of time. see encoding profiles. ::troubleshooting quality keeps dropping. auto is doing its job on a connection that cannot hold the higher rung. on a home network, check whether the traffic is going out to the internet and back rather than staying local. only one quality is offered. the title was encoded at one, or is being played as it is. which rungs exist comes from the profile it was encoded with: see encoding profiles. :: where to go next - watching - encoding overview

title: Your profile
description: Who you are signed in as, which server you are on, and signing out.
content: your profile the profile screen is the way into everything you can change. on a phone it is a tab; on a desktop it is the menu behind your avatar in the top bar. what is on it you. your name and picture, as your account carries them. the server. which one you are pointed at, and whether it is reachable. switching servers happens here. your account. the way through to display, subtitle and device settings. signing out. ends the session on this device only. your other devices stay signed in. switching servers only when your account can reach more than one. it changes what you browse, without signing you out. where to go next - display - subtitles - devices

title: Display
description: Language, theme, and the small choices about how screens behave.
