content: display everything about how the app looks and behaves on this device. this device device name. what this device is called in your device list. naming it now saves guessing later, when the list has four browsers in it. language. the language the app speaks. it also decides which translated titles and details you get. theme colour scheme. light, dark, or following the system. theme colours. the palette the app uses. colour from artwork. with this on, a title's own artwork tints the screen you are looking at. screensaver how long the app waits before starting its screensaver, or off. playback and browsing fullscreen on play. start playback in fullscreen rather than in the page. open the latest season. open a series on its most recent season rather than the first. backdrops. show the large background images. turning them off makes for a plainer, lighter screen. carousel buttons. draw the row arrows over the artwork instead of beside it. progress colours. colour the progress marks on cards. these are per device, so a phone can be plain and a desktop lavish. where to go next - subtitles - your profile

title: Subtitle style
description: How subtitles look, with a preview while you set it.
content: subtitle style how subtitles are drawn, set once and used everywhere. the screen shows a preview as you change it, so you can see the result instead of imagining it. what you can set font. reithsans, arial, courier new, georgia or verdana. size. as a proportion, so it scales with the screen rather than being fixed to one. text colour and opacity. background colour and opacity. the box behind the words. fully transparent by default. edge style. how the letters are separated from the picture: none, drop shadow, text shadow, raised, depressed or uniform outline. a shadow or an outline is what keeps white text readable over a bright scene. window colour and opacity. the band behind the whole subtitle area, rather than behind the words. where it applies the style is saved on this device and used by the player here. setting it on the phone leaves the television as it was. subtitles that style themselves some subtitles carry their own styling: positioned signs, songs, and anything designed to sit against the picture. those are drawn as their author intended and keep their own look. your settings apply to plain subtitles, which is nearly all dialogue. where to go next - subtitles - display

title: Your devices
description: The devices signed in to your account, and forgetting one.
content: your devices every device you sign in on appears here: phones, browsers, televisions. it is your own list, not the server's. what each row shows the device's name, whether it is online or asleep, and when it was last seen if it is not here now. naming a device when you first sign in on it is what keeps this list readable. see display. forgetting one the button on the right removes a device, after asking once. use it for a browser you will not open again, or a phone you no longer have. forgetting is not permanent: signing in on that device again puts it back. what it does is end its access now. the list updates itself when it changes, so a device removed on one screen disappears on the others without a reload. ::troubleshooting the list is empty. devices appear once they have signed in. a browser that has only ever been signed out is not in it. a device i own says asleep. it is registered and not currently connected. a television with the screen off usually looks like this, and casting to it asks it to wake. :: where to go next - casting - devices for what the server owner sees.

title: The dashboard
description: Where you administer a server you own, and what the overview shows.
content: the dashboard administering a server happens inside the app, under dashboard. it appears if you have the permission for it, on the server you are pointed at. opening the dashboard lands on the system overview, because a page listing what the sidebar already lists would be a stop on the way. the overview cards, each answering one question: the server. its name, version, address and how long it has been up. hardware. what the machine can encode with, from the benchmark. tasks. what the queue is doing. see logs and the queue view for detail. activity. what has happened lately. see activity. resources. processor, memory and disk as they move. this one is live, and appears once the dashboard's live connection is up. getting around the sidebar groups the screens: your content, the system, monitoring, and the advanced settings. each is documented on its own page here. who sees what some screens need only the manage permission. a few, such as plugins and content analysis, are owner-only, because they let code run or put the machine under load. ::troubleshooting no dashboard in the sidebar. your account does not administer this server. the owner grants that in users. the resource card is missing. its live connection is not up. everything else on the page still works, because the rest is fetched rather than streamed. :: where to go next - libraries - users - storage

title: Libraries
description: The dashboard screen for managing libraries, folders and content.
content: libraries the libraries screen in the dashboard is where you create libraries, point them at folders, and add content to them. for what the library types mean and how to choose folders, see library management. this page is about the screen itself. the library list every library, with how many folders each one has. new library creates one. refresh all libraries re-reads metadata for everything, which is rarely what you want; refreshing a single title from its own page is faster. select a library to open its settings. library settings library name and media type. the type decides how file names are read, so changing it on a library that already has content means that content is re-read against a different kind of match. special season display name sets what specials are called in this library. series use "specials" by convention. subtitle download languages picks which languages are fetched for new content. auto-encode files found by scanning controls what happens to files the server discovers in this library's folders. off by default: found files are listed in their original form, and play like anything else. switch it on when you want the whole shelf in the folder's format. it does not affect content you add yourself with add content, which is always encoded. encoding preset becomes available when auto-encode is on. see encoding profiles. changes to metadata and artwork settings apply to content added afterwards. existing titles keep what they have until you refresh them individually. folders a library needs at least one folder. most only ever need one. add new folder opens the picker. it browses the server's disks, not the device you are sitting at, and it can create a folder for you with new folder. each folder has its own encoder profiles, which is what lets one library keep content on two drives with different settings. change storage moves a folder to a different storage driver, for network shares and object storage. adding content add content takes files that already exist somewhere the server can read and brings them into the library, laid out and encoded the way that folder is set up. pick the source folder, pick the destination folder inside the library, tick the files, and add the selection. your source files are only read, never moved or changed. everything added this way is encoded, whatever the auto-encode switch says. rescan re-reads the library's folders and picks up anything new. where to go next - library management for types, folders and presets. - scanning and importing for adding files.

title: Storage
description: The places your server can keep media, and adding one.
content: storage a storage driver is a place your server can read and write. libraries point at a driver, so adding one here is what makes a new location available to them. what you can add local. a path on the server's own machine, or anything mounted into it. nfs. a server and an export, with the protocol version. s3 and compatible. a bucket and region, and an endpoint for anything that speaks the same protocol without being that service. webdav. a url. each row shows the kind and a summary of where it points, so a list of five is readable at a glance. mount it yourself where you can a share the server machine can mount belongs to local, pointed at the mount. mounting is the operating system's job and it does it better: through on linux, a unc path on windows, a volume with or in docker. reach for nfs or s3 or webdav here when that is not available to you, such as object storage or a machine whose mounts you do not control. adding one give it the details and save. credentials are kept in the machine's own credential store rather than beside the settings, and they are updated separately from the rest of the driver. the server's own local storage is there from the start and cannot be removed. probe before saving where the form offers it: a wrong address is much easier to fix while you are looking at it than after a scan has failed. using it a driver on its own does nothing. attach it to a library folder, on libraries. changing which driver a folder uses repoints where the server looks. it moves no files, so the media has to already be at the new location. ::troubleshooting a driver saves but a scan finds nothing. the path is reachable and empty, or points a level above or below the media. browse it from the folder picker to see what the server sees. removing a driver is refused. library folders still use it, and the message says how many. remove them from their libraries first. :: where to go next - libraries - storage

title: Users
description: Inviting someone, and deciding what they may do and see.
content: users who may use your server. people are invited by their nomercy account; no password is created here. inviting someone invite by email address, and choose which libraries they get while you are there. they need a nomercy account with that address. once invited, your server appears in their server list and they sign in with the account they already have. what you can grant access to content. the basic switch. without it, an invited account can sign in and see nothing. optical access. lets them use the disc drive: probe a disc and play from it. manage the server. gives them the dashboard, apart from the parts reserved to the owner. audio transcoding and video transcoding. whether playback that needs converting on the fly is allowed for them. turning these off means they get what plays as it is, and nothing that would put the machine to work. library access either all libraries, or a chosen few. the picker appears when you choose a few. this is what makes a shared server workable: a household member can have everything, and a friend one shelf. removing someone removing takes away their access. nothing of theirs is deleted from disk, and their own account is untouched. the owner one account owns the server, and that does not move. the owner can do everything a manager can, plus the owner-only screens such as plugins. where to go next - users - libraries

title: Devices
description: Every client connected to this server, and tidying the list.
content: devices every device that has signed in to this server, across all its users. your own devices are a separate, smaller list under your devices. what a device shows its name, its kind, who it belongs to, whether it is connected now, and when it was last seen. opening one shows what it has been doing. tidying up remove offline devices clears everything not currently connected, after confirming. it is the usual tidy-up on a server that has collected a year of browsers. clear activity logs drops the recorded activity for devices rather than the devices themselves. removing a device ends its access now. signing in on it again puts it back, so this is a tidy-up rather than a ban. where to go next - your devices - activity - users

title: Specials
description: Building a collection that mixes films and episodes in an order you choose.
content: specials a special is a collection you build: films and episodes, in a deliberate order. it is the grouping no metadata source can give you, such as a viewing order that crosses two series. everyone with access to the server sees it. that is what separates it from a playlist, which is personal. building one give it a name and a description, then add items and put them in order. artwork is yours to set: a poster, a backdrop and a logo. without them a special still works, and looks plainer beside the rest of the library. editing open a special to change its details, its artwork or its running order. rescanning it makes the server check the items are still there. where to go next - specials - playlists

title: Recommendations
description: Suggestions worked out from what your library already holds.
content: recommendations titles your server does not have, suggested from what it does. films, series and anime are worked out separately, because what makes a good suggestion differs. using it open a kind, browse the suggestions, open one to see why it was suggested and what it is. anything you decide to keep is added the way any title is. suggestions are worked out from your library, so they change as it grows. when the list looks thin the diagnostics view explains what the recommender had to work with. a small or one-sided library gives it little to reason from, and the honest answer is usually that rather than a fault. where to go next - libraries - recommendations for the endpoints behind this screen.

title: Ripper
description: Turning a disc into files: identify, choose titles and tracks, then rip.
content: ripper the ripper screen walks a disc from the tray into your library. watching a disc without ripping it is a different, simpler screen; this one is for keeping it. the drives every drive on the machine is listed with what is in it: empty, tray open, or a disc ready. the list keeps itself current, so putting a disc in updates the screen without a refresh. the tray can be opened and closed from here, which saves walking over to the machine. identifying the disc the server probes the disc and proposes what it is. where it is unsure it offers candidates with how confident it is in each, and you pick. nothing is written until you agree. if none of the candidates is right, search for the title yourself and assign it. choosing what to rip a disc holds many titles, most of them menus, trailers and warnings. the main feature is marked, and each title shows its length so a wrong pick is obvious. for the titles you keep, choose the audio and subtitle tracks by language. forced subtitle tracks are marked, since those carry the translated signs rather than the dialogue. where it lands pick the library and the folder, and the encoding profile to use. the default profile is used when you do not choose one. ripping starting a rip queues it. progress shows against the drive, and the screen can be left; the work is on the server, not in the page. ::troubleshooting a disc reports protection. the screen says so rather than failing quietly part way through. no drives listed. the machine has none the server can see. on linux this is usually the service's access to the device. identification finds nothing. search for the title and assign it by hand. a rip with a manual assignment is as good as an automatic one. :: where to go next - discs - encoding profiles - optical media

title: Encoder profiles
description: The profiles that decide how media is encoded, and how to build one.
content: encoder profiles a profile decides what the encoder does with a file. this screen lists them and lets you build your own. the list profiles are shown in a table you can sort and filter: by container, by tag, by whether they are built in, and by searching the name. built-in profiles come with the server. they cannot be edited, which is what makes them safe to fall back to. making your own clone the built-in that is closest and edit the clone. starting from nothing is possible and rarely what you want. clicking a row opens it beside the list, so you can read one without losing your place. setting a default one profile is the default. anything encoded without a specific choice uses it. checking before you commit a profile can be validated, and previewed against a real file. the preview is the honest answer to "will this re-encode or copy this file", which is worth knowing before a library's worth of work is queued. sharing profiles export and import. an import is checked against the publishers this server trusts; accepting an unsigned one is a deliberate choice. where to go next - encoding profiles for what the settings mean. - hardware - encoder profiles for the endpoints.

title: Hardware
description: What this machine can encode with, measured rather than assumed.
content: hardware two things live here: what the server found in the machine, and what it measured that hardware doing. detected hardware every accelerator the server can use, with what each one can encode and decode. a machine with nothing usable says so, and encoding then runs on the processor. the benchmark running the benchmark encodes real work with each combination and records what happened. that is what the server then uses when choosing how to encode. each device shows how many profiles it has been benchmarked with, so a partial picture is visible as a partial picture. the result is kept, so the page is cheap to open. running it again is worth doing after changing hardware or drivers. running the benchmark puts the machine under load for as long as it takes, so it is the owner's call and not something to start while people are watching. ::troubleshooting no hardware detected on a machine that has some. the server needs the driver and access to the device. in a container, the device also has to be passed in. the benchmark finishes with less than you expected. a combination that cannot run is left out rather than reported as slow. the detected-hardware list above says what was available to try. :: where to go next - hardware acceleration - encoder profiles

title: Content analysis
description: Looking inside a file: black bars, bitmap subtitles, speech, and intros.
content: content analysis four jobs that read a file and produce something the player can use. all of them are owner-only, because each puts the machine to work. each one takes a title, found by searching your library rather than by pasting an id. crop detection probes a file for the black bars around the picture, so a film shot wider than the frame can be shown without them. subtitle ocr some subtitles are pictures rather than text: the ones on dvds and blu-rays. ocr reads them into text, which can then be searched, styled and resized. you choose which subtitle stream to read and the language it is in. transcription turns the speech into a subtitle track, for a file with no subtitles at all. it can also translate to english while it goes. progress arrives while it runs, so a long file shows how far in it is rather than sitting silent. intro detection runs across a season, because a repeated opening is only findable by comparing episodes. what it finds becomes the skip button in the player. the screen shows how many episodes were scanned. where the results go all of it lands as content segments and subtitle tracks on the title itself. see content segments. where to go next - watching for the skip button these produce. - subtitles

title: Distribution
description: Extra machines encoding for this server, and what each is doing.
content: distribution encoding can be spread across more than one machine. this screen shows the machines that have joined and the work assigned to them. the screen appears only when distributed encoding is switched on. a single-machine server has nothing to show here and is sent to the system overview instead. what a worker shows cores and threads available. what it can take on. graphics devices and free slots. how many accelerated encodes it can run at once. utilisation. how busy its graphics hardware is now. failures. how many jobs it has failed. a worker that keeps failing is worth looking at rather than waiting on. last seen. workers keep a heartbeat going. one that stops sending it drops out of the list. cooldown. a worker that has just failed is rested before more work goes to it, and the remaining time shows here. the work tasks show as a total and a count of active ones, with which worker each is assigned to. where to go next - distribution workers for the endpoints behind this screen. - tasks and the queue

title: Plugins
description: Installing plugins, answering what they ask for, and turning one off.
content: plugins plugins add capability to your server. only the owner can install one, because installing one is letting code run inside your server. getting one the catalogue lists what your configured repositories offer, with what is already installed marked. install from there, or install a file you have. consent a plugin that asks for more than the ordinary set installs and waits, and the screen says it is waiting on you. read what it asked for, then allow or deny. a plugin that only reads media, supplies details or adds a screen is enabled when you install it. you can review what you granted later, and withdraw it. withdrawing disables the plugin and clears the grants. grants beyond that first decision, a plugin can ask for something specific while it runs, such as one network host. those appear at the top of the screen and are answered one at a time. managing an installed plugin open it to see what it is and what it can do. each can be disabled without uninstalling, which is the right move when you are working out whether it causes something. some changes need the server restarted before they take effect, and the screen says so where that is the case. ::troubleshooting a plugin shows as failed. it could not load. version compatibility is checked before loading, so a plugin built against a different server version is rejected rather than half-loaded. a plugin is installed and does nothing. it may be waiting for your consent. the screen marks that. :: where to go next - plugins overview - repositories and trust

title: Activity
description: What happened on this server, and who did it.
content: activity the activity log answers "what happened here". it is the people-shaped record; the log is the technical one. what is recorded | category | covers | |----------|--------| | auth | signing in and out | | connection | clients connecting and dropping | | playback | what was played, and where | | configuration | settings that changed | | failure | something that went wrong | | encoder | encode jobs starting, finishing or giving up | | library | scans, and files arriving or leaving | | security | addresses the server banned or released by itself | rows can be filtered by category, so "who watched what" and "what the encoder did" are separate views of one list. clearing it rows can be cleared by category, or everything older than a date. that keeps a long-running server's log useful rather than emptying it. privacy this shows what everyone on the server did, so reading it needs the manage permission. somebody with plain access can see their own playback and nothing else. where to go next - logs - devices

title: Logs
description: Reading the server log, filtered down to what you are looking for.
content: logs what the server itself wrote. for a record of what people did, read activity instead. filtering three filters, and using them together is what makes a busy log readable. type. which part of the server: the encoder, the queue, the scanner, and so on. the list comes from the server, so it matches what is actually being written. level. how severe. dropping down to warnings and errors is the fastest way to find something wrong. filter. free text matched in the message. live new lines arrive while the page is open, so a problem you are reproducing shows as you cause it. clearing the log can be cleared from here. it clears what is recorded, not the files the server writes on disk. see logs for where those live. where to go next - logs - activity - diagnostics

title: Live sessions
description: Transcodes running right now, and steering one.
content: live sessions a live session is the server converting a file while somebody watches it. this screen lists the ones running, with a count at the top. what a session shows the quality it is serving, with the resolution and bitrate behind that label, so "1080p" is backed by numbers rather than taken on trust. that is the screen to open when the machine is working hard and you want to know what it is working on. acting on one a session can be ended, moved to a different quality, or moved to a position, by naming its id. ending a session frees the machine. the person watching it will find their player reconnecting, so it is a thing to do knowingly. ::troubleshooting more sessions than people watching. a session that was abandoned rather than closed expires on its own after an idle period. everything is a live session. nothing plays as it is, which usually means the library is encoded in a form the clients cannot take directly. see encoding profiles. :: where to go next - streaming for the endpoints behind this screen. - hardware

title: Notifications
description: What the server has told people, and sending a message yourself.
content: notifications the notifications the server has sent, and a way to send one of your own. sending one choose a recipient, or everyone, then give it a title and a message. this is for telling people something they would otherwise find out by being surprised: the server going down for an hour, a library being reorganised. the list what has been sent, most recent first. opening one shows it in full. the list can be cleared, which removes the record rather than recalling anything. where they arrive wherever the person has notifications enabled: the app, and a phone that has allowed them. a device that was away gets what it missed the next time it connects. where to go next - users - activity

title: Common App Issues
description: Playback failures, login problems, and sync issues.
content: common app issues web app can't reach my server on my home network if you open the web app on the same network as your server and it never connects, your browser is almost certainly blocking the request as a security precaution. this is not a server misconfiguration, and there's nothing to fix on the server. symptoms - playback never starts, and live features the dashboard, live sessions, casting never connect. - the browser console repeatedly logs something like: - in firefox, a "local network access detected" permission banner appears until you allow it. why this happens app.nomercy.tv is served over the public internet. open it from a device on the same network as your server, and dns resolves your server's hostname, something like , straight to its private lan address. browsers treat a request from a public site into a private address as sensitive, and hold it until you grant permission. chrome and edge call this private network access. firefox calls it local network access. it applies to every public site reaching into your lan, not only this one. your server already does its part: it sends on the cors preflight and serves a valid public tls certificate. the piece that's missing is the one-time permission your browser wants from you, not a fix on the server side. this only comes up when you're on the same network as your server. from outside your home network your traffic goes through the server's public tunnel instead of its lan address, so there's no private-network prompt and nothing to allow. fix firefox version 149 and later, rolling out to everyone from firefox 151: accept the local network access prompt when it appears. if you dismissed it, go to settings → privacy & security → permissions → local network access and allow . chrome / edge: allow local network access when prompted. if you missed the prompt, open the site settings for and enable local network access sometimes labeled insecure private network. skip it entirely: the nomercy android app doesn't go through a browser, so this prompt never applies to it. opening the web app from outside your home network avoids it too, since that traffic never touches your server's lan address. firefox reconnects to the server in a rapid loop the console fills with repeated errors ending in , and the app never settles. firefox is the only browser that carries websockets over http/2, so it is the only one that shows this. chrome, edge and the android app connect normally against the same server. fix update your nomercy media server. current versions do not do this, and the loop stops on its own with no browser setting to change.

title: API Documentation
description: Learn everything there is to know about the NoMercy API and integrate NoMercy into your product.
content: ::hero api documentation use the app-web api to drive the browser client: sign in against a server, browse a library, and control playback from your own code. classname: 'lead' ::button url: '/installation', variant: 'text' installation ::icon arrow-right ::

title: MediaServer Overview
description: What the NoMercy MediaServer does, and how it differs from other media servers.
content: mediaserver overview mediaserver is the heart of nomercy. it turns discs and video files you own into a clean, permanent library. the one idea to hold on to it builds you a library. you give it content. it works out what each title is, files it where that title belongs, and names it the same way as everything else on the shelf. playback is a separate question, and it is already answered: the server converts anything a client cannot take directly, while it plays. what is on the shelf never decides whether something plays. two ways to fill a library nomercy can work either way, and the difference matters. import. you pick files or a disc and add them to a library. nomercy lays each title out in the library folder and encodes it with that folder's profile, so the shelf holds one codec rather than whatever each source happened to be. your own file is read, never moved or altered. scan. you point a library at a folder you already have. nomercy reads what is there, works out what each file is, and lists it. the files are left exactly as they are. you can mix them. neither one moves, renames, or deletes your files. which to use mediaserver is an organiser and an archiver. its purpose is to take what you own and turn it into a library that is laid out one way and kept in one format, so it is still yours and still readable years from now. import is that job done properly, and it is the route this documentation follows. a library folder that only ever receives imported titles has one layout and one codec, so there is nothing ambiguous about what is on it. scanning is fully supported and always will be. point it at a collection you have already organised yourself and it reads it, lists it, and plays it, leaving every file untouched. nothing about that path is second best. the two answer different questions. scanning asks the server to present what you already have. importing asks it to build the archive. what happens when you import a title 1. you point nomercy at a disc or a file. 2. it works out which movie or episode it is. 3. it encodes the title with the folder's profile: video, audio tracks, subtitles, chapters and preview thumbnails. 4. the result lands in your library folder, named and filed like everything else there. 5. every client sees it. your source file stays where it was, unchanged. playing back everything in a library plays, imported or scanned. where a client cannot take a file as it stands, the server converts it while it plays. so the codec your library is stored in is a choice about the library, not about playback. see encoding profiles. where to go next - installation guide to install the server. - first-run setup to claim it and link your account. - library management to set up your first library.

title: Installation Guide
description: Complete step-by-step guide for installing NoMercy.
content: installation guide pick the page for your platform below. each one covers the installer for that channel. choose your platform - windows - linux .deb - linux .rpm - linux arch - macos - docker - nas linux packages are published to apt, rpm, and arch repositories; docker images are published to . after installing once the server is running, open the setup page at , or at from another machine, and complete first-run configuration. on a desktop install that page opens by itself. setup links your nomercy account to the server and gets it a secure address. you can create the account during setup if you do not have one. see first-run setup. when it finishes you are taken to the nomercy app, where you create your first library. see library management. what is built | platform | architecture | |----------|--------------| | windows installer | 64-bit intel and amd | | macos installer | intel, and apple silicon through rosetta | | macos standalone binary | intel and apple silicon | | linux packages deb, rpm, arch | 64-bit intel and amd | | docker images | | setup needs an internet connection to link your account and get a certificate. troubleshooting if you encounter installation issues: - ensure port 7626 is available the server also binds a loopback-only health check on 7627 - review the installation logs - consult the faq or open an issue on github

title: First-Run Setup
description: Claim your server and link it to your NoMercy account.
content: first-run setup the first time your server starts it has no account attached, so it opens a setup page and waits for you there. this page walks that once-only step. you can create a nomercy account during setup. opening the setup page what happens depends on where the server runs. on a desktop machine, the server opens the setup page in your browser by itself. the address is . on a headless machine such as a nas, a docker host, or a system service, there is no browser to open. the server prints a code and a link in its terminal output instead, together with a qr code. open the link on any device that has a browser, phone or laptop or another computer, and enter the code. the qr code is a shortcut for phones. both routes reach the same place. you can also just browse to the setup page yourself from another machine on your network. signing in the setup page checks first whether you are already signed in to nomercy in that browser. if you are, it moves straight on and you never see a login screen. if you are not, you get two ways in. sign in on this device. choose login with nomercy. you go to the nomercy sign-in page and come back automatically. sign in on another device. use the code and qr shown on the page. this is the route to take when the machine you are setting up has no convenient browser. both are live at the same time. whichever you finish first is the one that counts. if you do not have an account yet the sign-in screen has a registration link. create your account there and verify your email address, then carry on. setup waits for you. take your time over it. the sign-in code has a short life and setup replaces it with a fresh one while you are still registering. if the code on screen has changed by the time you come back, use the new one. what the server does next once you are signed in, the server sets itself up without further input. 1. it registers itself against your account. 2. it gets its own internet address and dns entry. 3. it requests an ssl certificate so clients can reach it securely. the certificate is the slow part. the page reports progress while it works. do not restart the server during this step. when everything is in place the page shows all done!, tells you your server's address, and opens the nomercy app for you. your new server is waiting there. reaching your server from outside your home inside your own network your server works as soon as setup finishes. for access from elsewhere the server arranges a route by itself. it asks your router to open a port, and if that does not work it tries other routes without involving you. some routers refuse that request or ignore it silently. if yours does, and nothing else gets through, add the port rule on your router yourself. see networking. ::troubleshooting every page of the server says setup is required. setup did not finish. open again and complete it, or use the retry button. this state is expected until setup is done, so it is not a sign that anything is broken. setup ends with "the ssl certificate could not be acquired". choose retry. retrying is safe and is the normal fix. nothing works and the machine has no internet. setup cannot finish offline. signing in and registering both need a connection. once a server has completed setup once, it keeps working on your local network without one. windows asks about the firewall. allow it. the server needs to accept connections from your other devices. :: where to go next - library management to create your first library. - networking if you need access from outside your home.

title: Windows
description: Install NoMercy MediaServer on Windows.
content: windows windows uses a normal installer. nothing else has to be installed first: the server carries everything it needs, including its own .net runtime. install 1. download the installer from the latest release. the file is named . 2. run it and follow the prompts. 3. the server starts when the installer finishes, and opens the setup page in your browser. windows builds are 64-bit intel or amd. allow it through the firewall windows asks about network access the first time the server runs. allow it. if you dismiss that prompt, your other devices cannot reach the server. you can fix it afterwards in windows defender firewall by allowing on private networks. what runs afterwards the server runs in the background and starts with windows. a tray icon gives you start, stop, restart and a link to the logs. if the setup page does not open browse to yourself. if nothing answers there, the server has not started. check the tray icon, and check that nothing else is using port 7626. where to go next - first-run setup to claim the server and link your account.

title: macOS
description: Install NoMercy MediaServer on macOS.
content: macos macos has an installer package, and standalone binaries for people who would rather not use one. both are self-contained. each carries its own .net runtime. install with the package 1. download from the latest release. 2. open it and follow the prompts. 3. the server starts when installation finishes and opens the setup page in your browser. apple silicon the installer package is built for intel macs. it runs on apple silicon through rosetta. if you would rather run natively, take the standalone binary from the same release and run it directly. if macos blocks it macos may refuse to open a download from outside the app store. open system settings, go to privacy & security, and choose open anyway next to the blocked item. if the setup page does not open browse to yourself. where to go next - first-run setup to claim the server and link your account.

title: Linux (Debian and Ubuntu)
description: Install NoMercy MediaServer from the apt repository.
content: linux debian and ubuntu debian and ubuntu install from the nomercy apt repository, so updates arrive with the rest of your system updates. packages are built for 64-bit intel and amd. add the repository and install the package is self-contained. it carries its own .net runtime. updating complete setup a server installed this way runs as a service, so there is no browser to open and no terminal output to watch. browse to from any machine on your network. if you would rather work from the terminal, shows the setup link and the sign-in code. where to go next - first-run setup to claim the server and link your account.

title: Linux (Fedora, RHEL and CentOS)
description: Install NoMercy MediaServer from the rpm repository.
content: linux fedora, rhel and centos fedora, rhel and centos install from the nomercy rpm repository, so updates arrive with the rest of your system updates. packages are built for 64-bit intel and amd. add the repository and install the package is self-contained. it carries its own .net runtime. updating complete setup a server installed this way runs as a service, so there is no browser to open and no terminal output to watch. browse to from any machine on your network. if you would rather work from the terminal, shows the setup link and the sign-in code. where to go next - first-run setup to claim the server and link your account.

title: Linux (Arch)
description: Install NoMercy MediaServer from the Arch repository.
content: linux arch arch and its derivatives install from the nomercy pacman repository, so updates arrive with the rest of your system updates. packages are built for x8664. add the repository and install the signing key has to be added and locally signed before pacman will accept the packages, which is what the two lines do. the package is self-contained. it carries its own .net runtime. updating complete setup a server installed this way runs as a service, so there is no browser to open and no terminal output to watch. browse to from any machine on your network. if you would rather work from the terminal, shows the setup link and the sign-in code. where to go next - first-run setup to claim the server and link your account.

title: Docker
description: Run NoMercy MediaServer in Docker.
content: docker official images are published to . images are built for . pick a variant there is one image per hardware-acceleration target. pick the one that matches the machine. | variant | for | |---------|-----| | | no gpu acceleration | | | nvidia gpu | | | intel quick sync | | | amd gpu | encoding works on any of them. a gpu variant makes it faster on hardware that supports it. get the compose file the compose files ship with each release. download the one for your variant from the latest release. open it and edit it before you start anything. two things must be set, and a few more can be. set your media paths the file ships with placeholder mounts: replace the left side of each with a real path on your machine. keep the right side as it is, and keep : the server writes thumbnails and encoded titles back into these locations. remember the right-hand paths. inside nomercy your libraries live at , and , because that is what the container sees. typing the host path into nomercy finds nothing. media on a nas let compose mount the share, rather than the server. a volume with or is handled by the host kernel, and the container sees an ordinary directory. mount that volume where the placeholders above are, then point a local driver at it inside nomercy. this is faster than reaching the same share through nomercy's own nfs or smb driver, which does the protocol work inside the server process. set your host address the container needs the lan address of the machine it runs on, in . without it the server advertises an address your other devices cannot reach. optional settings | setting | default | change it when | |---------|---------|----------------| | | | you want timestamps in local time | | / | | your media is owned by a different user | | | detected | detection picks the wrong public address | | | | port 7626 is taken | | | | your router maps a different outside port | | | | you are chasing a problem and want more detail | the last four ship commented out. uncomment the ones you need. a volume holds the server's own database and settings. leave it alone; it is what makes your server keep its identity across restarts. start it complete setup browse to . the container log also prints a sign-in code and a link you can use from another device: where to go next - first-run setup to claim the server and link your account.

title: NAS
description: Run NoMercy MediaServer on a NAS.
content: nas a nas runs nomercy through docker. synology, qnap, unraid and truenas all provide a way to run a container, and nomercy is a normal container. read the docker page first. this page covers what is different on a nas. check the processor first images are built for only. many nas units, especially smaller synology and qnap models, run an arm processor. check your model's specification before going further. paths inside the container your nas presents your media at a path like . the container sees whatever path you mount it to. every path you enter in nomercy afterwards is the path inside the container. if you mount to , then in nomercy your library folder is under . this trips up almost everyone once. a nas holds its media locally, so mount the volume into the container and use a local driver in nomercy. the nfs and smb drivers are for reaching a share the machine cannot mount, which is not the case here. permissions the container needs to read your media, and it needs to write into the library folders you give it. if a scan finds nothing, or importing fails immediately, check the ownership of those folders on the nas before looking anywhere else. completing setup there is no browser on the nas. browse to from your computer. the container log also prints a sign-in code and a link you can open on your phone. where to go next - docker for the compose files and variants. - first-run setup to claim the server and link your account.

title: Library Management
description: Create libraries, choose the right type, and pick where your media lives.
content: library management a library is a shelf. it has a type, one or more folders on disk, and rules about what happens to content that arrives in it. most setups need three or four libraries and nothing more. create a library open the dashboard and go to libraries, then choose new library. each library needs three things. 1. a type the type is the most important choice on the page. it decides how nomercy reads file names and what it matches them against. | type | holds | what it looks like on disk | |------|-------|----------------------------| | movies | films | | | tv shows | episodic series | | | music | albums and tracks | | a film gets one folder. a series gets a folder, and inside it one folder per episode, named with the season and episode number. there are no season folders. music nests by first letter, then artist, then album. films and series are read differently, so put content in a library of the right type. a film in a tv shows library is read as if it were an episode, and matches badly or not at all. fixing that afterwards is more work than choosing correctly now. nomercy builds these folders itself for anything you import. you only need the shape when you point a library at files you already have. anime anime is a tv shows library scoped to anime. same shape, same folder depth, and the episodes are matched against themoviedb exactly as any other series is. two things change when you scope a library to anime. it reads absolute episode numbering, so a file named is understood as episode 1109 rather than nonsense. it files newly imported shows correctly, by checking anime sources at import to decide whether a series belongs in your anime library or your tv shows one. an anime film is still a film, so it goes in a movies library. 2. a folder choose add folder. the picker opens. the picker browses the disks of the machine running the server, not the device you are sitting at. if your server runs on a different computer, you are looking at that computer's drives. you can make the folder here. browse to where you want your media to live, choose new folder, name it, and select it. one folder per library keeps things simple. you can add more later if your media is spread across drives. 3. an encoding preset every folder gets a preset. it decides the codec everything imported into that folder is stored in, and how many quality steps are produced. this is the choice that makes a library uniform. titles arrive from twenty different sources; the preset is what makes the shelf hold one format instead of twenty. a new folder is given the standard preset automatically, so you can skip this and come back to it. the presets, what each one produces, and when to pick something other than the standard one are covered in encoding profiles. two ways content arrives this is worth understanding before you add anything, because the two routes behave differently. you add it, with add content. nomercy encodes each file using the library's preset and writes the result into the library folder. your original file is read, never moved or altered. the server finds it, by scanning. when a library folder already holds files, or files appear in it later, the server reads them and lists them. whether those are also encoded is controlled by the auto-encode files found by scanning switch in the library's settings. it is off by default, so found files are listed in their original form. which setup to use mediaserver is an organiser and an archiver. both setups below are supported, and they answer different questions: one presents a collection you have already organised, the other builds the archive for you. the recommended setup is one empty folder per library, filled only through add content. everything on the shelf is then laid out the same way and stored in the one codec the folder's profile produces. nothing on the shelf is ambiguous. you can also point a library at a folder you already have. the server scans it and lists what it finds. this is quicker to set up and suits a collection already organised the way you want it. your files stay exactly where they are and are not modified, and they play like anything else in the library. both work. mixing them in one folder makes it harder to reason about what is on the shelf, so pick one per library. ::troubleshooting the library stays empty after adding content. encoding a title takes time. check the task list on the dashboard to see the work queued and running. a film ended up as an episode, or was not recognised. check the library's type first. that is the usual cause. the picker does not show the drive i expect. it shows the server machine's drives. a drive attached to your laptop is not visible to a server running elsewhere. network shares have to be mounted on the server machine before they appear. :: where to go next - discs to rip a dvd or blu-ray. - scanning and importing for files you already have. - encoding to understand what a preset does.

title: Storage
description: Point NoMercy at disks, network shares and object storage.
content: storage your media does not have to live on the server's own disk. a storage driver tells the server how to reach somewhere else, and library folders then sit on top of it. only the server owner can add or change storage. what you can connect | type | for | |------|-----| | local | a disk on the server machine, or a path the machine already has mounted | | nfs | an nfs export, typically a nas | | s3 | amazon s3 or anything that speaks the s3 protocol | | r2 | cloudflare r2 | | webdav | a webdav server | a windows network share is reached through the local type, using its unc path. mount it yourself where you can if your operating system can mount the share, mount it there and use the local type pointed at the mount. that is the faster route, and it is the one to reach for first. a share mounted by the system is handled by the kernel, with its own caching and read-ahead. a share reached through the nfs or smb driver is handled inside the server process instead, which is more work for the same bytes. linux. add the share to so it mounts at boot, then point a local driver at the mount point. windows. point a local driver straight at the unc path, or map the share and use that. macos. mount the share and point a local driver at it under . docker. compose can create a volume that speaks nfs or smb itself, and the container then sees an ordinary directory. mount that volume into the container and point a local driver at it. preferring this over the in-server drivers is the same choice for the same reason. the nfs, smb, s3, r2 and webdav drivers are there for what the system cannot mount: object storage, a webdav host, or a machine where you have no control over mounts. they work, and they are the second choice when the first is available. adding storage go to storage in the dashboard and add a driver. each type asks for what it needs. local wants a root path, for example or . nfs wants the server address and the export. version defaults to 3, and you can set the user and group ids the server should present. nfs offers a connection test before you save, which is worth using: a wrong export path is otherwise a mystery later. s3 wants the bucket and region, optionally a prefix and a custom endpoint. r2 is the same, and its endpoint is required. webdav wants the url, and optionally a timeout. keys and secrets for s3 and r2 are stored separately from the driver's settings and are never sent back out of the server, so the dashboard shows only whether credentials are configured. how storage and libraries fit together a driver says where, a library folder says which part of it. one driver can carry many library folders. a single nas export can hold your films, tv shows and music folders, each pointing at a different path inside it. that is why adding storage is a separate step from adding a folder. you describe the location once, then use it as often as you like. changing a folder's storage a library folder has a change storage action. it repoints that folder at a different driver or a different path inside the same one. it changes where the server looks. it does not move any files. nothing is copied and nothing is deleted. if you are moving media between disks, move it yourself first, then repoint the folder to match and rescan. remote storage and encoding encoding a title needs a real file on disk, so the server fetches what it needs to a local working area, does the work, and writes the result back. it cleans up after itself. this works, and it means the speed of your network is part of the speed of your encoding. media on a fast local disk prepares faster than the same media over webdav. ::troubleshooting a scan finds nothing after connecting storage. check the path inside the driver. a driver that connects but points one directory too high or too low finds nothing, and that looks the same from the outside. a scan fails after working for weeks. the backend is most likely unreachable: a nas asleep, an export unmounted, a credential expired. the failure is recorded against the scan task with the reason the storage itself gave. everything is slow over a network share. encoding a title moves the whole file across and back. that is expected. a local disk is faster, and encoding is where you notice it most. slower through the nfs or smb driver than it should be. mount the share with the operating system and point a local driver at the mount instead. the kernel does that work better than the server can from inside its own process. :: where to go next - library management to point a library at your new storage.

title: How storage works
description: Drivers, scopes and the path contract that sits between the server and your disks.
content: how storage works your media can live on the machine's own disk, on a nas, or in a bucket. the rest of the server does not know which, and that is deliberate. this page explains the piece that makes it true. read storage first if you only want to add a location. the shape of it three layers, each with one job. the driver talks to one kind of backend. local disk, nfs, smb, s3 and anything s3-compatible, webdav. it knows about mount roots, bucket prefixes and base urls, and nothing else in the server does. the scope is a driver plus a path inside it. a library folder gets its own scope, so the folder is the whole world as far as that code is concerned. the facade is what the server actually calls: read, write, list, move, exists. every call is against a scope. adding a backend means writing a driver. no feature has to learn about it, because no feature ever asked what kind of storage it was using. why the local driver is the fast one the local driver does the least. it hands paths to the operating system and the kernel does the rest: caching, read-ahead, retries, and the protocol itself if the path is a mount. the nfs, smb, s3 and webdav drivers speak their protocol inside the server process instead. that is more work for the same bytes. so a share the system can mount should be mounted by the system, with a local driver pointed at the mount. the protocol drivers earn their place where that is impossible: object storage, a webdav host, or a machine whose mounts you do not control. see storage for how to set that up on each platform. the path contract six rules hold this together. they are worth knowing because they explain the errors you will see if something is set up wrong. paths are relative to their scope. code inside a library folder asks for , never for . the driver adds its own root. separators are forward slashes. backslashes are accepted and normalised, on every platform. an empty path means the root of the scope. that is what lets the dashboard browse a location from its top. absolute paths are rejected. a path already resolved to a real disk location means something bypassed the abstraction, so it is refused rather than obeyed. and null bytes are rejected structurally, before any backend is touched. this is the check that matters: it is what stops a crafted path reaching outside the folder it was given. the driver owns translation. local joins with the os root, nfs prepends the export, s3 prepends the bucket prefix, webdav prepends the base url. none of that is visible above the driver. two facades, on purpose most code uses the scoped facade and can only see inside its own folder. the dashboard's folder picker cannot work that way, because its whole job is to browse places that are not a library yet. it uses a lower-level backend that has no scope, and it is the only thing that does. that split is why a plugin cannot read your documents folder by asking nicely: it is handed a scope, and a scope has no way to express "somewhere else". tools that need a real path ffmpeg is a separate program. it cannot be handed an abstraction, so it needs an actual path on disk. for local storage that is simply the file. for a remote backend the server takes out a short lease: the file is staged locally, the tool is pointed at the staged copy, and the copy is cleaned up when the lease ends. this is why encoding from a network share is slower than encoding from a local disk. the bytes have to come across, and the result has to go back. folders that share a location several library folders often live on one disk or one share. the server works out that they share an endpoint, and groups them under a single driver rooted at the deepest directory they have in common. each folder then keeps its own path inside that driver. folders on genuinely different endpoints are never merged, however similar their paths look. the effect is one connection and one set of credentials for a share, rather than one per library folder on it. credentials a driver stores where to connect, not what to connect with. credentials are held in the machine's credential store and referenced by name, and they are updated on their own route rather than as part of the driver's settings. removing a driver removes its stored credentials with it. where to go next - storage to add a location. - how encoding works - libraries

title: Networking
description: How your server becomes reachable, and what to do when it is not.
content: networking your server needs to be reachable by your own devices. on your home network that works straight away. from outside, something has to let traffic in, and the server tries to arrange that by itself. the port the server listens on port 7626, and uses the same number on the outside by default. you can change either with the and options. it also opens 7627 for its own health checks. that one is loopback only, so nothing outside the machine can reach it, and it never needs a rule. how the server gets itself reachable setup does this without asking you anything. in order, it tries to: 1. open a port on your router. the server asks the router directly, using upnp, and then checks from the outside whether the port really answers. a router that accepts the request but does not actually forward anything is common, which is why the server verifies instead of trusting the reply. 2. connect through your router without a rule. if the port is closed, the server tries to establish a path anyway by coordinating with a helper server. 3. use a tunnel. as a last resort the server routes traffic through a tunnel, which works even when your router allows nothing inbound. if a tunnel has already been assigned to your server, that is tried first instead. when none of them work, the server stays reachable on your own network only, and keeps retrying in the background with growing gaps between attempts. adding the rule yourself some routers have upnp switched off, and some ignore the request without saying so. if your server works at home but not away from home, add the rule by hand in your router's admin page. forward external port 7626 to internal port 7626 on the machine running the server, for both tcp and udp. both, because the server speaks http/1.1 over tcp and http/3 over udp. the automatic mapping the server makes for itself creates both, so a hand-written rule should match it. a tcp-only rule still connects. clients that could have used http/3 fall back to the slower route. give the server machine a fixed address on your network while you are in there. your rule points at one address, and a router is free to hand that address to a different device later. ::troubleshooting it works at home, not away from home. nothing established an outside route. add the port rule above. it stopped working after a router restart or a power cut, and i added the rule by hand. the router most likely gave the server machine a different local address, so your rule now points somewhere else. give that machine a fixed address and update the rule. the server notices address changes and re-establishes its own route; a rule you wrote by hand is the part that cannot follow. nothing reaches the server at all, even at home. check the machine's firewall. on windows the prompt appears the first time the server runs and has to be allowed. :: where to go next - first-run setup if you have not claimed your server yet. - configuration for the rest of the server settings.

title: MediaServer Configuration
description: How to configure NoMercy MediaServer using startup flags, environment variables, and the dashboard.
content: where settings live settings are controlled in two places, and both are outside the filesystem: - startup flags or environment variables — port, ip address, log level, and a few launch-time options - dashboard — everything else: libraries, users, encoder settings, and general preferences open after the server starts to reach the dashboard. environment variables every flag has a matching environment variable. environment variables are applied when the corresponding flag is not passed. this is the primary way to configure docker deployments. | variable | equivalent flag | example | |:--|:--|:--| | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | | --- docker: the hostip requirement when running in docker, the container cannot auto-detect your host machine's lan ip. you must supply it via the environment variable, which the provided compose files map from a shell variable. the compose file contains: if you skip this step, the server starts but clients on other devices may not be able to discover or connect to it. you can also hard-code the value directly in the compose file instead of using the shell variable. for gpu-accelerated transcoding, use the matching compose variant: --- adding libraries via the web ui after first login, add your media libraries through the web dashboard. navigate to settings > libraries, then click add library. choose the library type movies, tv shows, or music, give it a name, and select the folder path where your media files live. the server will begin scanning immediately. library paths must be accessible to the server process. for docker, this means the folder must be mounted as a volume in your compose file. the provided compose template includes commented-out volume entries under , , and — uncomment and adjust those paths to match your actual media locations before starting the container. --- port forwarding to access your server from outside your home network, forward port or whichever port you configured on your router to your server's lan ip. once a certificate is issued during first-run setup, the server uses https automatically. --- next steps - mediaserver overview - return to overview - installation guide - installation reference

title: Users
description: Share your server with other people and control what they can reach.
content: users a media server is usually for a household rather than one person. this page covers inviting people and deciding what each of them can do. inviting someone open the dashboard, go to users, and choose to invite. you need their email address, and you can pick which libraries they get while you are there. the invitation goes to that email. they accept it with a nomercy account, creating one if they do not have one, and your server picks them up shortly afterwards. you are inviting an account, not creating one. their account is theirs, works on their own devices, and you never handle their password. who can do what access is a set of switches per person rather than a single rank. | setting | gives them | |---------|------------| | allowed | access to content at all | | manage | the dashboard, so they can administer the server | | optical access | use of a disc in the drive: browsing and watching it | | transcoding | whether the server may convert for their device while they watch | beneath those, each person has a list of libraries they can see. you can give someone everything, or hand a child an anime library and nothing else. the owner one account owns the server: yours. that is fixed, and the owner cannot be removed. only the owner can add people, remove people, and grant someone the ability to manage the server. someone with manage can run the dashboard day to day but cannot promote anyone else, which keeps administration from spreading by accident. nobody can edit their own permissions, including you. this is deliberate: it means a mistake cannot lock you out of your own server. optical access, separately access to a disc in the drive is its own switch because it means something different from library access. it lets a person browse and watch what is in the drive. it does not let them rip, eject, or change how ripping works, which stay with the people who manage the server. removing someone remove them from the users screen. their access ends: they stop being able to reach your content and your libraries stop appearing for them. removal ends access to your server. it does not touch their nomercy account, which is theirs and unaffected. one account, one person there are no separate profiles inside an account. each person gets their own account, and their watch progress, preferences and devices are their own. that is a deliberate difference from services where a household shares one login and picks a face at the start. here everyone signs in as themselves, on their own devices, and nobody resumes into someone else's episode. ::troubleshooting they accepted the invitation but do not see the server. your server takes a short while to pick up the change. if it persists, confirm they signed in with the same email you invited. they can sign in but see nothing. check their library list. someone with access to no libraries has an empty home screen rather than an error. they cannot play anything on one device. check their transcoding settings. a device that needs conversion cannot play anything if conversion is switched off for that person. :: where to go next - library management to set up the libraries you are sharing.

title: Blocking Abusive Traffic
description: How the server detects vulnerability scanners, bans them automatically, and publishes a deny-list your firewall can consume.
content: blocking abusive traffic any server reachable from the internet gets scanned. within minutes of a new hostname appearing in the public certificate transparency logs, automated tools start asking it for wordpress admin pages, files and php shells. none of that exists on a nomercy server, so every one of those requests is someone checking whether you are worth attacking. the server watches for that pattern and bans the address it comes from. offences accumulate inside a rolling window. crossing the threshold produces a ban, and the ban expires on its own. come back later and the next one lasts longer. it is the same shape as fail2ban, running inside the server rather than beside it. so it works whether you are reached through a cloudflare tunnel or a port forward on your router. what counts as an offence two things are treated as evidence. the first is a request for a path that belongs to software this server does not run. a request ending in , or containing , , , or , is scored heavily. no nomercy client, on any platform, ever asks for those. the second is a request for a path that never matched anything, from a caller who is not signed in. that is scored lightly, because a single one of those means very little on its own. two things are deliberately not offences, because getting either wrong would lock out real people: - a rejected request that did match a real endpoint. a client holding an expired token hammers the api with failures and none of them count, so nobody bans themselves by leaving a tab open over the weekend. - a missing static file. browsers ask for stale bundles and old icons after every deploy, and those misses are ignored entirely. addresses on your own network are never scored at all. that covers loopback, the private ranges , , , carrier-grade nat and ipv6 link-local and unique-local addresses. settings everything is in the dashboard under settings > security. there is nothing to put in a config file and no environment variable to set. | setting | default | what it does | |:--|:--|:--| | enabled | on | turns detection and enforcement off entirely when unchecked | | offence threshold | | score that triggers a ban. a known exploit path scores , an anonymous request that matched no route scores | | window | minutes | how long an offence stays on the tally | | ban length | minutes | length of a first ban. each repeat doubles it | | longest ban | days | ceiling the doubling never passes | | allowlist | empty | addresses and cidr ranges that are never scored | with the defaults, two exploit-path requests inside ten minutes are enough. ten anonymous requests for paths that do not exist are also enough. a scanner reaches either in seconds; a person browsing your library reaches neither. the allowlist takes a comma separated list of addresses and ranges, for example . use it for an office or a vpn exit you connect from, not for your lan, which is already exempt. seeing and lifting bans settings > security lists every active ban with the address, why it was banned, the last path it asked for, how many offences it racked up, and when the ban lifts. every ban has an undo button next to it. you can also ban an address by hand from the same screen. the server refuses to ban anything on your own network, so a slip of the keyboard cannot cut you off from your own dashboard. ::callout if you ever lock yourself out, the ban only affects the network path it came in on. reach the server on its lan address and the dashboard opens normally, because addresses on your own network are never banned. :: feeding the list to pfsense when the server is reached through a cloudflare tunnel, cloudflare is already blocking most of this traffic before it ever reaches your machine. when you use the regular port forwarding option instead, there is nothing in front of the server, so your firewall is the only place a bad address can be stopped before it costs you bandwidth. the server publishes its active bans as a plain text list, one address per line, at a url that only you know. pfblockerng on pfsense can pull that url on a schedule. the whole setup is one url, pasted once, and the firewall holds no credential of yours or ours. copy the url from settings > security, then in pfsense: 1. go to firewall > pfblockerng > ipv4 and press add. 2. give the alias a name, for example , and set list action to . 3. under ipv4 source definitions, paste the url, set format to and state to . 4. set update frequency to . 5. save, then go to update, choose force > reload, and run it. pfblockerng will now pick up new bans on its own schedule and drop expired ones when they leave the list. if the url ever leaks, press rotate on the same settings screen. the old url stops working immediately, so update it in pfblockerng afterwards. ::callout the list contains addresses that attacked you, which is information worth keeping private. that is why the url carries a secret token. treat it like a password and do not post it anywhere public. :: related - networking - port forwarding and tunnel setup - configuration - startup flags and the web ui

title: Discs (DVD and Blu-ray)
description: Rip a DVD or Blu-ray you own into your NoMercy library.
content: discs dvd and blu-ray the ripper reads a disc in your server's drive and adds it to a library. before you start the drive has to be attached to the machine running the server. a drive in your laptop is not visible to a server running on another machine. you also need a library to put the result in. see library management. rip a disc 1. put the disc in the server's drive. 2. open the dashboard and go to ripper. 3. the drive appears in the list on the left. when the disc has been read, it shows disc ready. 4. select the drive. the disc is scanned, and you get its name, its length, and the list of titles on it. 5. check the identification panel. if nomercy matched the wrong film, correct it here. 6. choose rip disc. progress appears as a task card. you can keep working while it runs. when it finishes, the title shows up on your home screen. fixing a wrong match correct the match before you start the rip, not after. the match decides the artwork, the title, and where the result is filed. discs with generic volume labels are the usual cause. a label like gives the matcher nothing to work with. ::troubleshooting the drive is not in the list. the drive has to be on the server machine. if it is, use refresh. the disc never reaches "disc ready". the drive may not be able to read that disc type. some drives read dvds but not blu-rays. try the disc in another player to rule out damage. the wrong film was matched. fix it in the identification panel before ripping. :: where to go next - scanning and importing for video files you already have. - library management to add another library.

title: Adding and scanning files
description: Add video files you already have, and understand what scanning does.
content: adding and scanning files you have files already: things you ripped before, or downloads of content you own. this page covers getting them into a library. there are two routes and they do different things. read library management first if you have not. add content this is the route that files a title onto the shelf for you and stores it in the library's format. 1. open the dashboard and go to libraries, then open the library you want. 2. choose add content. 3. source folder: type or browse to where your files are. this is a path on the server machine, or a share the server can reach. 4. destination folder: pick the library folder the results should go into. 5. tick the files you want. there is a select all if you want the lot. 6. choose add selection. nomercy queues one job per file. each is identified, encoded with the library's preset, and written into the destination folder under the name and layout the rest of the shelf uses. your source files are only read. they are not moved, renamed or deleted. when you are happy with the result you can remove them yourself. every file added this way is encoded, whatever the library's auto-encode switch is set to. choosing files by hand is treated as asking for them to be brought into the library's format. scanning the other route is to let the server find files itself. when you add a folder that already holds media, the server scans it and lists what it finds. it does the same for files that appear in a library folder afterwards. scanned files are listed in their original form. they are not converted unless you switch on auto-encode files found by scanning in the library's settings. they play like anything else in the library. the server converts whatever a client cannot take directly, while it plays. the trade is a shelf holding whatever format each file happened to arrive in, rather than the one your library's preset produces. getting matched correctly names matter. nomercy works out what a file is from its name and the folder around it. these match reliably: release-style names usually work too, because the year and the episode numbering are still in there. what causes trouble: - no year on a film with a common title. - a folder name that disagrees with the file name inside it. - episode numbering the name does not actually contain. you can correct a wrong match afterwards from the title's page. ::troubleshooting nothing appears after adding. check the task list on the dashboard. encoding a title takes real time and several may be queued behind each other. the files are on my laptop, not the server. move them to the server first, or share the folder and mount it on the server machine. the server can only read paths it can see. old formats take much longer. an avi or a ripped dvd folder has to be converted rather than repackaged. that is expected, and it only happens once. everything matched the wrong thing. check the library's type before anything else. films in a tv shows library are read as episodes. :: where to go next - discs for dvds and blu-rays. - metadata for fixing a wrong match.

title: Metadata and matching
description: How titles are identified, and how to correct a wrong match.
content: metadata and matching every title in your library is matched against themoviedb to get its name, artwork, cast, and episode list. this page covers how that match is made and what to do when it is wrong. how a match is made the server works from the file name and the folder around it. it pulls out a title, a year, and for series a season and episode number, then searches for that. the library's type decides what it searches. a movies library looks for films. a tv shows library looks for series. a library scoped to anime also searches themoviedb for series, and additionally reads absolute episode numbering. this is why the type matters so much. see library management. naming that matches reliably for films, the title and the year: for series, the series folder, a season
