folder, and episode numbering in the file: release-style names generally work too, because the year and the episode numbers survive in them. what causes a wrong match a missing year on a common title. several films share a name. without a year the server picks one, and it may not be yours. a misleading year. a year in the name that is not the release year sends the search somewhere else entirely. a folder that disagrees with the file. when the folder says one film and the file says another, one of them wins and it may not be the one you meant. the wrong library type. a film in a tv shows library is read as an episode of something. correcting a match open the title in the dashboard and choose to change the match. search for the correct title and select it. for discs, correct the match in the ripper before you start ripping. the match decides where the result is filed, so fixing it first saves redoing the rip. forcing a specific match when a title refuses to match correctly, put its themoviedb id in the filename. the id is the number in that title's themoviedb address. put it on the video file's own name. a folder carrying the id does not count. for a film, use the movie id. this pins the film exactly and no searching happens at all. for an episode, use the id of the series. the series is then fixed, and the episode is taken from the season and episode numbers in the filename. both skip the title search, which is where wrong matches come from. for an episode the still has to be right, because themoviedb reaches an episode through its series rather than by an id of its own. refreshing metadata artwork and descriptions are fetched once when a title is added. if a title was added before its artwork existed online, refresh its metadata from its page in the dashboard. changing a library's metadata settings does not retroactively update titles already in it. where to go next - scanning and importing for adding files. - library management for library types.

title: Specials
description: Build your own collections from films and episodes.
content: specials a special is a collection you build yourself. it holds films and episodes together, in an order you choose, and appears in the app as its own thing to watch. this is not the same as a show's specials season. that is covered at the bottom of this page, because the two share a word and nothing else. what you can put in one films and episodes, mixed freely, in any order. that mixing is the point. a run through a franchise can put the films between the episodes where they actually belong. a themed collection can pull one episode from each of six different shows. creating one go to specials in the dashboard and create one. give it a title, and artwork if you want it to look right on the home screen: a poster, a backdrop and a logo. then use the playlist editor to add films and episodes and drag them into order. watching one a special appears in the app like any other title. playing it plays its items in the order you set, one after the next. your position is remembered, so a long collection can be watched across several evenings. sharing specials belong to the server, so everyone who can reach the server can see them. people can like a special and add it to their watch list, and that part is per person. removing one delete it from the dashboard. deleting a special removes the collection only. the films and episodes in it are untouched and stay in their libraries. a show's specials season separately from all of this, tv shows often have a season 0 holding pilots, recaps and holiday episodes. nomercy calls that season specials by default, and you can change what it is called per library from the library's settings. that setting only renames a season in a show. it has no connection to the collections described above. where to go next - library management - metadata and matching

title: Encoding overview
description: What the server does to a title when you add it, and why.
content: encoding overview when you import a title, the server encodes it with the library folder's profile. this page explains what that produces and when it happens. why encode anything for one reason: so the library is uniform. your content arrives from everywhere. a disc, a file from years ago, a file from last week. left alone, the shelf holds a different format for every source it came from. encoding on import means the whole library is stored in the codec you chose, whichever one that is. playback is not part of this. the server converts anything a client cannot take directly, while it plays, so what is on the shelf never decides whether something plays. when the machine is the reason converting while someone watches is real work, and a heavy source is heavy work. a 4k dolby atmos remux asks more of a machine than a small server or a nas can manage in real time. encoding that title once, up front, into something the machine can send as it is, moves the work off playback entirely. the same goes for a ladder: several bitrates written ahead of time, so a client picks a step it can take instead of asking the server to make one. this is a decision about your hardware, not about your library. a machine that keeps up needs neither. what encoding produces this depends on the preset the library folder uses, and the presets differ a lot. see encoding profiles. every preset produces the audio tracks, subtitles as separate files including ones that were images in the original, chapter markers, and preview thumbnails for the seek bar. what differs is the video. a streaming preset writes the video at several sizes, so a phone on mobile data and a tv on the lan each get something sensible. the output is a folder of parts rather than one file, which is what makes seeking and quality switching instant. an archive or single-file preset writes one file at the source resolution. a remux preset copies the video across untouched and only changes the container. when it happens content you add with add content is always encoded. choosing files by hand is treated as asking for them to be brought into the library's format, whatever else the library is set to. content the server finds by scanning is not, unless you switch on auto-encode files found by scanning in the library's settings. found files are listed as they are, and are part of the library either way. discs are always encoded, because a disc holds a structure of titles and streams rather than a file. how long it takes longer than copying, shorter than you fear, and it happens once per title. speed depends mostly on whether the machine has a gpu the server can use. the docker images come in variants for nvidia, intel and amd hardware for exactly this reason. work is queued, so adding thirty films at once is fine. they are processed in order and you can watch the queue on the dashboard. where to go next - encoding profiles to choose what the output looks like. - library management to set a preset on a library.

title: Encoding profiles
description: The built-in presets and how to pick one.
content: encoding profiles a preset is the format your library is kept in: which video codec, which audio, how many quality steps, and which container. every library folder has one, and everything imported into that folder is stored the way it says. that is the whole point of it. pick the one you want your collection to be in and the shelf becomes one thing instead of an accumulation. every preset here plays. the server converts anything a client cannot take directly, while it plays, so this choice is about the library, never about whether something works. the exception is the machine itself. converting a 4k dolby atmos source in real time asks a lot, and a small server or a nas may not keep up. encoding those titles into something it can send as they are, or into a ladder of bitrates a client can pick from, moves that work off playback. see encoding overview. the default h.264 streaming universal is the default. it produces a full h.264 ladder from 144p up to 2160p. streaming presets these produce a ladder of quality steps, which is what lets a client switch quality mid-play without stalling. | preset | keeps the library as | |--------|----------| | h.264 streaming universal | h.264. the default. | | hevc streaming premium | hevc. roughly half the bitrate for the same picture. | | av1 streaming efficient | av1. the cheapest bitrate per step, and the slowest to produce. | | dash streaming universal | mpeg-dash rather than hls. | there are also hdr and tone-mapped ladders for hdr sources. fixed-resolution presets the ladders above adapt to each source. these pin every title in a library to one resolution instead, which suits a library where you want everything to land in the same shape. height clamps to the source, so a lower-resolution episode is never stretched to meet the name. | preset | what it does | |--------|--------------| | anime 1080p hevc 10-bit | hevc 10-bit at 1080p, tuned for animation. flat colour and hard line art get the bitrate that the default tuning spends on film grain. | | 1080p hevc 10-bit | hevc 10-bit 1080p at crf 18. visually lossless against a 1080p source. | | 1080p sdr hevc 10-bit | the same, for libraries you want kept in sdr. | | 4k hdr hevc 10-bit | hevc 10-bit 2160p with hdr carried through untouched. | archive presets these re-encode the video and copy the audio and subtitles untouched. they produce one file, not a ladder, so they are for keeping rather than for streaming to many devices. | preset | what it does | |--------|--------------| | hevc archive visually lossless | hevc 10-bit at crf 18. indistinguishable at normal viewing distance, typically 40 to 60 percent smaller. | | hevc space saver | hevc 10-bit at crf 22. the best size-to-quality trade for a large library. | | av1 archive maximum compression | av1 10-bit at crf 26. smallest files here, and slow to produce. | single-file presets one mp4 rather than a ladder. useful when you want a file you can copy somewhere else. | preset | what it does | |--------|--------------| | h.264 mp4 universal | h.264 with stereo aac. | | hevc mp4 high quality | smaller than the h.264 export at the same quality. | | h.264 mp4 1080p 2-pass 5 mbps | a fixed-bitrate 1080p file. | | legacy device h.264 baseline | the most conservative h.264 settings, for a file you are handing to something else entirely. | remux remux lossless mkv copies every track straight into an mkv. nothing is re-encoded. use it when the source is already exactly what you want and only the container is wrong. it costs one pass over the disk and no quality. it is not a streaming preset, so it does not produce quality steps. choosing decide what you want your collection to be, then pick the preset that says it: - storage is tight. hevc space saver. - the smallest library you can have, and you do not mind slow encodes. av1 archive. - the sources are already what you want, and only the container is wrong. remux. - every title at the same resolution. a fixed-resolution preset. - the machine cannot convert your heaviest sources in real time. a streaming preset, so the steps exist ahead of time. - no strong opinion. the default. a device that struggles with a title is not a reason to change preset. the server converts it while you watch. changing a library's preset applies to titles imported afterwards. titles already in the library keep the format they were encoded in. where to go next - encoding overview for when encoding happens at all. - library management to set the preset on a folder.

title: How encoding works
description: What a profile is, how one is resolved, and the six steps every encode runs.
content: how encoding works a preset in the dashboard is a name over a document, and that document is what the encoder reads. this page explains the document and the run. read encoding profiles first if you only want to pick one. what a profile is one record describing the output, not a list of ffmpeg flags. it names: - the container the result is written in - one video output, or none for an audio-only profile - the audio outputs, one per track you want produced - the subtitle outputs - thumbnails for the seek bar - a ladder, if this profile produces quality steps - packaging for hls or dash, and drm where it applies - the segment length, and whether the encode is one pass or two everything the encoder does is derived from that. nothing about it names a device or a client. policies, not switches alongside the outputs sit a handful of policies, which are what let one profile behave sensibly across very different sources. hardware preference. most profiles prefer a graphics card and fall back to the processor. the archival ones ask for quality instead, because a card's output is not what you want to keep forever. bit depth. what to do when the source is deeper than the output can carry: warn and step down, by default. hdr. carry it through where that is possible, rather than flattening it silently. crop detection. off unless the profile asks for it. custom arguments. an escape hatch for the case the model does not cover. inheritance a profile can name a parent, and a chain is resolved from the root down: each child merged over what came before it. that is what a clone is. cloning a built-in gives you a profile that carries one or two of your own values and inherits the rest, so it follows the original when the original improves. two limits keep this honest. a chain cannot loop, and it cannot run deeper than eight. both are refused rather than followed. because a stored profile is only its own layer, what it says and what the encoder will do are different documents. the dashboard's resolved view is the second one, and it is the one to read when a setting seems to have no effect. the ladder a streaming profile does not carry a fixed list of resolutions. it carries the rules for deriving one from the source. - the tiers it may produce, and the bitrate strategy for them. - never upscale, so a 720p source is not stretched to fill a 1080p rung. - a minimum gap between rungs, so two steps too close together are collapsed into one. - a maximum and minimum number of rungs. - a codec policy: the same codec throughout, or a split where lower rungs use one and higher rungs another. so the same profile gives a 4k source eight rungs and a 480p source one, without you maintaining two profiles. the six steps every encode runs the same sequence. each step is replaceable, which is how a plugin adds a way of encoding without a fork. analyse. probe the source: streams, codecs, resolution, durations, hdr metadata. validate. refuse a combination that cannot work, before any time is spent on it. plan. turn profile plus source into a concrete plan: which encoder, which graphics device, which filters, which rungs. this is where the ladder rules meet the actual source. build. turn the plan into the commands to run. execute. run them, and report progress as they go. finalise. write the master playlist, the chapters and the sidecar files that make the output a title rather than a pile of parts. above the six sits a strategy per container family: hls, dash, mp4, mkv, audio-only. a plugin registering its own strategy takes precedence over the built-in one for that family. when several machines share one title a distributed encode splits a title into slices across workers. they write into one output directory, so only the coordinator runs finalise. the workers stop after execute. without that rule they would race each other to write the master playlist. changing a profile a profile change applies to titles encoded after it. titles already in the library keep the format they were encoded in, and the encoding history records which profile produced each one. where to go next - encoding profiles to pick or build one. - encoding overview for when encoding happens at all. - how storage works

title: Hardware acceleration
description: Use a GPU to encode titles faster.
content: hardware acceleration encoding a title is the slowest thing the server does. a graphics card can do that work far faster than a processor, and the server uses one when it can. what is supported | vendor | used through | |--------|--------------| | nvidia | nvenc | | intel | quick sync | | amd | amf on windows, vaapi on linux | | apple | videotoolbox | h.264, hevc and av1 can all be accelerated, depending on what the card itself supports. an older card often accelerates h.264 and hevc but not av1. finding out what you have the server probes the machine at startup and remembers what it found. the dashboard shows the result under hardware, along with a benchmark of how fast each encoder actually is on your machine. that benchmark matters more than the specification sheet. the server uses it to choose, so a card that benchmarks poorly is not preferred just for being present. in docker the container needs to be given access to the card, which is why there is one image per vendor. use the compose file that matches: the plain image has no gpu access, so it encodes on the processor. quality against speed a hardware encoder is faster. a software encoder produces a slightly smaller file at the same picture quality, because it can spend more effort on each frame. presets carry a preference for this, and it is why the archive presets lean on software: an archive is written once and kept, so the extra time buys something permanent. a streaming ladder leans on hardware, because it is rebuilt whenever you change your mind. you do not choose the encoder directly. you choose a preset, and the preset's preference plus the benchmark decide. ::troubleshooting encoding is slow and the dashboard shows no gpu. on docker, check that you started the compose file for your vendor. outside docker, check that the machine's graphics drivers are installed; the server can only use a card the system already exposes. a gpu is detected but the server encodes on the processor anyway. not every card supports every codec. a preset asking for av1 on a card without av1 encoding falls back to software rather than failing. :: where to go next - encoding profiles - docker for the gpu images.

title: Formats
description: The video, audio and container formats the server works with.
content: formats this page lists what the server can read and what it can produce. most people never need it: the presets already pair sensible formats together. it is here for when you are choosing between them. video the server can produce h.264, hevc, vp9 and av1, and it can copy a video stream through untouched. | codec | where it fits | |-------|---------------| | h.264 | plays on the widest range of devices, including old ones. | | hevc | roughly half the size of h.264 at the same picture. needs a reasonably modern device. | | av1 | smallest of the four, slowest to produce, needs a recent device. | | vp9 | mostly of interest for the web. | | copy | no re-encoding at all. the original video is carried across unchanged. | copying is the only option that cannot lose quality, because nothing is re-encoded. it also carries hdr and bit depth across exactly, since those are properties of the stream being copied. audio aac, flac, opus, ac-3, e-ac-3, mp3, vorbis, truehd and dts, plus copy. copy matters more for audio than most people expect. lossless and object-based tracks such as truehd and dts-hd master audio cannot survive a re-encode intact, so the archive presets copy audio rather than touch it. stereo aac is what the streaming presets pair with by default. surround is carried as e-ac-3 where a preset offers it. containers | container | used for | |-----------|----------| | mkv | single-file output, archive and remux presets | | mp4 | single-file output meant to be copied elsewhere | | hls in mpeg-ts | streaming, the widest device support | | hls in fmp4 | streaming, needed for hevc and av1 | | dash | streaming, for clients that speak dash rather than hls | there are audio-only equivalents for music: mp3, aac, flac, ogg, and audio hls. the container is part of the preset, so choosing a preset chooses this for you. subtitles text subtitles are written as separate files next to the video, which is what lets you switch them without the server re-reading anything. subtitles that exist as images in the source, which is normal on dvds and blu-rays, are converted to text so they can be handled the same way. what can be read the server reads far more than it writes. anything ffmpeg can decode can be imported, including old formats like avi and divx and disc structures like videots. so a shelf of avi, divx and disc rips can be imported and end up as one format, whichever one your library's preset produces. where to go next - encoding profiles to pick a preset. - hardware acceleration

title: Encoding history
description: What the server recorded about every title it encoded.
content: encoding history the server keeps a record of every title it has encoded. you reach it from the dashboard, under encoding. it exists for two reasons: it answers "what did that actually cost me", and it is what the server uses to estimate how long queued work will take. what each entry records | recorded | tells you | |----------|-----------| | preset used | which settings produced this result | | gpu used | whether it ran on a graphics card, and which one | | duration | how long the job took | | input size and output size | what went in and what came out | | compression ratio | how much smaller the result is | | average speed | how many times faster than real time it ran | | average frames per second | throughput, useful when comparing presets | | date | when it ran | using it to choose a preset this is the honest answer to "which preset should i use", because it is measured on your hardware and your content rather than argued from a table. encode a few titles with one preset, then a few with another, and compare the compression ratio and duration columns. a preset that halves your storage at an acceptable speed is the right preset for you, whatever anyone else recommends. estimating the queue the dashboard's estimate of remaining work comes from this history: recent speeds against the size of what is still queued. a new server has nothing to average, so early estimates are rough and settle as history accumulates. where to go next - encoding profiles - hardware acceleration

title: NoMercy Connect
description: Control playback on one device from another.
content: nomercy connect connect lets one device play while another controls it. start something on the tv and drive it from your phone, or pick up on your phone what the tv was playing. how it works at any moment one of your devices is the active one. it is the device actually playing. everything else showing that session is passive: it mirrors what is happening and can send commands. the server decides which device is active, rather than the devices negotiating between themselves. that is what keeps two clients from both believing they are in charge, and it is why the controls on your phone match the tv rather than drifting from it. choosing a device the device picker lists what you can play on. it shows devices that are connected right now, and it also shows devices the server knows about that are currently asleep, so a tv that is off is still something you can send playback to. picking a device makes it the active one. your current device becomes a remote for it. what you can control play and pause, seek, skip forward and back, volume and mute, and the queue. the queue is shared, so reordering on your phone changes what the tv plays next. taking over you can move playback the other way, back onto the device you are holding. it picks up where the other device was. casting is separate chromecast is its own path. casting hands playback to a chromecast device, which is not a nomercy client and is controlled differently. the distinction matters when something misbehaves. connect is nomercy device to nomercy device. casting is nomercy to a chromecast. ::troubleshooting a device is missing from the picker. it has to be signed in with the same account. a tv that has never been signed in does not appear. the tv is listed but does not respond. it may be asleep. the server can wake devices that support it; ones that do not need waking by hand. controls on the phone do not match the tv. leave and re-enter the session on the phone. it re-reads the current state from the server. :: where to go next - devices to name and manage your devices.

title: CLI overview
description: Control a running NoMercy server from the terminal.
content: cli overview is a command-line client for a running server. it is installed alongside the server on every platform, and it is the practical way to work with a machine that has no screen. it talks to the server over a local channel, so it works on the machine the server runs on. it is not a remote-control tool. the commands | command | does | |---------|------| | | start the server | | | stop the server | | | restart the server | | | show whether it is running, and its addresses | | | read or follow the log | | | show cpu, memory and disk use | | | show what work is queued and running | | | print the current configuration | | | change one setting | | | list installed plugins | | | turn start-on-boot on or off | | | download and stage an update | every command accepts . checking on the server answers the first question you usually have. answers the second one, when something feels slow: if a command says the server is not running every command except needs the server up, because they all ask the running server for the answer. this message means exactly what it says rather than that something is broken. a server in a container run the command inside the container: where to go next - starting and stopping - logs

title: Starting and stopping
description: Start, stop, restart and check the server from the terminal.
content: starting and stopping four commands cover the server's life cycle. start on a machine where the server is installed as a service, it is already running after a reboot and you rarely need this. stop the server finishes what it is doing before it exits. an encode in progress is checkpointed, so stopping does not throw away the work; it resumes from where it stopped when you start again. restart use this after changing a setting that says it needs a restart. it is a stop and a start, with the same safety around work in progress. status tells you whether the server is running and which addresses it answers on. this is the fastest way to find the address to open in a browser, which matters on a headless machine where nothing told you. ::troubleshooting every command says the server is not running. start it with . if that fails too, read logs to find out why. the server starts and then stops again. the log says why. the usual causes are port 7626 already being in use and a data directory the server cannot write to. stop takes a while to return. it is finishing an operation rather than hanging. let it complete; killing the process is what causes work to be lost. :: where to go next - logs to find out why something failed. - autostart to control start-on-boot.

title: Logs
description: Read and follow the server log from the terminal.
content: logs the log is where the server explains itself. when something did not work, this is the first place to look and usually the last. read the recent log follow it live is the short form. useful while you reproduce a problem: start following, then do the thing that fails, and watch what appears. show more or fewer entries is the short form. filter by level, when you only want the bad news: the levels are verbose, debug, information, warning, error and fatal. by type, when you know which part of the server you care about: combining them the options work together, which is how you get a readable answer out of a busy server: finding the setup link on a headless machine the log carries the setup address and the sign-in code: where to go next - starting and stopping - queue to see work in progress rather than log lines.

title: Configuration
description: Read and change server settings from the terminal.
content: configuration settings live in the server, not in a file you edit. the dashboard is the normal place to change them. the cli is there for a machine with no screen. see the current configuration this prints what the server is actually using, which is the useful thing when a setting was changed somewhere and you want to confirm it took. change a setting take the key from the output of , so you are setting something that exists rather than something you assumed. some settings apply immediately and some need a restart. restart with: prefer the dashboard everything here is also in the dashboard under settings, with the valid choices shown and a description next to each one. use the dashboard when the machine has a screen. where to go next - starting and stopping - configuration reference for what the settings mean.

title: Plugins from the CLI
description: List the plugins a server has installed.
content: plugins from the cli plugins extend the server. the dashboard is where you install and configure them. the cli can tell you what is installed, which is what you need when you are diagnosing something over a terminal. list installed plugins when a plugin is the suspect a plugin that fails to load says so in the log: comparing that against tells you whether a plugin you expected is actually loaded. where to go next - plugins overview for what plugins are and how to install them. - logs

title: Queue
description: See what work the server has queued and running.
content: queue the server does its heavy work in a queue: encoding titles, fetching artwork, building preview thumbnails. when a title has not appeared yet, the queue is the answer. see the queue this shows what is waiting and what is being worked on right now. reading the result work is processed in order, so a long list is not a stall. a title added after thirty others waits for those thirty. encoding a title is the slow part, and how slow depends on the machine and whether the server can use a gpu. see encoding overview. if the queue is empty and a title still has not appeared, the work never started. the log says why: where to go next - logs - resource use with , when work is running but slowly.

title: Updating
description: Update the server from the terminal.
content: updating this downloads a new version and stages it. the staged version takes over when the server next restarts: splitting it that way means the download happens while you are watching, and the interruption happens when you choose. updating a package install a server installed from the apt, rpm or arch repository updates with the rest of your system instead: updating a container pull the image and recreate: your library, database and settings live in the mounted volume, so they survive this. ::troubleshooting the update downloaded but the version has not changed. a staged update applies on restart. run . the server did not come back after an update. read the log with . a staged update that cannot start leaves the reason there. :: where to go next - starting and stopping - upgrading

title: Autostart
description: Control whether the server starts with the machine.
content: autostart a media server is expected to be there. autostart makes it come back on its own after a reboot or a power cut, without someone signing in to start it. check turn it on turn it off what it does per platform on windows the server is registered to start with the machine. on macos it runs as a launch agent. on linux it runs as a systemd service. a server installed from a linux package or run in docker already starts on boot, so there is nothing to enable there. docker handles it through the policy in the compose file. where to go next - starting and stopping

title: Plugins overview
description: What plugins can add to your server, and how they are kept in check.
content: plugins overview a plugin adds capability to your server without changing the server itself. only the server owner can install one. what a plugin can extend | extension point | lets a plugin | |-----------------|---------------| | media source | find media somewhere the server does not look on its own | | metadata | supply titles, artwork and details from another source | | encoder | decide the encoding profile for a title | | scheduled task | run work on a schedule | | authentication | take part in signing users in | | user interface | add screens and navigation to the dashboard | a single plugin can do several of these. the user interface point is worth understanding: the plugin describes the screen and each client renders it in its own style. one plugin therefore looks native on the web, on a phone and on a tv without shipping three interfaces. where plugins come from repositories. your server starts with the official nomercy repository configured, and you can add others. you can also install a plugin from a file, as a carrying its manifest or as a bare . see repositories and trust for how a repository is trusted and what that changes. consent this is the part worth reading before you install anything. a plugin declares what it needs. a plugin that only reads media, supplies metadata or adds a screen is treated as ordinary and is enabled when you install it. a plugin that wants more, such as reaching the network, adding its own endpoints, or opening a socket, installs but stays switched off until you allow it. it cannot switch itself on. you see it listed as waiting for consent, you read what it asked for, and you decide. consent can be withdrawn later. withdrawing it disables the plugin and clears what you granted. grants beyond that first decision, a plugin can ask for something specific while it runs: one network host, the ability to write into one named library, permission to play a source outside your library. each request arrives separately with the reason the plugin gave, and you approve them one at a time. a plugin cannot widen its own reach by asking once and taking everything. what this protects you from plugins run inside the server, so this is a permission model rather than a wall. the protections that exist are real, and knowing their shape is better than assuming more: - a plugin only reaches the network hosts it declared or you granted. - a plugin needing anything beyond the ordinary set cannot run until you say so. - its version compatibility is checked before it loads, so a plugin built against a different server version is rejected rather than half-loaded. - downloads from a repository are checked against the checksum the repository published. install plugins you have reason to trust, the same way you would with any software that runs on your machine. where to go next - installing plugins - repositories and trust - writing a plugin

title: Installing and Managing Plugins
description: Install, enable, disable, and remove plugins.
content: installing and managing plugins everything here lives on one screen, under dashboard > plugins. it is owner-only on every client, because approving what a plugin may do is the server owner's decision and nobody else's. two ways in you can hand the server a file, or point it at a repository and pick from what that repository offers. both end in the same place: the plugin is on disk, disabled, waiting for you to look at what it asked for. a file you already have. press install on the plugins page and pick the plugin's . the upload is staged outside the plugins folder and only moves in once it passes verification, so a file the server rejects is never left somewhere it would be found on the next start. a repository. open the catalogue, add a repository by name and index url, then install from the list. the server resolves the download against its own copy of that index, so the browser never names a url. if the repository published a checksum it is checked before anything is copied into place, and if it did not, the prompt says so before you agree. publishing your own index is one json file. see publishing a plugin repository. approving what a plugin asked for a plugin declares what it needs before it runs: outbound hosts, hooks, whether it serves rest or a socket, and which screens it contributes. anything past the baseline installs disabled and cannot start itself. the plugin's page shows that declaration in full, hosts included, rather than the word "network". approving is one action that records your consent, records the grants that came with it, and starts the plugin. withdrawing takes all of that back and stops the plugin, and you can approve again later. some plugins ask for something afterwards that their manifest could not know up front, such as a host they only learn about at runtime. those requests sit at the top of the plugins page until you allow or deny them, because a plugin waiting on you is a plugin not doing its job. turning one off disable stops the plugin and leaves it installed with its configuration intact. use it to find out whether a plugin is behind something you are seeing. some changes need the server restarted before they take effect. the plugin's row says so when that is the case, and says why. when it says nothing, the change is already live. removing one uninstall removes the plugin and its files from the server. anything it stored goes with it and is not recovered, so the dashboard asks first. updates the catalogue compares what each repository offers against what is installed, and puts anything newer at the top of its own page. the comparison happens on the server, so every client agrees about whether an update exists. updating is the same operation as installing, against a newer version. when a plugin fails to load a plugin that broke on startup is listed apart from the ones you turned off. it is not off, because nobody chose this, and enabling it again fails the same way until the cause is fixed. the server log says what went wrong. configuring one a plugin's settings live inside the plugin, on the screens it registered. those appear on its page and in the sidebar once it is enabled, and the server hands each screen back to the plugin to draw.

title: Publishing a Plugin Repository
description: The index file a repository serves, and what the server does with it.
content: publishing a plugin repository a repository is one json file on a web server. the media server fetches that url, reads the plugins it lists, and shows them in the catalogue. there is nothing else to run and nothing to register with us: if you can serve a file over https, you can publish plugins. the index the server asks for the url you gave it and expects this document back. field names are matched case-insensitively, trailing commas are allowed, and comments are skipped, so a hand-maintained index is not a trap. repository fields the two top-level strings are for humans. only changes what the server does. | field | required | what it is | |---|---|---| | | yes | the repository's own name. shown nowhere yet; kept so an index identifies itself. | | | no | a homepage for the repository. | | | yes | every plugin this repository offers. an empty list is valid and means you publish nothing today. | plugin fields one entry per plugin, not per version. the is the identity the server matches against what is installed, so it has to be the same guid the plugin's own manifest declares. | field | required | what it is | |---|---|---| | | yes | the plugin's guid, identical to the in its . | | | yes | the plugin's name. the server names the downloaded assembly after this. | | | yes | one line, shown in the catalogue. | | | no | shown beside the name. | | | no | where someone reads more before installing. | | | yes | every version you still offer, in any order. | version fields the server picks the highest version it can parse, so a version that does not parse sorts below every one that does rather than breaking the entry. | field | required | what it is | |---|---|---| | | yes | dotted numeric, for example . this is what gets compared. | | | yes | a direct link to the . the server fetches this; a browser never sees it. | | | no | the plugin platform version this build targets. | | | no | sha-256 of the file at . see below. | | | no | what changed. | | | no | when this version was published. | checksums publish one. the server verifies the file it downloaded against before anything is copied into the plugins folder, and a mismatch aborts the install. a version without a checksum still installs. the catalogue marks it unverified and the owner is told, in the confirmation prompt, that nothing can be checked before it lands. that is a choice you are making on their behalf, so make the other one. what the server will not do your index says where a download lives, and that is the only place an install from your repository can reach. the dashboard sends a plugin id and a version, never a url, so nobody using the web app can point an install somewhere you did not publish. listing a plugin does not grant it anything. every plugin still declares its capabilities in its own manifest, still installs disabled when it asks for more than the baseline, and still waits for the server owner to approve what it asked for. a repository is a place to find plugins, not a way to skip consent. serving it static hosting is enough. the server issues a plain get and reads the body, so object storage, github pages, a raw file from a git host, or nginx serving a directory all work. two things to get right. serve it over https, because the server refuses any other scheme when a repository is added. and set your cache headers deliberately: the catalogue is only as fresh as what your host hands back when the owner presses refresh.

title: Repositories and trust
description: Where plugins come from, and what marking a repository trusted changes.
content: repositories and trust a repository is a catalogue of plugins your server can install from. trust is decided per repository, by you. the default repository your server starts with the official nomercy repository configured and marked trusted. adding a repository add one from the plugins section of the dashboard by giving its catalogue address. refreshing it pulls the current list, and the available plugins then show alongside what you already have, with updates flagged. only the server owner can add or remove a repository. what trusted means marking a repository trusted says: plugins from here do not need me to approve their capabilities. a plugin from a trusted repository skips the consent step described in plugins overview and starts enabled, even when it asks for the network or its own endpoints. a plugin from an untrusted repository installs the same way, then waits for you. trust attaches to the repository, never to a name inside a plugin's own manifest. a plugin cannot describe itself as trustworthy; trust only comes from you having marked the place it came from. whether to trust one trusting a repository is trusting its owner with your server, continuously. it applies to every plugin they publish now and to every update they push later. trust the official repository. trust others only when you would also let that person run software on your machine unattended. leaving a repository untrusted costs you one approval per plugin and keeps the decision in your hands. what is checked regardless trusted or not, every install is checked for two things. version compatibility. a plugin built against a different server version is rejected rather than loaded. checksum. a plugin downloaded from a repository is checked against the checksum that repository published, so a file altered in transit does not install. a note on the name elsewhere in the dashboard you may meet trusted publishers under encoding. that is a different feature: it verifies signatures on imported encoding profiles. it has nothing to do with plugins. where to go next - plugins overview - installing plugins

title: Writing a plugin
description: Build a plugin for NoMercy MediaServer.
content: writing a plugin a plugin is a .net assembly the server loads at runtime. this page covers the shape of one; the interfaces themselves are documented in the contract package. starting from the template the repository ships a project template under , which is the fastest correct start. there are sample plugins under as well, including a minimal one, one that adds dashboard ui, and ones that fail deliberately so you can see how the server reacts. the shape of a plugin implement . it gives the server a name, a description, an id and a version, and receives an when it initialises. then implement whichever extension points you need: | interface | for | |-----------|-----| | | finding media the server would not find | | | supplying titles, artwork and details | | | overriding the encoding profile for a title | | | work on a cron schedule | | | taking part in authentication | | | adding navigation and screens | and are available when you need dependency injection or your own settings. building a user interface describes screens rather than rendering them. you return a description of the view and each client draws it in its own idiom: web, phone and tv. write the screen once and it looks native everywhere, which is the reason for the indirection. declaring capabilities your manifest declares what the plugin needs: hooks it implements, network hosts it will reach, where it mounts ui, and whether it serves endpoints or sockets. declare the narrowest set that works. a plugin needing only media source, metadata or ui is installed and enabled straight away. anything asking for network access or its own endpoints waits for the server owner to consent, which is friction you inflict on every one of your users. network access is limited to the hosts you declared. reaching elsewhere fails unless the owner grants that host. asking at runtime when you cannot know something in advance, such as a host the user configures themselves, ask for it while running through . give a real reason: the owner sees it and decides on it. packaging ship a containing your manifest and assembly, or a bare for something trivial. to publish through a repository, list it in a catalogue with a download address and a checksum. the server verifies the checksum on install. compatibility the server checks that your plugin targets a compatible version before loading it. a plugin built against a different version is rejected outright rather than loaded and left half-working. rebuild against the contract package when the server has a major update. where to go next - plugins overview for the consent model your users will meet. - repositories and trust for distribution.

title: Backups
description: What the server backs up on its own, and what you should copy yourself.
content: backups the server keeps its own recovery points. they protect against a bad upgrade on the same machine, and they do not protect against losing the machine, because they live on it. what the server does for you it snapshots its databases automatically, twice over: before every database change that an upgrade brings. if a version arrives with a schema change, a snapshot is taken before that change is applied. once a day. so there is a recent recovery point even on a server that goes months between upgrades. it keeps the five most recent snapshots and removes older ones. they are written under the server's data directory, in a folder. snapshots are taken through the database's own backup mechanism rather than by copying files, so a snapshot taken while the server is running is consistent. what you should copy yourself the server's data directory is the thing worth backing up, because most of it cannot be regenerated. | platform | directory | |----------|-----------| | windows | | | linux and macos | | inside it, two things matter most. the databases, under . they hold your libraries, what you have watched, your users and your settings. the folder. this is the keyring that encrypts the server's secrets. without it, the encrypted parts of the database cannot be read even though the database itself is intact, so a backup of the databases without this folder is only a partial backup. copy the whole data directory and you have both. what the backup leaves out your media. libraries live wherever you put them, and are covered by however you back up the rest of your files. artwork and details, which the server fetches again by itself. in docker everything above lives in the volume. back up the volume and you have the server. restoring stop the server, put the data directory back where it was, and start it again. where to go next - upgrading - moving to another machine

title: Upgrading
description: Move the server to a newer version safely.
content: upgrading upgrading is a normal update plus a restart. the server handles its own data. how to upgrade it depends on how you installed it. linux packages upgrade with the rest of your system: docker pulls a new image: windows and macos stage an update through the server itself: the download and the interruption are separate steps, so the restart happens when it suits you. what happens on the first start if the new version changes the shape of the database, the server updates it during startup. you do not run anything. before it makes that change, it takes a snapshot of the databases. that snapshot is what a failed upgrade falls back to, and it is why an upgrade is a low-risk operation rather than a leap. your content is unaffected upgrades change the server, not your library. your titles stay as they are, watch progress is kept, and nothing needs re-importing. ::troubleshooting the version has not changed after updating. a staged update applies on restart. run . the server did not come back. read the log: a version that cannot start records the reason there, and the snapshot taken before the upgrade is in the folder under the data directory. a container came back empty. the data volume was not mounted. check the compose file still has the volume, then recreate. :: where to go next - backups - updating from the cli

title: Moving to another machine
description: Move your server and library to new hardware.
content: moving to another machine two things move separately: your library, which is portable, and your server's identity, which is tied to the hardware it was set up on. read this before you start, because the order matters. your server's identity a server identifies itself with a fingerprint taken from the machine it runs on, built from the motherboard and system drive. that identity is what its address, its dns entry and its certificate are issued against. new hardware produces a new fingerprint, so a server on a new machine is a new server, and copying the old machine's data does not carry the old identity across. that is the part to plan around. everything else moves cleanly. what moves cleanly your media. copy the library folders. they are ordinary files. your data directory, which holds your libraries, watch progress, users and settings. see backups for where it lives per platform. moving 1. copy your media to the new machine, or connect the same storage to it. 2. install nomercy on the new machine and complete setup, signing in with the same account. it registers as a new server and gets its own address and certificate. 3. copy the data directory across from the old machine, replacing the new one's, then restart the server. 4. check the library folder paths in the dashboard. if the media sits at a different path on the new machine, update each folder to match and rescan. 5. open the app, pick the new server, and confirm your libraries and watch progress came across. 6. once you are satisfied, retire the old server. keep the old machine intact until step five passes. it is your fallback. in docker moving a container is easier because the identity problem is smaller. copy the volume to the new host, bring the container up with the same compose file and the same media mounts, and the server keeps its own identity. the mount paths inside the container must match what they were, since your libraries refer to container paths. your users people you invited follow the account, not the machine, so they do not need re-inviting. they select the new server the same way you do. ::troubleshooting the app shows two servers. expected while both exist. remove the old one once you are satisfied with the new one. the libraries are there but every title is missing. the folder paths do not match the new machine. correct each folder's path in the dashboard and rescan. :: where to go next - backups - storage if the media moved to a different disk or share.

title: Reading the logs
description: Where the log lives and how to get an answer out of it.
content: reading the logs the log is where the server explains what it did and why something failed. it is the fastest route to an answer for almost every problem. the quickest way that skips the routine chatter and shows only what went wrong. most problems are visible in that output without any further filtering. where the file lives | platform | path | |----------|------| | windows | | | linux and macos | | files roll daily, so a problem from yesterday is in yesterday's file. in docker, read the container's output instead: levels from most detail to least: verbose, debug, information, warning, error, fatal. the server runs at information, which records what it is doing without recording every step of it. raise it to debug while reproducing something that only happens occasionally, and put it back afterwards; debug is noisy enough to make a busy server's log hard to read. filtering to one part of the server the log is tagged by area, so you can look at one thing at a time: areas worth knowing: for encoding titles, for scheduled work, for discs, , and for first-run problems, for sign-in, and for clients failing to connect, and for metadata lookups. watching a problem happen start following, then do the thing that fails. what appears while you do it is the relevant part, which is much easier than searching a file afterwards. reading an error errors name the operation and the reason. read the reason rather than the stack of technical detail under it; the reason is usually the whole answer, and it is usually something ordinary like a path that does not exist or a device that refused a connection. where to go next - common issues - diagnostics for checking the server's health directly.

title: Common issues
description: The problems people hit most, and what fixes each one.
content: common issues grouped by where you notice the problem. each one names the check that confirms it before you change anything. setup will not finish ::troubleshooting every address on the server says setup is required. setup did not complete. open and finish or retry it. until it completes the server answers this on every other address by design, so it is not a fault. setup ends with the certificate not acquired. choose retry. this is the normal fix and it is safe to repeat. setup cannot get past sign-in. it needs an internet connection to reach the sign-in service and register. neither works offline. :: the app cannot find the server ::troubleshooting no servers listed. almost always a different account. the account that owns the server is the one that sees it. confirm the email matches. the server is listed but unreachable. check it is running with . if it runs, check whether you are outside your own network; that is a separate problem covered in networking. it worked at home and stopped when you left. nothing established an outside route. see networking. :: content does not appear ::troubleshooting nothing arrived after adding files. check . encoding titles takes real time and they are processed in order. the queue is empty and it still has not appeared. the work never started. says why. a scan found nothing. check the folder path, and check the library type. a folder one level too high or too low finds nothing and looks identical from outside. everything matched the wrong title. check the library type first. films in a tv shows library are read as episodes. see metadata and matching. :: playback problems ::troubleshooting it plays on one device and not another. the server converts while you watch for devices that need it. if one device fails, check that person's transcoding settings in users. playback stutters over the internet but is fine at home. the connection is the limit. a streaming preset gives clients smaller versions to fall back on; a single-file preset does not. no subtitles. subtitles are written when the title is encoded. something imported without them will not gain them later without being encoded again. :: the server is slow ::troubleshooting everything is slow while titles are being encoded. expected. check . encoding is the heaviest thing the server does, and a graphics card changes it dramatically. see hardware acceleration. slow with media on a network share. encoding moves the file across and back. if you reach the share through nomercy's nfs or smb driver, mount it with the operating system instead and point a local driver at the mount. see storage. :: where to go next - reading the logs - diagnostics

title: Diagnostics
description: Check the server’s health and find out which part is unhappy.
content: diagnostics when something is wrong, the useful first question is which part is wrong. these checks answer that before you start reading logs. is it running this also prints the addresses the server answers on, which is the thing you need on a machine with no screen. is it healthy the server answers health checks over http: | check | tells you | |-------|-----------| | | it is alive and answering | | | it is alive and its database is reachable | | | the state of each part: database, sign-in, network, registration | is the one to reach for. it reports each component separately, plus the version and how long the server has been up, so it distinguishes "the whole server is down" from "the server is fine but registration failed". the server also answers a plain health check on port 7627, on the loopback address only. that one exists for docker's own health monitoring and is not reachable from another machine. is it busy shows processor, memory and disk use. worth checking before concluding something is broken, because a server encoding several titles is busy rather than stuck. shows what work is queued and running. an apparently missing title is usually waiting here. narrowing it down work outward from the server: 1. — is the server running at all? 2. — which component is unhappy? 3. — what did it say when it went wrong? 4. — is the work simply still queued? most problems are answered by step two or three. where to go next - reading the logs - common issues

title: Error messages
description: What the messages you are most likely to see actually mean.
content: error messages the server writes errors in plain language rather than numeric codes, so this page explains the ones whose wording does not tell the whole story. from the command line "nomercy mediaserver is not running, or is not reachable on its management socket." every command except asks the running server for its answer, so they all need it up. start it with . if that fails too, the log says why. during setup "registered, but the ssl certificate could not be acquired." your server exists and is linked to your account. only the certificate is missing. choose retry; this is the expected fix and repeating it is safe. "setup required" on every address. not an error. until setup finishes, the server deliberately answers this everywhere except the setup page itself. during a scan a scan task that failed with a storage message. the reason comes from the storage backend rather than from nomercy: a refused connection, a missing export, a rejected credential. the text is the backend's own, which is why it reads differently from the rest of the server's messages. fix the backend, then rescan. during playback a title that will not play on one device only. not usually a server error. check that person's transcoding permissions, since a device needing conversion cannot play anything when conversion is off for them. when a title will not match nothing in the log, and the title is simply absent or wrong. matching does not fail loudly, because a wrong match is a plausible answer rather than an error. check the library type, then fix the match by hand. see metadata and matching. finding the rest anything not here is in the log with its reason attached: where to go next - common issues - reading the logs
