title: What is nomercy-music-player
description: A headless, plugin-driven audio engine with crossfade, a swappable audio backend, synced lyrics, and a Web Audio equalizer, built on nomercy-player-core.
content: / source: packages/nomercy-music-player/src/index.ts, src/types.ts / what is nomercy-music-player is a headless audio engine. it ships no chrome. you get the audio transport and a typed surface to drive it. everything on screen is code you write, or a plugin you add. what it handles for you: - gapless queue playback - crossfade between tracks - a swappable audio backend: a plain element, or a full web audio graph - synced lyrics - a plugin system it is built on /nomercy-player-core, which carries lifecycle, queue, plugin runtime, i18n and auth. this library adds the one piece the kit cannot: an audio backend, plus the methods that only mean something when listening. crossfade between queue items, and lyrics. who it's for anything where someone listens: a streaming app, a podcast or radio client, a music dashboard inside a bigger product. reach for it when you want the ui to be yours, rather than someone else's chrome under css overrides. composing a third kind of player, neither video nor music? start one level down at /nomercy-player-core. why it exists listening has one genuinely hard job: getting from one track to the next without a gap or a click, and with a real overlap when the app wants a crossfade rather than a cut. a swappable audio backend owns that job. , the default, drives a plain . routes through an graph, which buys sample-accurate crossfades and a tap point for an equalizer or a visualizer. both sit behind the same typed surface, so reads the same either way. queueing, transport, volume, auth and plugins are not listening-specific, so they come from the core. a fix there reaches every player built on it. the setup, then freedom, model create an instance bound to a container, call once, wait for it, then do whatever you want. is the factory. it returns the existing instance for an id already in use, or mounts a fresh one into the at that id, creating its own audio element inside it. is the only strict part. it walks the pipeline every kit-composed player runs, before resolves: config snapshot, plugin registration, stream, auth, playlist, media readiness. call it twice and it throws, so a half-configured instance is not a state you can reach. once resolves, no ui is prescribed. build controls against the typed methods, or add plugins for lyrics, cast or media session. every path calls the same , and underneath. what you get - , created through the factory, generic over your own playlist item type. - a swappable audio backend: by default, for sample-accurate crossfades and a web audio graph tap, selectable at setup or at runtime through . - crossfade between queue items with a configurable duration and curve. music defaults , unlike a hard-cut transition. - audio output device selection , , for routing playback to a specific speaker or bluetooth device. - a web audio equalizer and audio graph, from the kit's chain, available on either backend, lazily creates the web audio source node the first time a plugin requests it. - synced lyrics through the opt-in : fetches , parses it through the kit's cue parser registry, and fires line-enter/line-exit events for a karaoke-style ui. - a plugin system: media-session, cast, key-handler, scrobbling, and auto-advance ship as opt-in plugins instead of bundle weight everyone pays for. - everything from underneath: lifecycle, queue, transport, volume, i18n, and auth-aware fetch, so it never gets reimplemented per medium. where it sits : backend, crossfade, lyrics.' , n: 1, name: 'nomercy-player-core', pkg: 'dependency', knows: 'lifecycle, queue, transport, plugins, i18n, auth.' , /> next steps - quick start: install the player and get a real song playing, copy-paste.

title: Quick Start
description: Install nomercy-music-player and play a real song with the baseUrl pattern. One copy-paste example that works first try.
content: music player: quick start this gets a real song playing in the preview below: "where dreams drift" by ketsa, streamed from the fixture catalogue, using the baseurl pattern every nomercy player and app is built around. install that's the only package you need. is a regular dependency of , npm installs it for you, there is no peer dependency to add by hand. play your first song here it is loaded for real: an mp3 streamed from , through the native controls that mounts. press play in the bar to start it. below the player is the exact code that produced it, ready to copy: :::snippetfile="music-quickstart" runnable preview="first" ::: the player is headless: it mounts a plain element into your container, and gives it the browser's own control bar. loads the first track so those controls have something to play. add the container and style it however your app needs, here it sits as a full-width bar along the bottom: the baseurl pattern is the one config field every playlist should set. item paths above stay relative, exactly the shape a real media server sends, and the player prepends as a plain string prefix, keeping the whole base path: - the server sends the base with no trailing slash and each item path with a leading slash . - move to a different server, a different environment, or a signed-url cdn, and you change one config value; nothing in your catalogue is hardcoded to today's origin. - never pre-join an absolute url into an item yourself. that is the player's job, and doing it twice breaks the moment the base changes. next steps - guided tour: transport: play, pause, and moving through the queue, the first stop on the full method surface. - build a player: put a real overlay ui on top of the player, one control at a time.

title: Transport
description: play(), pause(), stop(), togglePlayback(), and next()/previous(), the queue-driven playback commands every music UI wires first.
content: / source: packages/nomercy-player-core/src/core/mixins/transport.ts / transport doesn't reimplement transport. every method below is 's transport contract: a cancellable dispatch, then a call into the active audio backend. music adds nothing to the surface here, only a real audio element or web audio graph for it to drive. play, pause, stop , , , and all return a that resolves once the backend call settles: every one of these accepts : . defaults to and gets stamped onto the emitted event, so a connect plugin syncing playback across devices can tell its own remote-triggered apart from a real click. moving through the queue and move the queue cursor and load the resulting item. the queue covers the cursor itself. honours : - reloads the current item without moving the cursor. - wraps back to the first item at the end. - fires when there is no next item. ignores repeat. it steps back one item, and no-ops at the start of the queue: there's no music-only variant of either, the shuffle-aware, repeat-aware logic lives once in the kit and every player built on it gets it for free. guard first every transport method calls the kit's guard before doing anything else. calling before resolves, or after , throws a typed instead of silently reaching into missing state, the same contract core: transport contract documents in full, including the / shape of the event. see it running music ships no play button, so this builds the smallest bar that can drive the methods above. :::snippetfile="music-tour-transport" preview="first" ::: next steps - time & seeking: time, duration, and rewind/forward for the scrubber this bar is missing.

title: Time & Seeking
description: time(), duration(), timeData(), rewind()/forward()/restart(), and seekByPercentage(), the position surface a scrubber reads and drives.
content: / source: packages/nomercy-player-core/src/core/mixins/time.ts, src/core/mixins/transport.ts / time & seeking position and duration come straight from , same as transport, and so does the event's payload: the kit's full snapshot, because a progress bar almost always wants percentage and remaining time in the same read. reading and seeking reads the current position in seconds. seeks to a new one. there is no separate . position is reported by two different events, for two different reasons. ordinary playback ticks the event per frame, plus the throttled event. a deliberate jump fires the cancellable → → cycle. it is the same split the web platform draws between and /. the tick against the jump: returns the total track length once metadata resolves before then. and read how far ahead playback has downloaded. bundles all of it into one snapshot, , , , , , computed together so the values agree at the moment of the call instead of drifting across separate reads: relative seeks and compute a relative target from the current position and run the same cancellable → → cycle; both default to a 5 second step when called with no argument. seeks to and resumes playback, an atomic intent, not a seek-then-play sequence, so a cancelled seek skips the resulting too: seeks to a position expressed as - percent of , the calculation a progress bar's click handler would otherwise have to do by hand. the event payload core's defines as the full snapshot, everything a scrubber needs in one payload, identical across the music and video players: is an alias for in seconds, is elapsed time as - of , is how many seconds are loaded ahead of the position, is seconds left. it is the same shape returns, so subscribe to this instead of polling from a render loop. see it running the scrubber reads position from the event and length from . drag it and it ignores incoming updates until you let go. :::snippetfile="music-tour-time" preview="first" ::: next steps - volume: volume, mute/unmute, and the volume gain state a slider or mute icon reads.

title: Volume
description: volume(), mute()/unmute()/toggleMute(), volumeUp()/volumeDown(), and volumeState(), the gain surface a slider or mute icon reads.
content: / source: packages/nomercy-player-core/src/core/mixins/volume.ts / volume volume is another kit surface inherits unchanged, there's no music-specific volume behavior, the backend just needs a real gain to move. reading and setting the level reads the current level as a number in ; sets it, clamped to that range, and returns a once the backend applies it: doesn't add a volume field of its own, but it inherits from the kit's , set it at for a declarative initial level, when omitted: read a saved preference into that same field before runs instead of calling after . mute and are absolute; flips based on the current state. all three dispatch first, same cancellable shape as transport, and no-op never dispatch when already in the target state: and nudge the level by a sane default when omitted, clamped to the same as a direct call, the pair a keyboard shortcut binds to. reading the gain stage returns a typed or , the value a mute-icon component reads instead of tracking its own boolean, since it stays correct even when something other than that icon a keyboard shortcut, a connect sync changes the mute state: , , and / events carry / payloads respectively, subscribe to those instead of polling the getters from a render loop. see it running drag the slider and click mute. the button reads on every change, so it cannot drift out of step with the player. :::snippetfile="music-tour-volume" preview="first" ::: next steps - the queue: queue, item, and the mutators a playlist ui reads and drives.

title: The Queue
description: queue(), item(), queueAppend()/queueRemove()/queueMove()/queueShuffle(), and the baseUrl + relative-path shape every track carries.
content: / source: packages/nomercy-player-core/src/adapters/media-list/default.ts, src/core/mixins/queue.ts, packages/nomercy-music-player/src/types.ts / the queue behind is one cursor-aware instance, the same structure core: the queue documents. adds the item shape , everything else, the queue mechanics, is unchanged kit code. the track shape carries the canonical display field, also works since it's inherited from the base shape but is what the rest of this library reads, , , , , , and : stays relative and supplies the origin, the pattern quick start introduces. there's no → normalization step here, a track is already in its canonical shape the moment it enters the queue. is resolved differently, see now playing & lyrics for why cover art usually needs a fully-qualified url instead. reading and moving the cursor returns the current items as a readonly array; reads the active item, moves the cursor and loads it. reads the cursor's position, its size: / read what / see transport would load, without moving the cursor or triggering a load, useful for a "coming up next" label or for picking the target of a manual crossfade. mutating the queue every mutation method below fires a typed event , , ... that a reactive track-list ui subscribes to instead of re-reading after every call. | method | what it does | | --- | --- | | | add to the end. | | | add to the front. | | | add at a specific position. | | / | remove by id or position. | | | reorder in place. | | | empty the queue. | | | randomize order; the cursor follows the currently-playing track to its new position. | | | sort with your own comparator. | removing the item before the cursor decrements the cursor automatically, so it keeps pointing at the same logical track, none of these ever silently jump playback to the wrong entry. playitem and playnow races: fires a fire-and-forget , and a called immediately after can reach the backend before the source is even set. and exist to close that race, both route through internally, which only calls inside the resolved 's own continuation: see it running three real tracks. shuffle reorders the queue in place and the cursor follows the playing track to its new position. :::snippetfile="music-tour-queue" preview="first" ::: next steps - crossfade: crossfadeto, the manual dual-buffer fade between two queue items.

title: Crossfade
description: crossfadeTo(item, opts), isTransitioning(), and the crossfadeEnabled/crossfadeDefaults config that makes music the one player in the trio that overlaps tracks instead of cutting between them.
content: / source: packages/nomercy-music-player/src/index.ts, src/adapters/audio-backend/iaudiobackend.ts / crossfade moving from one track to the next without a gap, or with a real overlap instead of a hard cut, is the one job that's genuinely specific to listening. is 's own method, not something inherited from the kit. crossfadeto call it with any queue item to fade the current track out while the target fades in, over a configurable duration: internally it loads the target into a second audio element, or a second web audio node graph on , primes it, ramps both gains over the window, then swaps it in as primary and advances the queue cursor. that fires the same event a normal does. reports while a fade is in flight. a second during that window is ignored rather than stacked. falls back to on the config, then to 5 seconds. is or . linear is the default for a manual ; equal-power is perceptually smoother, with no volume dip at the midpoint. it resolves per call first, then from . the automatic track-boundary fade, run by , uses equal-power on its own. seeks the incoming track to a start position in milliseconds before the fade begins. the event sequence is cancellable the same way every other event is, a listener can and no buffers are touched, keeps playing, fires instead of . automatic crossfade between queue items manually calling is one use of crossfade. the other is automatic: defaults for music, so the queue's own natural track-boundary transition already overlaps instead of cutting. / both default control that window: that automatic behavior is , a medium-neutral kit primitive, not something this page reimplements. see adapter: transition strategy for the full mechanism, above is the explicit, on-demand version of the same idea. backend precision the default drives the fade with a loop, not sample-accurate, expect sub-frame-length seams at track boundaries. routes through a real graph for a sample-accurate ramp instead: see it running trigger a crossfade and watch the status line. it is driven by the three events, not by a timer guessing at them. :::snippetfile="music-tour-crossfade" preview="first" ::: next steps - equalizer: the web audio effect chain both backends expose, shared with the rest of the trio.

title: Equalizer
description: AudioGraphPlugin + EqualizerPlugin: the shared kit Web Audio chain and its 10-band parametric equalizer, available on either audio backend.
content: / source: packages/nomercy-player-core/src/plugins/audio-graph/index.ts, src/plugins/equalizer/index.ts / equalizer an equalizer isn't music-specific code living in this package, it's 's shared + pair, available to any player built on the kit. just makes them the plugin most listening apps reach for first. registering the chain owns the web audio signal chain, , the media source node, and . inserts itself into that chain and requires it to already be registered: both plugins register before , so they install as part of the setup pipeline. that is the rule every plugin in the trio follows. register either one after and its still runs, inline and fire-and-forget rather than inside that pass. completion then surfaces through the event or , not through resolving. , the default, creates the web audio source node the first time asks for it. so registering the equalizer neither forces nor costs anything on a player that never taps the graph. driving it sets one band directly; applies a named preset in one call. the full options table, event list, and persistence rules live on core: plugin: equalizer, this page only covers what's specific to reaching for it from a music player. see it running two buttons swap between two of the plugin's presets. both plugins are shared kit plugins, registered in . :::snippetfile="music-tour-equalizer" preview="first" ::: next steps - audio output devices: audiooutputs, selectaudiooutput, and routing playback to a specific speaker.

title: Audio Output Devices
description: audioOutputs(), selectAudioOutput(), and audioOutput(deviceId), routing playback to a specific speaker or Bluetooth device.
content: / source: packages/nomercy-player-core/src/core/mixins/audio-output.ts / audio output devices picking which speaker plays audio matters constantly for a listening session, headphones now, a bluetooth speaker in ten minutes, a desk speaker after that. the device-routing surface lives in the kit, is simply the library most consumers reach for it from. listing devices enumerates available output devices without prompting for permission: browsers gate device labels behind a permission grant, without one, still returns entries, just with an empty on some devices. render what you get, a picker button covers the rest. picking one opens the browser's own output picker chrome ≥105 only, everything else throws a structured and resolves with the chosen device, or if the user cancels: reads the currently-selected device id for the system default; routes playback there by calling on the backend's media element, and throws when the browser doesn't support it. see it running the list is enumerated without a permission prompt. picking a device opens the browser's own picker, which needs a real click. :::snippetfile="music-tour-audio-output" preview="first" ::: next steps - lyrics: the synced-lyrics plugin, parsing a timed lyrics file into cues and firing an event on every active line change.

knows what a component is. vue owns nothing about the player. the player owns nothing about vue. a composable is the seam. it subscribes to player events, writes the values into s, and returns both the reactive state and the player instance, so a template can call methods directly. the composable is until runs. a template reads it through , the same as any other ref that starts empty. and the handler below guard the same way. that shape is correct however the caller renders the container: always-present markup, , or a route transition. the composable never assumes the dom is ready before vue says it is. using it in a component below takes and as props instead of owning them, the same two values 's already needs, just threaded one level up so whoever mounts the component supplies the real catalogue: is a top-level ref, so the template above reads it unwrapped , no , vue does that unwrapping automatically for refs returned from a composable and used directly in the template. inside itself the handler, it stays an explicit ref: . mounting it is the real fixture catalogue the same ketsa/bent wyre tracks the quickstart and the testbed use, passed down as a prop, not hardcoded inside the component above: providing the player globally when several components need the same instance, a mini-player, a queue sidebar, a lyrics panel, provide it once at the root instead of re-deriving state in each. unlike the composable above, this is safe at 's top level rather than inside . is a static element in , a sibling of that vue never renders, so it exists in the dom before this module runs: a typed key avoids the string-collision risk a bare provide key carries in a larger app. wrap the injected instance in its own local composable subscribing to the events that component actually cares about rather than passing raw player state through more / layers. pinia store pattern when several unrelated components need the same reactive state, not just the same title: Recipe: Crossfade & Gapless Playback
description: Choosing between an overlapping crossfade and a true hard-cut gapless boundary, switching modes at runtime, and firing a manual crossfadeTo() independent of either.
content: / source: packages/nomercy-music-player/src/index.ts, packages/nomercy-player-core/src/adapters/preload/default.ts / recipe: crossfade & gapless playback crossfade covers and the config fields that shape the fade. this recipe is the task on top of it: picking the right automatic boundary behavior for your catalogue, and switching it at runtime instead of only at . two boundary strategies, one interface the automatic transition between queue items, the behavior that fires with no method call at all when a track ends, is owned by an from . two ship in the kit: | strategy | behavior | default for | |---|---|---| | | overlapping fade, before the outgoing track ends through into the incoming one. | music | | | hard cut at the natural end, no overlap. the incoming item is already warm from preloading, so the cut has no buffering pause either. | video | both are medium-neutral, nothing about is video-specific, it's simply not the music default. reach for it when your catalogue is a continuous mix, a live recording, or a gapless album where the tracks are mastered to touch exactly, cases where an audible overlap would sound wrong rather than smooth. is worth setting alongside even though the strategy itself already reports , it also gates the automatic transition path other plugins may be listening for, so the / / events never fire for a catalogue that never crossfades. switching modes at runtime swaps the active strategy on a live player, useful for a per-playlist or per-genre setting instead of a fixed -time choice: the swap cancels any transition already in flight, emitting with reason , and the new strategy takes effect from the next boundary the preload pipeline evaluates. manual crossfadeto either way is independent of whichever automatic strategy is active, it's a direct call, not something the transition strategy gates. a gapless-configured player can still fade into a specific track on a user action a "blend into this" button, a dj-style manual mix point: see it running the toggle below flips between the two modes; "crossfade now" fires a manual regardless of which mode is active. :::snippetfile="music-recipe-crossfade-gapless" live="false" ::: next steps - recipe: synced lyrics ui: building a full scrolling lyrics panel on top of .

content: / source: packages/nomercy-music-player/src/plugins/lyrics/index.ts / recipe: synced lyrics ui lyrics covers registering and reading the single active line. this recipe builds the fuller ui most listening apps actually want: every line visible at once, in a scrollable panel, with the active one highlighted and scrolled into view as playback moves through it. rendering the whole cue list up front returns every parsed cue for the current track, not just the active one. render it once, on the plugin's event, rather than building rows incrementally as lines become active: matching the active line by identity, not text and hand back the cue's object directly, the exact same reference already put in the map. using that reference as the map key means the active-line lookup works correctly even when a song repeats a line a chorus, where matching by text content would highlight every occurrence instead of only the current one: handling the no-lyrics case not every track carries a , lyrics covers why that's silent rather than an error. a panel built this way should show something explicit rather than sitting empty: only fires once a lyrics file was actually found, parsed, and attached, when is missing entirely the plugin clears state without emitting anything, clear the panel on the event's cursor change so a previous track's lyrics don't linger on screen. see it running every line of 's sidecar renders below; the active line brightens and scrolls into view as playback reaches it. :::snippetfile="music-recipe-lyrics-sync" live="false" ::: next steps - recipe: equalizer presets: a preset-picker ui built on the shared kit .

content: / source: packages/nomercy-music-player/src/plugins/scrobble/index.ts, src/plugins/scrobble/iscrobbler.ts / recipe: scrobbling plugin: scrobble covers the threshold rules and the default no-op backend. this recipe is the other half: implementing a real so listens actually go somewhere, last.fm, listenbrainz, or your own server's activity log. implementing iscrobbler two methods, both -returning so the plugin can await network calls without blocking playback on their result: is optional on the interface, a backend with no "currently listening to" concept can omit it entirely, only calls it when present. wiring it in both thresholds default to the real last.fm rule already, whichever is reached first wins, override them only when your service's own rules differ. handling backend failures without breaking playback a failed or call never throws back into playback, the plugin catches it and reports through its own error channel instead: reading in-progress state and on the plugin instance read the current item's accumulated listened time and whether it already crossed the threshold, useful for a small "scrobbling in 0:42..." indicator instead of only reacting to the final event: next steps - recipe: queue & playlist panel: rendering as a clickable "up next" list.

title: Plugin: Scrobble
description: ScrobblePlugin: threshold-based listen reporting (Last.fm 50%-or-4-minute rule by default) to any IScrobbler backend, no-op until you wire one in.
content: / source: packages/nomercy-music-player/src/plugins/scrobble/index.ts, src/plugins/scrobble/iscrobbler.ts / plugin: scrobble id tracks listened time per track, against the player's own , and events. it reports to a configured backend: once per item on cursor change, and once accumulated listened time crosses a threshold. the default scrobbler is a no-op, so the plugin is inert until a real backend is wired in. time is tracked and never reported. recipe: scrobbling implements one. options | option | type | default | purpose | |---|---|---|---| | | | | the reporting backend. | | | | | fraction of the track's duration counted as "listened enough" — last.fm's 50% rule. | | | | | absolute listened-seconds ceiling. whichever of this or is reached first wins — last.fm's 4-minute rule. | | | | | tracks shorter than this are never scrobbled. | events namespaced onto the player's own bus as : | event | payload | fires when | |---|---|---| | | | right after resolves, once per item. | | | | right after resolves, once per item, the first time the threshold is crossed. | the iscrobbler port is optional, a backend with no "currently listening" concept can omit it. , the shipped default, implements both as immediately-resolving no-ops. how listened time is tracked a normal playback tick advances the event by well under a second; anything ≥2 seconds between ticks is treated as a seek or a track change and doesn't count toward listened time. this means scrubbing back and forth through a track doesn't inflate the listened total the way naively summing every delta would. methods exposes the tracked state read-only, for a ui that wants to show elapsed listened time or badge a track as scrobbled without waiting on the plugin's own events: | method | signature | notes | |---|---|---| | | | seconds of listened time accumulated for the current item so far, the same running total is checked against once it crosses the threshold. | | | | whether the current item already crossed the scrobble threshold. latches for the rest of that item's playback. | rules & restrictions - a failed or never interrupts playback. the plugin catches the rejection and reports it through its own error channel, or . - once a track is scrobbled it stays scrobbled. latches for the rest of that item's playback, so replaying it without advancing does not scrobble again. - tracking resets on every change, including a mid-track . listened time never carries across tracks. how to extend it implement against a real service and pass it as : see recipe: scrobbling for a full implementation built on the / read surface above. next steps - plugin: auto-advance: the other queue-driving plugin, deciding what plays next rather than reporting what already played.

is fetched exactly as given, it is not resolved against the way is. store a fully-qualified url, or resolve it yourself in a override, see lyrics: lyricsurl isn't resolved against baseurl. - a missing , with no resolver returning one, clears plugin state quietly. no fetch, no error. - a fetch or parse failure reports through the plugin's error channel, or , rather than throwing. a bad lyrics file never interrupts playback. - parsing needs a cue parser registered for that url's format. a file resolves to the built-in parser. a custom format needs its own registered first, through . see core: cue parsers. - title: Adapter: Audio Backend
description: IAudioBackend: the port every player-level method reads through for actual playback, including the dual-buffer crossfade primitives. Two shipped implementations, swappable via backendFactory.
content: / source: packages/nomercy-music-player/src/adapters/audio-backend/iaudiobackend.ts, src/adapters/audio-backend/html5-audio.ts, src/adapters/audio-backend/web-audio.ts / adapter: audio backend is the one port every music-specific player method , , , , and the rest reads and writes through, itself never touches an element or the web audio api directly. two implementations ship: the default and . this is the swap point for a custom backend, webcodecs, a native-shell bridge, a test double. the interface method conventions mirror the player class itself: stateful values are overloaded functions / , actions are bare verbs , , , and seeking goes through , there is no separate method at this layer either. the two shipped implementations | backend | | signal path | use for | |---|---|---|---| | | | plain . lazily creates a only the first time a plugin requests the analyser graph, so a consumer without an equalizer or spectrum plugin pays zero web audio cost. | the default, the safe fallback for environments where web audio is restricted or undesired. | | | | → → → destination, routed through a real . throws immediately at construction if is unavailable, it never silently degrades to a no-op graph. | sample-accurate crossfades, or when a plugin needs full web audio graph access. | switch at via , or at runtime: both back the identical surface, so every player-level method, included, reads the same either way. crossfade: the dual-buffer contract on the player delegates the dual-buffer work to whichever backend is active. three calls do it: - allocates and loads a second playback handle, without touching primary playback. - pre-rolls it to a start position and waits for it to be ready. - ramps both gains over the window, then swaps the secondary in as primary and disposes the old one. the curve is linear by default, constant-power with . and exist for tests and for callers inspecting mid-crossfade state. precision differs by backend. drives the fade with a loop. that is not sample-accurate, so expect a sub-frame seam at track boundaries. ramps through real automation, which is sample-accurate. it allocates a fresh element and pair per crossfade, because binds an element to a context permanently and the same element cannot be reattached. reports whether a backend can allocate a second playback handle at all, both built-in backends return . a custom backend that returns causes to throw a a subclass with code before any crossfade event fires or buffer is touched, rather than attempting the transition. auth on manifest and segment requests is how reaches 's own manifest and segment requests on an hls audio stream, not just the kit's calls. wires this automatically from , resolving the bearer value fresh sync or async getter on every request rather than capturing it once. rules & restrictions - constructs the instance on first call and caches it. call it before and you get an instance not yet wired to a loaded source. - one backend is active per player at a time. swapping mid-session with disposes the previous one and emits . - a swap is not a crossfade. whatever was playing stops, and the new backend comes up with no source, so reload the current item to resume. - , and exist for eme and drm coordination on protected audio. a backend that never touches encrypted content implements them as no-ops. - and are the tap points the kit's chain needs for the equalizer, spectrum and visualizers. see equalizer. is optional: a backend with no separate pre-volume source node omits it, and the plugin falls back to . how to extend it provide a at , it receives the resolved kind and full config, and returns any implementation: a custom backend implementing the full contract, crossfade methods included, works with every player-level method unchanged, never branches on which backend is active. next steps - title: Adapter: Similarity Engine
description: ISimilarityEngine: a reserved "find similar tracks" port with no default implementation and no current consumer, not re-exported from the package entry points.
content: / source: packages/nomercy-music-player/src/adapters/similarity-engine/isimilarityengine.ts / adapter: similarity engine is a reserved port for "find items similar to this seed". it is there for a future radio mode or "more like this", and for /nomercy-music-player/plugins-adapters/auto-advance when its local genre and decade scoring is not enough. today it is a defined contract with no shipped implementation and no plugin wiring it in. it is documented so it is visible rather than silently absent, not because there is something to configure. current status: reserved, not wired - no default adapter ships. unlike audio backend, which always has behind it, there is no or equivalent. - no plugin in this package calls . 's does its own local scoring today and does not depend on this interface, see plugin: auto-advance. - not re-exported from either public entry point. the subpath re-exports the audio-backend module only, and declares no subpath. - importing it today means reaching into an internal file path, which is not supported. if you need this shape now, define a matching interface of your own. the interface, for reference returns results ordered by descending similarity, most similar first. the scale behind is deliberately implementation-defined, a tag-based engine and an ml-embedding engine don't score similarity on comparable numbers, callers should treat it as relative within one engine, not as a portable threshold across implementations. where a real implementation would plug in once wired, an implementation would come from one of: - server-driven, the nomercy media server's own recommendation endpoint. - audio-feature-based, bpm / key / energy similarity computed from the audio itself. - tag-based, genre / decade / mood overlap, a generalized version of what already does locally. - ml embedding, vector proximity over a precomputed embedding space. - external service, last.fm similar-tracks, or an equivalent third-party api. next steps - reference: music player types: every other music-owned type, including the ones that are actually wired.

title: Native quickstart
description: One dependency and one view, on Android, the desktop, iOS and tvOS.
content: the native music player is the same library as the web one, ported rather than reimplemented. same method names, same events, same error codes. all of it generated from one contract and checked against it on every build. what differs is the toolkit underneath. android and the desktop draw in compose, apple draws in swiftui. both mount the same engine. android and desktop one coordinate for the engine, one for the chrome. an application that already draws its own controls takes the first and leaves the second. then the two surfaces a music app needs. is the bar that sits at the edge of every screen; is what it expands into. both read one and send one set of commands, so the two can never disagree about what is playing. ios and tvos add the swift package and take the drop-in product. the swiftui half mirrors the compose one name for name: and over the same state, with and as the pieces underneath. apple gets swiftui rather than compose because an application already drawing its chrome in swiftui does not want a second toolkit in the process. writing a plugin scrobbling, lyrics and auto-advance are plugins rather than player features, and so is whatever you need that this list does not have. the scaffold is a working plugin to copy: :::snippetfile="plugin-authoring" ::: next the methods reference lists every call the music surface answers for, and the migration guide covers moving an app off its own embedded player.

title: Migrating an app to the native player
description: Moving a Kotlin or Swift app off its own embedded audio player.
content: most apps arrive here with an audio player already in them: a media3 session wired into a service, or an avaudioplayer with a hand-drawn bar. the move is not a rewrite. the engine you have keeps decoding; what changes is who owns the queue, the crossfade and the state the bar reads. what to delete anything tracking whether playback is running, anything holding the queue and its cursor, anything deciding what plays next under shuffle or repeat, and anything converting a position into a scrubber fraction. those four are where two clients of one server drift apart, and the library holds one answer for each. keep your engine setup, your data source, your auth headers and your media session. kotlin wrap the engine you already build. where your screen read the engine directly, read or collect . where it advanced the queue itself, call and let the announcement reach the bar, the full screen and the notification at once. swap the chrome last. gives you the state and the commands the shipped surfaces take, and a screen can mount beside its own while you move one control at a time. swift the swiftui surfaces take the same state object the compose ones do, bridged through the framework. an app conforms what it has and gets and over it. what you gain by moving plugins, and one queue. scrobbling stops being a hook inside your playback code, and becomes something that registers and unregisters cleanly. lyrics stop being a screen that polls the engine, and become something that listens. a queue that lives in the player rather than in a screen is one the lock screen, the car and a cast target all read the same way.

title: What is nomercy-player-core
description: The shared kit nomercy-video-player and nomercy-music-player are built on: lifecycle, plugins, queue, adapters, i18n, and auth, ready to compose into your own player.
content: / source: packages/nomercy-player-core/src/index.ts / what is nomercy-player-core is not a player. it is the kit both nomercy players are built from. it holds the lifecycle machine, the plugin runtime, the queue, the event bus, i18n, auth, and every swappable adapter a media player needs before it can play a frame. and each add one thing on top: a media backend, and a few methods for their own medium. the rest they get from here. who it's for building a player for something the trio does not cover: a podcast player, a live radio player, a custom streaming protocol. you get the lifecycle, queue, plugin and auth machinery already written and already tested, instead of writing it a third time. if you want to play video or music for end users, use /nomercy-video-player or /nomercy-music-player instead. they have done this work. why it exists video and music playback differ in one place: how a frame is decoded, and how a ui reacts to it. everything else is the same. queueing the next track, tracking phase, running plugins, resolving auth headers, switching language. a movie and a song need identical machinery. so it lives once. both players compose it rather than reimplementing it, and a fix here reaches both in the same release. setup is strict, the rest is yours call once. the kit then walks a fixed pipeline: calling twice, or calling it after , throws. there is one way in, and a half-configured instance is not one of them. above that, nothing is prescribed. the kit ships no ui, no dom beyond a container, and no opinion about what your play button looks like. every behaviour outside the lifecycle is a named interface with a working default, and any of them can be replaced: , , , , , , , , , . plugins extend behaviour without forking anything. through the cancellable pipeline a plugin can veto, delay or rewrite a mutation before it lands. what you get - lifecycle: / / and a phase machine → → → / → that every mixin and plugin can trust. - shared playback primitives: transport, time, volume, queue, and backlog methods, composed once and reused by both real players instead of hand-copied. - plugin runtime: a base class, typed registration, and a cancellable dispatch pipeline , for behavior that shouldn't require forking the player. - adapter ports: swappable interfaces for the media backend, stream source, storage, event bus, cue parsing, translation, platform capabilities wake lock, network, visibility, fullscreen, pip, realtime channel, preload strategy, transition strategy, and shuffle strategy, each with a working default. - auth-aware fetch: one pipeline 401 refresh-and-retry, 403 propagates, never conflated used by every kit-internal request and available to plugins via . - i18n engine: a translator with the kit's own strings built in english eager, every other kit locale loaded lazily on demand, consumer async-loadable bundles, and a title-token interpolation system for per-library tokens like season/episode. - cue parsing: built-in vtt, sprite-vtt, and lrc parsers behind a registry you can add your own formats to. - typed errors: a hierarchy , , , , , , ... with severity, scope, and a retry policy, instead of raw thrown strings. - composition primitives: , , and , the exact three functions and use to become players. quickstart shows them composing a real, minimal one. where it sits both rows at layer 2 sit on the same foundation and never talk to each other. they do not share code because one imports the other. they share it because both are composed from this kit. next steps - quickstart: compose a minimal player from the kit and mount it, in real, typechecked code.

content: / source: packages/nomercy-player-core/src/core/mixins/lifecycle.ts, src/core/mixins/player-state.ts / core: lifecycle & setup is the one strict step every player library composed from the kit shares: call it once, and a fixed pipeline runs before anything else can happen. the pipeline snapshots your config and wires the cross-cutting policies: visibility, network, wake lock, metrics, preload and transition orchestration. then it runs an ordered async sequence. each stage emits its own name on success, or a matching on failure. a failure short-circuits the rest and rejects . playlist resolution is the exception. it never throws. a fetch or parse failure emits , and the pipeline still reaches and with an empty queue. returns a promise that resolves once the pipeline reaches , or rejects if a stage failed or ran first. it's memoised, so calling it from multiple places in your player library returns the same promise rather than re-running anything. call a second time on the same instance and it throws . that guard is checked first and stays tripped across a in between. reuse after teardown needs a fresh instance, not a second . the narrower guard fires only when runs for the first time on an instance that was disposed before ever ran. there is exactly one way in. the phase machine underneath the pipeline sits a closed set of phases. reads the current one. the event fires on every transition. so a ui layer or a plugin drives an overlay off phase changes alone, instead of piecing state together from a dozen flags. two guard methods sit on top of the phase machine, and every transport method , , , , , and the rest calls the first one before doing anything else: - content: / source: packages/nomercy-player-core/src/adapters/event-bus/default.ts, src/adapters/event-bus/ieventbus.ts / core: the event bus every event a player emits, from to a plugin's own custom events, flows through one class: . what it is is a small, dependency-free pub/sub implementation, generic over an event map that types each event name to its payload shape. both and extend it directly, so every player instance already has , , , , , and before a single kit mixin is composed onto it. under the hood it is a plain , not the dom's , and that is deliberate. a lets remove a listener by reference without matching options, which composes with in a way does not. snapshots the listener set before iterating, so a listener calling on itself mid-dispatch cannot corrupt the pass. it also catches exceptions per listener, so one bad handler cannot abort the rest of the chain. the firehose registers a listener called for every emit, with as its arguments. this is what and every debug overlay in the trio is built on. with no function removes every listener across every event, which is what calls to guarantee a disposed player leaks nothing. using it in a player library you rarely construct an yourself. your player class extends it, and its typed event map is whatever interface you declare. the usual starting point is the kit's extended with your own events. the example below builds a standalone bus with a small custom map, so the mechanics are visible without a player around them. :::snippetfile="tour-event-bus" live="false" ::: the cancellable variant plain is fire-and-forget: it can't be cancelled, delayed, or mutated by a listener. every event , , , and the equivalent on a 's own custom events runs through a different dispatcher built on top of this same listener registry, one that gives listeners a mutable, preventable payload. that's the subject of the next page. next steps - transport contract: the cancellable dispatch pattern, demonstrated on / / .

title: Player and Plugin
description: The this-versus-this.player boundary that organises the whole trio: what you extend is this, what you talk to is this.player, and that line decides whether a behaviour is a player concern or a plugin concern.
content: / source: packages/nomercy-player-core/src/core/plugin/base.ts, src/core/state.ts, packages/nomercy-video-player/src/index.ts / core: player and plugin there is one rule underneath everything else in this trio, and once it is named the rest of the library stops feeling like a pile of methods and starts feeling like one shape. the rule is about what means. what you extend is . what you talk to is . a plugin subclasses , so inside a plugin is the plugin. its own machinery is bare : , , , , , , , , . each is scoped to the plugin and cleaned up when the plugin goes away. the player is not part of the plugin. it is a collaborator the plugin holds a reference to, reached through : the player is built the same way, one layer down. is not a class full of methods. it is composed. stamps the shared core mixins onto its prototype transport, time, volume, queue, and the per-library file adds the few methods its medium needs. inside any of those mixin bodies, is the player. , , are the player's own methods calling each other. there is no in there. in there, already is the player. so the boundary is symmetric. from a plugin, the player is the collaborator: . from inside the player, a plugin is the collaborator, reached the mirror way, through : for the thing you are, for the thing you are talking to. that is the entire rule. the rule is also a decision because marks what a piece of code is part of, the same boundary answers the question every new feature runs into: where does this behaviour live? if a behaviour is part of what the player is, it belongs on the player: a core mixin when it is identical for video and music, a per-library method when it carries a domain twist. you call it from inside, consumers call it from outside, and every plugin gets it for free through . if a behaviour is something layered onto a player from outside, it belongs in a plugin: , its state and lifecycle scoped to , the player reached through . autohide is the worked example. controls fading after a few idle seconds sounds like a ui detail, so it is tempting to build it inside whatever plugin draws the controls. but "am i being interacted with right now" is a fact about the player. it is true whether or not any ui is mounted, and every ui wants the same answer. so activity tracking is a player concern. the player watches its own container, keeps and on its element, and emits . a ui plugin does not compute it. it reads those classes, or subscribes to the event. ask "is this part of the thing, or a consumer of the thing". the boundary tells you which side to build on. why this is the shape of the trio the same boundary, read at each layer, is why the three packages fit together the way they do. and do not share code by importing each other. they share it because both are composed onto their own prototype. the core mixins are for both players at once. that is why a fix there reaches both in one release. it is also why a method that branches on "is this music or video" does not belong in core. a branch means the behaviour is not really shared, so it is not really part of the thing both players are. plugins ride on top of all of it without forking any of it, because a plugin only ever talks to 's public surface. it never reaches inside the composition. that is what lets one /nomercy-player-core/tour/plugin-base base work against a video player, a music player, or a third library you compose yourself. the plugin does not know which player it is talking to, only that exposes the shared contract. next steps - the plugin base: every helper on the side, and how registration wires a plugin to its player. - adapters & dependency injection: the third kind of collaborator, the swappable ports a player is built from.

player in memory. listen / partial / the memory-safe dom listener. drop-in for : same signature, same behavior, plus automatic teardown. the lifecycle registry records the exact four-tuple: target, event, handler, and options. on dispose it replays each record through with the same options, so capture-phase and passive listeners detach correctly. after dispose, further calls are silent no-ops. / partial / a raw on or outlives the plugin. the handler closes over , so it pins the plugin, the player, and everything they reference for the life of the page. this is the single most common player memory leak, and exists to make it unwritable. on / partial / subscribes to events with auto-dispose on teardown. two forms: the string form listens to player and core events , , . the payload type comes from the player's event map through the generic. the class form listens to another plugin's events: . the kit prefixes the event with the target plugin's namespace, so becomes on the wire. the payload type comes from that plugin's generic. there is no untyped string fallback for plugin events. import the class. when your plugin declares , that class is loaded before yours anyway, so the registration. the handler survives the plugin. once / partial / same two-form contract as , for a single occurrence. the handler auto-removes after its first dispatch. if the event never fires, the handlers run in subscription order. if your plugin must see an event before another plugin acts on it, raise your and make sure the flow you care about iterates ; do not rely on registration order title: Timing
description: Timers, animation-frame loops, abort controllers, and observers that the lifecycle registry cancels for you: timeout, interval, frame, abortable, and lifecycle.observe.
content: / source: packages/nomercy-player-core/src/core/plugin/base.ts, src/adapters/lifecycle-registry/default.ts / core: timing anything time-based a plugin starts must stop when the plugin does. five helpers guarantee that: each one registers itself with the lifecycle registry, and a single dispose cancels them all. timeout / partial / schedules a one-shot callback. wraps with two additions: the timer is cancelled automatically on dispose, and an error thrown inside is caught and logged instead of escaping into the player. returns the numeric timer id, the same shape returns. keep it only when you may need early; most callers discard it. after dispose, the call returns and schedules nothing. / partial / a raw fires after the plugin is gone. the callback then touches disposed state, or throws into whatever code happens to be on the stack. interval / partial / schedules a repeating callback. wraps , cancelled automatically on dispose. errors are caught per tick, so a single failing run logs and the interval keeps going. returns the numeric interval id for early cancellation; after dispose. / partial / a raw is the worst version of the timer leak: it never stops, ticking against a dead plugin for the life of the page. frame / partial / starts an auto-cancelled loop. you write the render callback; the kit owns the loop, the delta accounting, and the cancellation. visualization plugins use this exclusively. the callback receives two arguments each frame. is the elapsed milliseconds since the previous frame, so animation speed stays correct across display refresh rates. is the frame timestamp, the same value hands its callback. the return value is a stop function. calling it cancels this one loop and nothing else: other frame loops keep running, and the registry stays alive. dispose cancels every outstanding loop anyway, so the stop function is only for ending one loop early. a thrown frame is caught and logged; the loop continues. in an environment without node, ssr, no loop starts and the returned stop function is a no-op. / partial / a hand-rolled raf loop needs its own cancellation flag, its own delta math, and its own dispose wiring, and forgetting any of the three burns cpu on a player that no longer exists. abortable / partial / creates an whose signal fires automatically on dispose. pass to any abort-aware api. the plugin's own helper already wires this internally; reach for when integrating third-party or platform apis that accept a signal but know nothing about the plugin lifecycle. called after dispose, it returns a controller that is already aborted, so downstream apis refuse to start instead of running unowned. / partial / without it, the in-flight work you started keeps running after teardown, and its completion callback lands on a disposed plugin. lifecycle.observe / partial / registers a , , , or any object with a method, and disconnects it on dispose. this one lives on directly rather than as a wrapper method on the plugin. it returns the observer unchanged, so the registration chains straight into the observe call: / partial / after dispose the call still returns the observer, but registers nothing. an unregistered observer keeps watching its targets forever. a on the player container holds the container, the callback, and the plugin in memory after every other reference is gone. example one plugin exercising all five: a delayed overlay hide, a periodic save, a frame loop with its stop function, an abortable signal, and a resize observer. :::snippetfile="handbook-timing" live="false" ::: next steps - listening: the event surface these timers usually drive. - the plugin base: the one-page overview of every helper.

content: / source: packages/nomercy-player-core/src/plugins/equalizer/index.ts, src/plugins/equalizer/presets.ts / plugin: equalizer id is a 10-band parametric equalizer plus a pre-gain stage, built from s inserted into audio graph's chain. options | option | type | default | purpose | |---|---|---|---| | | | | 10 frequency bands. element 0 must be the pseudo-band. | | | | — | preset name to apply on . | | | | — | additional presets beyond the built-ins. | | | | | min/max/step/default per slider, for a ui to read directly. | | | | — | storage key. omit to disable persistence. | | / | | / when set | load/save automatically through . | | | | | ramp time for gain changes, avoids audible clicks. | is . events , , , , . rules & restrictions - , register audio graph first, the equalizer throws otherwise. - is a fixed contract: it must be the pseudo-band, not a real frequency. - persistence goes through , the plugin's own scoped, namespaced storage, never raw . swapping the storage adapter moves equalizer persistence with it, same as everything else that uses . - pre-gain has a sticky-zero snap: values within ±0.05 of zero round to exactly zero, so a ui slider settles cleanly at the middle instead of hovering at 0.0003. how to extend it next steps - plugin: mixer: the master gain and pan stage at the tail of the same chain.

title: Plugin: Mixer
description: MixerPlugin: master gain (dB) and stereo pan, inserted as the last effect in the AudioGraphPlugin chain, with optional storage-backed persistence.
content: / source: packages/nomercy-player-core/src/plugins/mixer/index.ts / plugin: mixer id is a master gain and stereo-pan stage, inserted as the last effect in audio graph's chain, gain then panner then destination, so it always acts on the fully-processed signal from every other effect. options | option | type | default | purpose | |---|---|---|---| | | db | | initial master gain. | | | -1..1 | | initial stereo pan. | | | | — | storage key. omit to disable persistence. | | | | | clamp ceiling and floor, negated for . | | | | | ramp time for gain/pan changes. | events , , , . rules & restrictions - , same missing-dep guard as every other effect in the chain. - clamps to ; clamps to . out-of-range calls don't throw, they saturate. - ordering is fixed: this plugin is meant to be the last effect. inserting your own effect after it defeats the "acts on the final mix" guarantee the plugin is built around. how to extend it next steps - plugin: spectrum: fft analysis, feeding visualization instead of the audio path.

title: Plugin: Canvas
description: CanvasPlugin: a shared <canvas> mount and requestAnimationFrame render loop host every visualizer plugin builds on, zero rendering cost when not registered.
content: / source: packages/nomercy-player-core/src/plugins/canvas/index.ts / plugin: canvas id mounts a on the player container and runs a shared loop that every renderer registered with draws into on the same frame, instead of each visualizer running its own raf loop. options | option | type | default | purpose | |---|---|---|---| | | | player container | where the canvas is appended. | | / | | auto | omit both to track the mount element via . | | | | | render loop target rate. | | | | or | backing-store scale for crisp output on high-dpi screens. | | | | | whether the canvas clears before each frame or accumulates. | | | | | whether the canvas intercepts pointer events. | events , , . rules & restrictions - opt-in by design: without this plugin registered, no canvas is created and no animation frame is ever requested, a player that doesn't use visualization pays zero rendering cost. - throws a if called before has run. - throws a if the environment can't produce a 2d context. how to extend it register a renderer directly for a one-off effect, or build on visualization for anything that needs frequency/waveform data too. next steps - plugin: visualization: the base class that layers canvas rendering on top of spectrum data.

title: Plugin: Spectrum
description: SpectrumPlugin: FFT analysis on top of AudioGraphPlugin, producing a per-frame VisualizationFrame consumed by Visualization and any custom renderer.
content: / source: packages/nomercy-player-core/src/plugins/spectrum/index.ts / plugin: spectrum id reads audio graph's analyser node once per animation frame and produces a : frequency and waveform buffers both byte and float, per-band energy / / , and beat/bpm fields when a beat provider is registered. visualization is the primary consumer, but any plugin can read frames directly. options | option | type | default | purpose | |---|---|---|---| | | | inherits audio graph's analyser | analysis resolution. | | | | inherits audio graph's analyser | analyser smoothing. | | | | | allocate separate left/right analysers instead of one summed channel. | | | | — | reserved, currently unused. | events , . rules & restrictions - , throws without it. - allocates two extra s and four extra typed-array buffers per frame, only turn it on when a consumer actually needs per-channel data. - synthetic mode + exists for passive nomercy connect receivers that have no local audio stream to analyse: it bypasses the entirely and re-emits the last pushed frame verbatim. / on a synthetic frame are not overridden by the canvas raf clock the way a real-analysis frame's are. how to extend it next steps - plugin: visualization: the base class that turns these frames into pixels.

title: Plugin: Visualization
description: VisualizationPlugin: the abstract base for canvas-based visualizers, layering Canvas (RAF + mount) and Spectrum (frame data), subclass and implement render().
content: / source: packages/nomercy-player-core/src/plugins/visualization/index.ts / plugin: visualization default id , subclasses must set their own is an abstract base class, not something you register directly. it exists to give every canvas-based visualizer the same two dependencies wired up: canvas for the mount and raf loop, spectrum for frequency/waveform data, so a visualizer author writes only the drawing code. options | option | type | default | purpose | |---|---|---|---| | | | | clear the canvas before each call. | | | | | reserved, only is currently active. | events , . rules & restrictions - , the player refuses to register a visualizer without both already present. - cannot be registered directly, it's . needs a concrete subclass. - degrades gracefully rather than throwing: if the dependencies are missing or spectrum analysis is unavailable, it emits and returns early, the rest of the player keeps running. - kit rule for extension authors: bridges to p5.js, three.js, or shader-based rendering belong in a separate optional package built on top of this class. they should never reach into kit internals; override only . owns clearing/compositing and owns frame data, a visualizer subclass owns neither. how to extend it subclass it and implement the one abstract method. the kit ships a reference implementation, id , importable from the subpath, worth reading as a real example of the pattern below. next steps - plugin: cast sender: outside the audio-graph chain, the kit's chromecast bridge.

title: Plugin: Cast Sender
description: CastSenderPlugin: the Chromecast Web Sender SDK bridge, meant to be subclassed per medium, override defaultContentType() and buildMetadata().
content: / source: packages/nomercy-player-core/src/plugins/cast-sender/index.ts / plugin: cast sender id bridges player transport state to and from an active chromecast session via the cast web sender sdk. it's written as a shared base class: and each subclass it, overriding the two methods that differ per medium. options | option | type | default | purpose | |---|---|---|---| | | | — | your registered cast receiver app id. | | | | — | also surface an airplay control path. | | | | — | custom message namespace for a non-default receiver. | | | | | resume local playback when the cast session ends. | | | | subclass's | mime type hint sent to the receiver. | | | | | marks the content as a live stream for the receiver ui. | events , , , , , . rules & restrictions - chrome/chromium web sender sdk only. in firefox, safari, or a non-chromium browser, emits and throws a , everything else stays a harmless no-op rather than crashing. - requires the global / sdk to already be loaded on the page, the plugin doesn't load the script for you. - volume arrives on the kit's own 0-100 scale and is divided to 0-1 at the boundary, which is the 0-1 float range the receiver's sdk expects. how to extend it subclass it and override the two per-medium methods. this is exactly what and do, neither reimplements the session/connection handling. next steps - plugin: embed: the cross-origin bridge for a player running in an iframe.

title: Plugin: Embed
description: EmbedPlugin: a cross-origin postMessage bridge between a host page and a player running inside an <iframe>, with an explicit inbound-origin allowlist.
content: / source: packages/nomercy-player-core/src/plugins/embed/index.ts / plugin: embed id bridges a player running inside an to the host page via : it forwards player events out , , , and more and accepts a small transport command set in , , , , and more. options | option | type | default | purpose | |---|---|---|---| | | | none | inbound origins accepted. empty means no inbound commands are accepted at all, outbound events still forward. | | | | | which player events forward to the host. | | | | result of an in-iframe check | apply embed-specific layout/behavior tweaks automatically. | rules & restrictions - security default is closed, not open: with no configured, zero inbound origins are trusted. you opt in explicitly. - outbound targeting: with exactly one origin in , outbound messages are pinned to it. with multiple origins or , outbound falls back to , the plugin's own docs recommend pinning to one origin in production rather than relying on the multi-origin fallback. - the host needs , , and for full functionality. the permission specifically is load-bearing, without it the browser's mediasession integration never activates inside the frame. - media session already works correctly inside an iframe on its own, this plugin doesn't need to bridge it. how to extend it on the host page, listen for events with and post commands shaped like , to the iframe's . next steps - plugin: key handler: keyboard shortcuts, the other common "host page integration" surface.

title: Plugin: Key Handler
description: KeyHandlerPlugin: a single keydown listener routing combo strings to player callbacks, with sane defaults and input-field awareness. Subpath-only import.
content: / source: packages/nomercy-player-core/src/plugins/key-handler/index.ts / plugin: key handler id is a keyboard-binding router: one listener that dispatches combo strings , , to callbacks. it isn't re-exported from the package's main entry, import it from the subpath. options | option | type | default | purpose | |---|---|---|---| | | | | where the listener attaches. | | | | — | your own combo-to-callback map. | | | | | merge with the defaults instead of replacing them. | | | | — | extra gate, return to suppress handling entirely. | | | | | throttle window. disables throttling. | | | | | turn off the hardware key bindings specifically. | rules & restrictions - default bindings: toggles playback, / seek ±5s, / adjust volume, toggles mute, plus the eight w3c hardware media keys , , and the rest. - keys are silently ignored when the event target is an , , , or any element, so the player never steals keystrokes from a form on the same page. - gates every binding individually, it doesn't touch the non-hardware defaults , arrows, . how to extend it next steps - plugin: media session: the os-level equivalent, hardware media keys and lock-screen controls.
