title: Plugin: DRM
description: DrmPlugin: EME key-system coordination for Widevine/FairPlay/PlayReady, license fetch routing with optional request signing, and safe no-op degradation without EME.
content: / source: packages/nomercy-video-player/src/plugins/drm/index.ts / plugin: drm id coordinates encrypted media extensions eme license acquisition for widevine, fairplay, and playready, and carries hdcp / output-protection requirements. registration and license-fetch routing are real; the actual key-system handshake is gated behind , so environments without eme headless test runners, older browsers stay quiet instead of throwing. options | option | type | purpose | |---|---|---| | | | eme key system identifier, , , , etc. | | | | license server url. required before can be called. | | | | fairplay service certificate. optional for widevine/playready. | | | | sign the license request hmac, proprietary auth before it goes out. | | | | transform the challenge body before sending. | | | | transform the license response body after receiving. | | | | output protection requirement. | events | event | payload | fires when | |---|---|---| | | | the key-system handshake fails. | | | | eme isn't available in this environment, either at plugin registration or at handshake time. | how activation works the plugin listens for the player's event, when the incoming item carries a hint a consumer-supplied field on your own item shape, not part of the canonical , it attempts the eme handshake for that key system, falling back to the plugin's own option when the item doesn't specify one: posts the challenge to , wrapped through when provided, and through / for payload shaping either direction: rules & restrictions - missing at registration time emits immediately and the plugin does nothing further, it does not throw and does not retry. - throws if was never configured, this is a real, addressable configuration error, not a soft failure. - all license network i/o goes through the kit's , the same auth pipeline every other plugin uses, so the config from bearer token, custom headers, request signing already applies without extra config here. - returns whenever eme isn't supported or the handshake hasn't completed, always guard before use. how to extend it subclass to add key-system-specific certificate handling or a different license transport a websocket-based drm proxy, for instance: next steps - adapter: video backend: the backend that mounts the media source eme and drm attach to.

title: Plugin: Touch Zones
description: TouchZonesPlugin: a 3x6 tap-zone grid for seek/playback/volume, single-tap vs double-tap dispatch, and cumulative seek-feedback indicators.
content: / source: packages/nomercy-video-player/src/plugins/touch-zones/index.ts / plugin: touch zones id renders a transparent tap-zone overlay for touch input. single-tap shows or hides the controls, or toggles playback. double-tap seeks or adjusts volume. that is the model most streaming apps have trained people to expect. it sits at a z-index between the video element and the controls overlay, so it catches taps meant for the video area without blocking buttons on a control bar above it. options | option | type | default | purpose | |---|---|---|---| | | | | milliseconds between taps that still counts as a double-tap. | | | | | seconds to seek on a double-tap in the left/right zones. | | | | | stop the center zone's single-tap from toggling playback. mirrors 's own , both plugins ship independent click handlers on different dom layers, so the same override is needed on both when a consumer wants a custom center-tap behavior. | zone layout a 3-column x 6-row grid. desktop/tablet touch gets three columns spanning the full height seek-back, playback+fullscreen, seek-forward; mobile additionally splits two rows off the top and bottom of the center column for volume up/down, detected via presence or . | zone | single-tap | double-tap | |---|---|---| | left seek back | dismiss controls if visible, no-op otherwise, already woke them. | seek back . | | center playback | toggle playback unless . | toggle fullscreen. | | right seek forward | dismiss controls if visible, no-op otherwise, already woke them. | seek forward . | | top / bottom of center, mobile only | dismiss controls if visible, no-op otherwise, already woke them. | volume up / down. | each seek zone shows a floating circular indicator chevron icon plus accumulated seconds, e.g. "-30s" after three rapid taps that lazily mounts on first use and collapses back to zero after roughly a second of no further taps in that direction. rules & restrictions - single-tap "toggle controls" reads a visibility snapshot captured at , in the capture phase, before 's bubble-phase wake handler can touch the dom. - without that, a tap from a hidden state would show the controls on , then hide them again when the deferred handler read the just-added class. the flicker makes the tap look like it did nothing. - mobile detection is a one-shot capability check at startup, or , not a live pointer-type check. a touch-capable laptop driven with a mouse still gets the mobile volume zones. - emits to coordinate with 's auto-hide timer. this plugin has no chrome of its own to hide. how to extend it there's no subclass hook for zone geometry, the grid positions are internal. a different zone layout a 5-zone grid, a corner-only seek gesture is a new plugin built against the same player methods , , , , , rather than a subclass: next steps - plugin: desktop ui: the control bar this plugin's events show and hide.

title: Adapter: Video Backend
description: IVideoBackend: the port every player-level method reads through for actual media playback. Default Html5VideoBackend, swappable via backendFactory for MSE/WebCodecs/native-shell.
content: / source: packages/nomercy-video-player/src/adapters/video-backend/ivideobackend.ts, src/adapters/video-backend/html5.ts / adapter: video backend is the one port every video-specific player method , , , , and the rest reads and writes through, itself never touches or directly. the shipped default, , passes hls through natively on safari and falls back to everywhere else, this is the swap point for mse, webcodecs, or a native-shell bridge instead. the interface method conventions mirror the player class itself: stateful values are overloaded functions / , actions are bare verbs , , , and seeking goes through , there is no separate method at this layer either. the shipped implementation wraps a real element. native hls on safari, everywhere else. the import is dynamic, so the bundle cost is zero on safari, and never branches on browser. it applies hdr-aware level constraints itself, capping or lifting hls renditions as the display's hdr capability changes. it emits the full map, which bridges onto its own public events: , , , , , , and the standard media element events. two things are deliberately not the backend's. bandwidth estimation, and , belongs to the kit's mixin. dropped-frame metrics come from polling . both work the same whichever is active. reports whether the backend consumes natively, when , the kit skips its own post-load seek fallback, supports this directly , so a resume-at-offset load fetches the correct segment from the first request instead of downloading and discarding the stream's beginning. auth on manifest and segment requests is how reaches 's own manifest and segment requests, not just the kit's calls. wires this automatically from , resolving the bearer value fresh sync or async getter on every request rather than capturing it once, see recipe: auth tokens via baseurl + auth. rules & restrictions - constructs the instance on first call and caches it. call it before and you get an instance not yet wired to a loaded source. - one backend is active per player at a time. swaps it mid-session, disposes the previous instance and emits . - a swap is not a crossfade. whatever was playing stops, and the new backend comes up with no source, so reload to resume. see reference: video player methods. cast handoff is a separate concern, through at plugin level. - , and exist for eme and drm coordination. see plugin: drm. a backend that never touches encrypted content implements them as no-ops. - and are optional. implement them only to support web audio taps such as the equalizer and spectrum visualizers re-exported from the kit. a backend that never builds a web audio graph omits them and pays nothing. how to extend it provide a at , it receives the resolved kind and full config, and returns any implementation: is currently always from the kit's own resolution unless your factory or a plugin requests otherwise, and are reserved labels for a custom factory to branch on, not backends this package ships. next steps - adapter: chapter source: a much smaller, optional adapter for chapter lookup outside the built-in surface.

title: Adapter: Chapter Source
description: IChapterSource: load(item), current(time), all(), unload(). A standalone sync-lookup contract for custom UI, not wired into setup() or the built-in chapters() reader.
content: / source: packages/nomercy-video-player/src/adapters/chapter-source/ichaptersource.ts, src/adapters/chapter-source/vtt-chapters.ts / adapter: chapter source is a small contract for chapter lookup. load once per item, then answer "which chapter is active at this time" synchronously, cheaply enough to call on every scrubber hover. unlike adapter: video backend, it is not a config field. the player's own , and read directly and never consult this interface. see chapters. it exists for two things: custom ui that wants the same lookup shape without re-deriving it, and chapter data that does not live on the item. the interface the shipped implementation reads straight from . that field is either populated by a consumer as canonical , or derived by from the server's millisecond-based array at queue-ingest time. see the queue & playlist. it fetches and parses nothing. the list is already resolved by the time runs, and this class only does the synchronous lookup on top of it: rules & restrictions - returns an empty array for an item with no field. that is a legitimate "no chapters" state, not an error. - and stay synchronous in any implementation. they are called from hot paths, scrubber hover and -driven ui, where an shows as lag. - does not use it either. its chapter-marker rendering reads directly, the same source of truth this adapter's default reads, without going through the interface. how to extend it implement the four methods against a source doesn't already cover, a chapters endpoint separate from the item payload, or any format your server doesn't already ship as the item's field: call yourself from a listener in your own overlay code, there is no automatic hook that invokes it. next steps - adapter: thumbnail source: the same standalone, sync-lookup shape applied to scrub-preview thumbnails.

title: Adapter: Thumbnail Source
description: IThumbnailSource: load(item), lookup(time), unload(). Sprite-sheet scrub-preview lookup, standalone like Chapter Source, sharing DesktopUiPlugin sprite helpers but not wired into that plugin.
content: / source: packages/nomercy-video-player/src/adapters/thumbnail-source/ithumbnailsource.ts, src/adapters/thumbnail-source/vtt-sprite.ts / adapter: thumbnail source answers "what sprite sub-region shows this timestamp" for a scrubber's hover preview. load once per item, then a synchronous on every hover-move. like adapter: chapter source, it is a standalone contract rather than a field. 's own scrub preview calls the same sprite-parsing helpers directly, without going through this interface. the adapter is for a custom scrubber built outside that plugin. the interface /// are all zero for a source that packs one standalone image per cue instead of a sprite sheet, covers both shapes with the same fields. the shipped implementation reads , fetches a webvtt sprite manifest cue body format , the format nomercy's media-server sprite generator produces, and compatible with ffmpeg tileify output and the common web-player sprite convention, and preloads the sprite image so stays synchronous once loaded: rules & restrictions - resolves rather than rejecting when the item has no . that means "no preview available", not an error. - must stay synchronous in any implementation, it runs on every pointer-move across the scrubber. - the default implementation caches one item's sprite set at a time, so call again on every item change. there is no per-item eviction to configure. how to extend it implement against a different manifest format, or a source that returns one full-size frame per cue instead of sprite sub-regions: wire from a listener and from your scrubber's pointer-move handler in your own overlay code, same as adapter: chapter source, there is no automatic hook. next steps - adapter: subtitle style store: the persistence-focused adapter, saving user preferences instead of looking up media metadata.

title: Adapter: Subtitle Style Store
description: ISubtitleStyleStore: load()/save(style)/clear(), a persistence contract for subtitleStyle() preferences. The kit keeps style in memory only; wiring a store is left to the consumer.
content: / source: packages/nomercy-video-player/src/adapters/subtitle-style-store/isubtitlestylestore.ts, src/adapters/subtitle-style-store/storage-backed.ts / adapter: subtitle style store see subtitles & text tracks keeps the user's font, color, and edge-style choices in memory and emits on every change, it never persists anything on its own. is the contract for the other half: load a saved preference after and apply it, save on every change so it survives the next session. the interface the shipped implementation persists through the kit's /nomercy-player-core/plugins-adapters/adapter-storage port, the same swappable storage interface the kit's plugins persist their preferences through via , under the key namespaced automatically when the storage backend itself is namespaced: the constructor takes an instance directly, not the player, the player has no public accessor for its own active storage adapter only plugin code reaches it, via . construct the store with the same instance passed to , or with a fresh the kit's own default when didn't override it: wiring it end to end returns , not the full shape, because a store might only have persisted a subset of fields across app versions. already merges a partial onto the current style, so passing the loaded value straight through is correct even when it's incomplete. rules & restrictions - the player never calls any of these three methods itself, wiring load-on-ready and save-on-change is entirely the consumer's responsibility, exactly like the pattern in recipe: swap an adapter for other kit-level ports. - only removes the persisted record, it does not reset the live value, call yourself alongside it for a "reset to defaults" action that also affects the currently-rendered subtitles. how to extend it implement the three methods against a remote store for cross-device sync, or any other backing store you already have: next steps - reference: types: the full field list this adapter persists.

title: Native quickstart
description: One dependency and one view, on Android, the desktop, iOS and tvOS.
content: the native video player is the same library as the web one, ported rather than reimplemented. same method names, same events, same error codes. all of it generated from one contract and checked against it on every build. what differs is the toolkit underneath. android and the desktop draw in compose, apple draws in swiftui. both mount the same engine. android and desktop one coordinate for the engine, one for the chrome. an application that already draws its own controls takes the first and leaves the second. then one view. reads the device it is on and mounts the touch chrome or the focus chrome accordingly, so the same call is a phone player and a television player with different hands on it. :::snippetfile="kotlin-quickstart" ::: the engine is on android and on the desktop. both implement the same , so everything above the seam is identical and the only per-platform line is the one that constructs the engine. what the desktop needs installed nothing. the desktop engine decodes through libvlc, and libvlc arrives with the dependency rather than from the machine: the first time a player is constructed, the library fetches the prebuilt runtime for that operating system and architecture, checks it against the digest it was published with, and unpacks it into a per-user cache. later runs read the unpacked copy. a vlc that happens to be installed is used only when there is no payload for the platform yet. that way one build behaves the same on every machine, rather than inheriting whichever version somebody had lying around. to supply your own, point at a directory holding it. that one is taken instead, with the digest check and download skipped. ios and tvos add the swift package and take the drop-in product. draws the controls and reads everything it shows off the object you hand it. is the projection it observes, and it forwards to anything conforming to , which is seven members. :::snippetfile="swift-quickstart" ::: apple gets swiftui rather than compose because an application already drawing its chrome in swiftui does not want a second toolkit in the process. next the methods reference lists every call the video surface answers for, and the migration guide covers moving an app off its own embedded player.

title: Migrating an app to the native player
description: Moving a Kotlin or Swift app off its own embedded player.
content: most apps arrive here with a player already in them: an exoplayer wired directly into a screen, or an avplayer with hand-drawn controls. the move is not a rewrite. the engine you have keeps decoding; what changes is who owns the state above it and who draws the controls. what to delete the parts worth removing are the ones this library already answers for, and the list is longer than it looks. - anything tracking whether playback is running - anything converting a position into a progress fraction - anything remembering a selected subtitle across a track change - anything deciding when the controls hide those are the four places two clients of the same server drift apart, and the four the library holds one answer for. keep your engine setup, your data source, your auth headers and your surface. kotlin wrap the engine you already build rather than replacing it. is a , so everything the core reference lists is on it. where your screen read , read or collect . where it called , call and let the announcement reach anything else listening. swap your controls last. takes the player and an optional surface, and a screen can mount it beside its own chrome while you move one control at a time. swift conform what you have to rather than adopting a new engine. it is seven members: the , an observe callback, three transport calls and three selection calls. hand that to and the chrome works over it. the engine adapter for the kotlin core is not shipped yet. until it is, an apple app conforms its own avfoundation code to and gets the full chrome over it, which is the path the quickstart shows. what you gain by moving plugins. once the player owns the state, a feature is a plugin rather than a change to a screen: it registers, listens, contributes ui, and unregisters cleanly. the plugin scaffold is a working one to copy, and the shipped testing kit tests it without a device.
